title: Personalizing the treatment of head and neck cancer in vitro: The 3D-OTC model.
xenium_reason: Text indicates reuse of public Xenium data
evidence_text: Personalizing the treatment of head and neck cancer in vitro: The 3D-OTC model. BACKGROUND: Treatment of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) remains challenging and the survival rates of affected patients remain poor. A three-dimensional organotypic co-culture (3D-OTC) model where patient derived tumor tissue is cultured on human-derived fibroblasts (dermal equivalent, DE) was evaluated regarding its comparability to primary tumor tissue and its applicability in drug resistance testing. METHODS: 3D-OTC models were cultured from n = 10 HNSCC patients for up to 21 days. The growth pattern at the DE was compared to tumor budding of corresponding resection specimens. Furthermore, we immunohistochemically determined the immune cell infiltrate of primary tumor tissue and corresponding 3D-OTC models. Spatially resolved gene expression analysis (“Xenium in situ”) was performed for separate regions of interest within the 3D-OTC specimens and within primary tumor tissue. Up-regulated and down-regulated genes of the 3D-OTC samples were included in gene set enrichment analysis and up-regulated genes between invasive (invading the DE) and non-invasive tumor cells within the 3D-OTC samples were included in drug resistance testing using publicly available databases. RESULTS: The growth pattern observed at the DE was associated with tumor budding in primary tumor tissue. The density of CD3-/CD20-/CD56-positive cells was lower in 3D-OTC samples compared to primary tumor tissue. No such changes were observed for CD68-positive cells and no significant changes in the density of the immune cell infiltrate were detected during the cultivation period. The centroids and dispersion of the gene expression of the 3D-OTC samples did not differ from the corresponding primary tumor tissue. The regions of interest within the 3D-OTC samples showed distinct functional states in gene set enrichment analysis. The comparison of genes up-regulated in invasive tumor parts of the 3D-OTC samples could explain resistance of tumor subclones to certain chemotherapeutics. CONCLUSIONS: The 3D-OTC model morphologically and transcriptomically resembles primary tumor tissue and its biology while preserving the tumor microenvironment. Furthermore, the 3D-OTC model allows the standardized evaluation of tumor tissue by the definition of transcriptomically separate regions of interest and thus, could help to evaluate the impact of personalized therapeutic interventions on the tumor and its microenvironment in vitro.

Single-Nucleus Transcriptomic Atlas Reveals Disease-Associated Cellular States in Human Glomerular Diseases.

Introduction

Glomerular diseases are a major cause of chronic kidney disease and kidney failure worldwide, yet the cellular mechanisms underlying their heterogeneity remain incompletely understood. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) enables high-resolution characterization of transcriptional alterations across diverse kidney cell populations.

Methods

We performed snRNA-seq on snap-frozen kidney biopsy tissues obtained from treatment-naïve patients with minimal change disease (MCD), membranous nephropathy (MN), IgA nephropathy (IgAN), and diabetic kidney disease (DKD), together with control kidney samples. In total, 333,938 nuclei from 37 individuals were analyzed to define disease-associated transcriptional programs across kidney cell types.

Results

Upregulated transcripts formed disease-specific programs that were shared across multiple cell types, whereas downregulated transcripts were largely cell type-specific and conserved across diseases. We identified disease-associated cellular states, including a glomerular epithelial population exhibiting a hybrid transcriptional profile shared between podocytes and parietal epithelial cells (PECs); a podocyte subpopulation with endocytosis-related gene expression, correlated with proteinuria severity and treatment response; and expansion of periostin (POSTN)-expressing myofibroblasts, inversely associated with estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) and spatially colocalized with podocyte injury. Each cellular state was independently recovered in external single-cell cohorts.

Conclusion

Single-nucleus transcriptomic profiling of human kidney biopsy tissues reveals disease-specific and shared cellular programs across major glomerular diseases. This resource provides insight into the cellular mechanisms underlying glomerular injury and identifies disease-associated cell states that may contribute to disease progression. Graphical abstract Keywords glomerular diseases single nucleus RNA sequencing pmc-status-qastatus 0 pmc-status-live yes pmc-status-embargo no pmc-status-released yes pmc-prop-open-access yes pmc-prop-olf no pmc-prop-manuscript no pmc-prop-legally-suppressed no pmc-prop-has-pdf yes pmc-prop-has-supplement yes pmc-prop-pdf-only no pmc-prop-suppress-copyright no pmc-prop-is-real-version no pmc-prop-is-scanned-article no pmc-prop-preprint no pmc-prop-in-epmc yes pmc-license-ref CC BY-NC-ND Glomerular diseases significantly contribute to the global burden of kidney disease and frequently lead to kidney failure. 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 Although they share common clinical manifestations such as proteinuria and progressive loss of kidney function, they differ considerably in their histopathologic features, mechanisms, and clinical trajectories. 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 Understanding the molecular heterogeneity underlying these diseases is therefore critical for improving disease classification and identifying potential therapeutic targets. Because the kidney is composed of diverse and highly specialized cell populations, disease mechanisms may manifest through cell type-specific transcriptional alterations. Recent advances in single-cell and snRNA-seq have enabled high-resolution characterization of kidney cell populations and injury-associated transcriptional states. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 These approaches have provided important insights into kidney biology and disease mechanisms, including the identification of rare glomerular cell types such as podocytes that are often underrepresented in conventional transcriptomic studies. 14 However, most single-cell studies of kidney disease have focused on individual disease entities or tissues obtained from nephrectomy specimens, limiting the ability to compare transcriptional alterations across multiple glomerular diseases using diagnostic human biopsy tissues. To address this gap, we performed snRNA-seq on snap-frozen kidney biopsy tissues obtained from patients with 4 major glomerular diseases—MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD—together with control kidney samples. By integrating transcriptomic profiles across disease groups and controls, we aimed to identify both shared and disease-specific transcriptional programs across kidney cell types and to characterize disease-associated cellular states within the human glomerulus. Methods Ethical Considerations and Patient Consent The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board of Seoul National University Hospital (IRB Nos. H-2203-053-1303 and H-1404-117-575). The study samples were collected from the KORNERSTONE project, a multicenter, prospective cohort study and biobank for glomerular diseases, run under the National Biobank Project of the Republic of Korea. 15 Patients provided informed consent for the collection of the biospecimens, their use in this study, and their use in a public database. The study was conducted under the National Research Project Single Cell Atlas of Immune Disease ( http://www.scaid.org/ ). Kidney Tissue Collection The study subjects were enrolled in the KORNERSTONE project before their first diagnostic kidney biopsy. At our institution, three biopsy cores were typically obtained per patient and first evaluated by an attending nephropathologist for routine clinical diagnostics (light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy). Intact biopsy tissue not required for diagnostic evaluation was immediately snap-frozen at the bedside for biobanking. For snRNA-seq, the remaining cores were used in their entirety; because standard biopsy cores traverse the cortex and may variably extend toward the corticomedullary region, the sequenced material represents mixed cortical regions. We selected patients with preserved kidney function (eGFR ≥ 30 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 ), to minimize disease-nonspecific transcriptomic effects of advanced fibrotic changes. Inclusion required primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti-phospholipase A2 receptor antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without other glomerulonephritis pathologies; patients with urine protein creatinine ratio > 3 g/g (MCD, MN, and DKD) who were immunosuppression-naïve were prioritized to capture active disease. In this study, we included a total of 30 patient kidney samples (from 7 MCD, 6 MN, 13 IgAN, and 4 patients with DKD). Clinical data from the initial visit and treatment initiation were analyzed. For control kidney tissues, we used the normal kidney cortex obtained during radical nephrectomy surgery for kidney cancer. We carefully reviewed the clinical histories to exclude patients with diabetic or hypertensive kidney disease and selected those without proteinuria or obstructive changes in the kidney. To minimize ischemic bias, an intraoperative gun biopsy was obtained from the exposed kidney before renal artery clamping, away from cancerous lesions. Tissues were snap-frozen and delivered to central storage. A total of 7 control patients were included in the study. Results Baseline Characteristics of the Study Subjects We collected data from 37 participants, including individuals with MCD ( n = 7), MN ( n = 6), IgAN ( n = 13), and DKD ( n = 4), as well as a control group ( n = 7). All patient samples were obtained from immunosuppressants-naïve individuals with typical clinical presentations, including primary MCD with overt nephrotic syndrome, anti- PLA2R antibody-positive MN, IgAN, or DKD without another diagnosis. Control kidney tissues were obtained from chemotherapy-naïve patients undergoing nephrectomy for renal cell carcinoma, using noncancerous lesions in cortical tissue. The baseline demographics of the study subjects are presented in Supplementary Table S1 . The mean spot urine protein creatinine ratio for each condition was 8.09 ± 4.87 g/g for the MCD group, 7.98 ± 6.49 g/g for the MN group, 1.05 ± 1.36 g/g for the IgAN group, and 3.68 ± 1.78 g/g for the DKD group. The control group had no proteinuria. The baseline eGFR was 89.8 ± 26.8 ml/min per 1.73 m 2 in the study subjects with typical clinical features. We analyzed a total of 333,938 nuclei from biopsy tissues ( Figure 1 a) and identified 12 main cell clusters, annotated based on known canonical markers, including podocytes, PECs, various tubular cells, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, and immune cells ( Figure 1 b, c). We next examined the distribution of these subtypes across clinical groups and observed pronounced, disease-specific heterogeneity ( Figure 1 d). To validate these annotations, we compared our data with an external dataset from the Kidney Precision Medicine Project. 9 This comparison revealed a high correlation in marker gene expression profiles ( Supplementary Figure S1 A). Furthermore, upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in our DKD samples showed a similar pattern to those in the Kidney Precision Medicine Project dataset ( Supplementary Figure S1 B). Finally, we performed more detailed subclustering and annotation for each major cell type ( Supplementary Figure S1 C, Supplementary Table S2 ). Figure 1 Study design and single-nucleus transcriptional profiling of kidney biopsy samples from control individuals and patients with glomerular diseases. (a) A schematic showing the overall study design. (b) Human glomerular disease single-nucleus transcriptional atlas ( n = 333,938). UMAP plot showing different cell types identified by snRNA-seq. (c) Dot plot representation of the marker genes for the annotated kidney cell types. The dot size indicates the percentage of relative gene expression for each marker gene. The dot color reflects the average expression level of the specified gene within each cell type. (d) Stacked bar plot showing the per-condition proportions of cell types in each condition. Cell type proportions were calculated relative to the total number of cells within each sample and compared between disease groups and Controls using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with Benjamini–Hochberg correction. Cell types showing statistically significant differences compared with Controls are marked with white asterisks. (e and g) Heatmap illustrating DEGs (|log2FC| > 0.25, adjusted P value < 0.05) categorized into 16 modules through k-means clustering across various cell types in glomerular disease patients in comparison to those in the control group. (e) Heatmap of upregulated DEGs associated with each glomerular disease. Gene modules specific to each glomerular disease are indicated by the corresponding-colored boxes. (g) Heatmap generated by downregulated DEGs, arranged by cell type. Gene modules specific to each cell type are indicated by the corresponding-colored boxes. (f and h) Bar plots of the −log10( P value) from enrichment analysis of DEGs from different modules, as shown in heatmaps. Pathways represented by upregulated DEGs are colored in orange (f), and those associated with downregulated DEGs are highlighted in sky blue (h). CNT, connecting tubule; DCT, distal convoluted tubule; CDPC, collecting duct principal cell; CDIC, collecting duct intercalated cell; DKD, diabetic kidney disease; Endo, endothelial cell; FIB, fibroblast; IgAN, IgA nephropathy; IMM, immune cell; MCD, minimal change disease; PLA2R MN, phospholipase A2 receptor 1-associated membranous nephropathy; POD, podocyte; PEC, parietal epithelial cell; PT, proximal tubule; TAL, thick ascending limb; tL, thin limb; VSMC, vascular smooth muscle cell. Disease-Dominant, Cell Type-Common, Cell Type-Dominant, and Disease-Common DEGs in Glomerular Diseases Our analysis of DEGs revealed a dichotomous pattern—upregulated DEGs were largely disease-specific but shared across cell types, whereas downregulated DEGs were cell type-specific but common across diseases ( Supplementary Table S3 ). We identified disease-dominant upregulated gene modules enriched in each condition ( Figure 1 e and f; Supplementary Table S4 ). The MCD-dominant module was enriched for transporter-related genes (e.g., SLC13A1 , SLC36A2 ; Module 5). The MN-dominant module included genes associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition (e.g., SPP1, VIM ) and the interferon response (e.g., HIF1A, IFNAR2 ; Module 8). The IgAN-dominant module was associated with previously reported pathways, including aldosterone-regulated sodium reabsorption (Module 2). In DKD, upregulated modules were associated with differentiation and metabolic processes (Module 15) ( Figure 1 f; Supplementary Table S5 ). Representative genes within each module also showed preferential expression in the corresponding disease group at the sample level ( Supplementary Figure S2 A). Module score analysis confirmed significantly higher in scores in the corresponding disease groups compared with others ( Supplementary Figure S2 B). In contrast, downregulated DEGs exhibited a cell type-restricted pattern shared across diseases ( Figure 1 g and 1h; Supplementary Table S4 ). In podocytes, genes related to the actin cytoskeleton (e.g., IQGAP2 , MICAL2 ) 16 , 17 and cell-cell adhesion were reduced (Module 12). In PECs, genes negatively regulating mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling were downregulated (Module 14). 18 Tubular cells showed decreased expression of metabolic pathways, including fatty acid metabolism, in proximal tubule- and thick ascending limb-specific modules (Modules 1 and 3). 19 , 20 In collecting duct principal cells, the downregulated module included the glucocorticoid receptor and NR4A1 . Endothelial cells demonstrated reduced expression of SPRED2 , with gene ontology analysis indicating negative regulation of the MAPK cascade (Module 9; Supplementary Table S6 ). 21 For each cell type, module scores were significantly lower in diseased samples than in controls, without differences in unrelated cell types ( Supplementary Figure S2 C). Disease-Associated Intermediate Epithelial State Between Injured Podocytes and Activated PECs Subclustering of glomerular cells identified a distinct population positioned between podocytes and PECs on uniform manifold approximation and projection ( Figure 2 a). 22 These cells coexpressed canonical markers of both lineages along with a distinct transcriptional profile ( Figure 2 b, Supplementary Figure S3 A). A pseudotime analysis further demonstrated the transcriptional proximity of this population to both podocytes and PECs ( Figure 2 c). This population was enriched for PEC activation and proliferative signaling programs, including MAPK- and epidermal growth factor receptor-related pathways involving ERBB 2, EGF , FGFR , and CD 24, together with cluster-defining genes such as CASR and PRDM 16 ( Supplementary Figure S3 B and C). 18 , 23 This cluster also showed significant upregulation of genes known to be highly expressed in proliferative PECs ( Figure 2 d). 22 Importantly, the proportion of this cluster was significantly correlated (Pearson's r = 0.35, R² = 0.13, P = 0.031) with clinical severity index that we defined ( Figure 2 e). Marker genes for this cluster were also present between podocytes and PECs in the uniform manifold approximation and projection of the external transcriptomic data for podocytes and PECs ( Supplementary Figure S3 D). 9 Figure 2 Detection of an intermediate epithelial population sharing podocyte and PEC features. (a) UMAP of subclustered cell types belonging to the glomerulus ( n = 13,475) are colored according to subclustered cell type with a hematoxylin and eosin-stained image of the glomerulus. Podocyte and PEC populations were subclustered from the glomerular epithelial compartment, whereas mesangial cells and glomerular endothelial cells were identified through subclustering of the VSMC and endothelial compartments, respectively. (b) Violin plots showing the expression of podocyte and PEC marker genes. (c) Trajectory and pseudotime analysis of podocytes and PECs. The panel illustrates the trajectory in order of subsets of podocytes and PECs. (d) Heatmaps showing the relative expression of genes from previous studies indicating proliferative PECs in each podocyte and PEC subset. 22 (e) Scatter plot of the proportion of Intermediate cells versus renal dysfunction severity. The score is calculated as (proteinuria + 1) × 100 / eGFR, ensuring it rises with increased proteinuria (a marker of kidney damage) and lower eGFR (indicating poorer kidney filtration). The fitted linear regression line with 95% confidence interval (shaded area) is shown. Pearson's correlation coefficient (r), R², and corresponding P value are indicated in the plot. (f) Representative Xenium in situ hybridization images of human kidney tissues from control, and patients having MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. Green and red dots indicate NPHS1 , and ALDH1A2, respectively. The dashed box indicates the magnified region shown below. MCD, minimal change disease; (g and h) Immunofluorescent stain images of human kidney tissues from control and patients having MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. (g) Green, cyan, and red indicate WT1, claudin 1(encoded by CLDN1 ), and PRDM16, respectively. (h) Green and red dots indicate Podocin (encoded by NPHS2 ) and CASR, respectively. (i) Bar graph of immunofluorescence-based quantification of Podocin–CASR coexpression across conditions ( Supplementary Table S8 ). For each glomerulus, coexpression is defined as the percentage of the glomerular ROI in which Podocin (green) and CASR (red) are both above threshold. Statistical analyses were performed using the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test and unpaired t -test for proportion comparisons; ∗∗ P value < 0.01, ∗∗∗ P value < 0.005, ∗∗∗∗ P value < 0.0001. DKD, diabetic kidney disease; IgAN, IgA nephropathy; MCD, minimal change disease; MN, membranous nephropathy; PEC, parietal epithelial cell. Spatial validation reinforced these findings. Xenium in situ demonstrated coexpression of ALDH1A2 and NPHS1 in glomerular diseases ( Figure 2 f). At the protein level, immunofluorescence staining revealed that WT1, Claudin1 (encoded by CLDN1 , Figure 1 c), and PRDM16 ( Supplementary Figure S3 A) were coexpressed in all disease samples ( Figure 2 g). In addition, coexpression of Podocin (encoded by NPHS2 ) and CASR was also observed ( Figure 2 h and Supplementary Tables S7 and S8 ). Across conditions, both modalities showed increased abundance in glomerular diseases compared with controls ( Figure 2 i, Supplementary Figure S3 E). 24 To further characterize the glomerular niche surrounding this population, we performed CellChat analysis using glomerular and peri-glomerular populations together with spatial neighborhood analysis in Xenium data. Intermediate cells showed convergent incoming signaling associated with transforming growth factor (TGF)-β, platelet-derived growth factor, complement, and EGFR–MAPK-related pathways, including epidermal growth factor and neuregulin signaling from multiple glomerular cell populations ( Supplementary Figure S3 F). Consistent with these findings, Xenium neighborhood analysis demonstrated increased expression of TGFB1 , PDGFRB , C3 , STAT1 , and ETS1 in cells spatially proximal to Intermediate cells, supporting the presence of an active glomerular injury niche associated with epithelial plasticity and PEC activation. Disease-Specific Gene Expression in Podocytes and Podocytes With Endocytosis Feature We further focused on podocytes, given their crucial role in glomerular pathophysiology. Comparison of downregulated DEGs between controls and disease groups revealed 2 dominant patterns—genes commonly reduced across all glomerular diseases ( n = 101) and genes selectively reduced in DKD ( n = 124; Figure 3 a). The commonly downregulated DEGs were primarily associated with the regulation of cell migration and the negative regulation of the immune system ( Figure 3 b). This latter finding is consistent with the prominent interferon-γ response observed in the disease groups ( Figure 3 c). Furthermore, this common signature included the downregulation of genes involved in the Wnt signaling pathway, which is known to exacerbate podocyte injury and contribute to the development of proteinuria. 25 Figure 3 Transcriptional characterization of podocytes across glomerular diseases. (a and d) Venn diagram constructed using downregulated (a) and upregulated DEGs (d) obtained from comparisons of podocytes between each GN and the control group. Upregulated DEGs were enriched in disease-specific gene modules across glomerular diseases, highlighting the strong disease specificity of transcriptional activation programs ( Figure 3 d). Upregulated DEGs in MN showed enrichment of epithelial-mesenchymal transition-related genes, whereas IgAN was associated with genes involved in cell-substrate junction assembly ( Figure 3 e). Across diseases, slit diaphragm-associated genes including TJP1 and MAGI2 were consistently downregulated, along with VCL , which contributes to maintenance of the glomerular filtration barrier. 26 , 27 , 28 Additional disease-specific patterns were observed, including detachment-associated genes ( NOX4, TCF21 , and SLIT2 ) 29 , 30 , 31 , 32 in MCD and regeneration-related genes ( PROM1 and PAX8 ) 33 , 34 in DKD ( Figure 3 f and Supplementary Figure S4 A and B and Supplementary Table S9 ). The expression of GADD45A , VIM, and CDH6 , 35 , 36 , 37 which are known to be associated with epithelial-mesenchymal transition, was found to be specifically elevated in MN. Podocytes were divided into 3 clusters and annotated using marker genes ( Figure 3 g and Supplementary Figure S4 C). One population was characterized by high expression of genes associated with cubilin and amnionless complex, including LRP2 , CUBN , CLCN5 , and PRKCA , and was therefore designated the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure S4 C and D). 38 A similar transcriptional pattern cluster was also observed in podocytes in independent external single-cell datasets, including in patients with chronic kidney disease ( Supplementary Figure S4 E, F, and G). 9 Compared with conventional podocytes, podocyte endocytosis showed increased PAX2 , 39 and reduced expression of CDKN1C , 40 PODXL, and NPHS2, together with higher proliferation module scores ( Supplementary Figure S4 H and I). Importantly, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis cells significantly increased with baseline proteinuria severity (quasibinomial generalized linear model, β = 0.042, P = 0.001, pseudo-R 2 = 0.226), whereas patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment exhibited higher podocyte endocytosis module scores, suggesting an association between this transcriptional state and poor treatment response ( Figure 3 h and i). Accordingly, the gene module score was significantly greater in the MCD and MN groups than in the other glomerular disease groups and the control group ( Figure 3 j). These findings suggest that the activation of endocytosis-related gene programs in podocytes reflects the severity of proteinuria and may also have prognostic implications. We validated the presence of “podocyte endocytosis” at both the transcriptomic and protein levels through the coexpression of LRP2 and NPHS1 in Xenium in situ and megalin (encoded by LRP2 ) and WT1 in immunofluorescence ( Figure 3 k–l and Supplementary Table S7 ). Additionally, the proportion of podocyte endocytosis tended to be higher in glomerular disease in Xenium in situ and IF ( Supplementary Figure S4 J and K). To further characterize the signaling environment associated with podocyte endocytosis, we performed CellChat analysis across glomerular and peri-glomerular populations. Among the inferred pathways, Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling showed preferential communication toward the podocyte endocytosis state ( Supplementary Figure 4 L). Bradykinin signaling originated from multiple glomerular populations, whereas complement and interleukin17 signaling were primarily inferred from juxtaglomerular apparatus cells, PECs, and podocytes. Together, these findings indicate an injury-related signaling microenvironment around podocyte endocytosis cells. Drug2Cell (Wellcome Sanger Institute, Cambridge, UK) 41 identified candidate compounds targeting podocyte endocytosis, including phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitors (Apremilast, Roflumilast, and Crisaborole) and the cyclic guanosine monophosphate-modulating agent isosorbide ( Supplementary Figure S4 M), suggesting that modulation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate and cyclic guanosine monophosphate pathways may offer promising therapeutic avenues for targeting podocyte endocytosis-related injury. Stromal Activation and Myofibroblast Expansion Across Glomerular Diseases Stromal cells (including vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts) were subclustered into 12 clusters ( Figure 4 a, Supplementary Figure S5 A). 9 Across glomerular diseases, stromal cells showed consistent enrichment of TGF-β signaling, with the strongest activation observed in the myofibroblast cluster ( Figure 4 b and c). Trajectory analysis restricted to fibroblast-lineage cells revealed a differentiation continuum from fibroblasts to myofibroblasts present across all disease groups ( Figure 4 d), consistent with the established role of TGF-β signaling in myofibroblast activation. Along this trajectory, gene programs transitioned from mesenchymal differentiation to extracellular matrix organization, reflecting acquisition of myofibroblast functions ( Supplementary Figure S5 B). The expression levels of genes corresponding to the trajectory of the myofibroblast-enriched state and myofibroblast-associated genes, such as SULF1, NOX4, and COL16A1 , were consistently increased in glomerular diseases ( Supplementary Figure S5 C). Correspondingly, the proportion of myofibroblasts was significantly increased in disease samples compared with controls ( Figure 4 e). A heatmap analysis of fibroblast-associated cell types (e.g., fibroblasts, medullary fibroblasts, adaptive fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts) using their DEGs revealed a gene module (Module 4) that was commonly upregulated across all glomerular diseases (module 4, Supplementary Figure S5 D and Supplementary Table S9 ). This module was significantly enriched for markers of myofibroblasts, TGF-β signaling-related genes, and genes of the Wnt pathway. Consistent with this, functional analysis of the module showed enrichment for biological processes related to myofibroblast function, such as extracellular matrix organization ( Supplementary Figure S5 E). The presence of this shared profibrotic pathway indicates that a common fibrotic program is activated across these diverse glomerular diseases. The myofibroblast gene module score was significantly increased across all glomerular diseases ( Supplementary Figure S5 F). Importantly, this module score was inversely correlated with eGFR(linear regression r = -0.47, R 2 = 0.22, P -value = 0.003), directly linking the fibrotic signature to declining kidney function ( Figure 4 f). Consistent with this, the proportion of myofibroblasts itself was also higher in the disease groups and was significantly associated with lower baseline (quasibinomial generalized linear model β = −0.013, P -value < 0.001, pseudo-R 2 = 0.339) and follow-up eGFR (quasibinomial generalized linear model β = −0.009, P -value = 0.012, pseudo-R 2 = 0.171) in regression analyses ( Figure 4 g and h). These associations persisted throughout the follow-up period, supporting a potential relationship between myofibroblast expansion and progressive kidney dysfunction. Cell-cell interaction analysis highlighted Periostin pathway as a disease-specific pathway originating from myofibroblasts ( Figure 4 i). This pathway primarily targeted PECs and, in primary glomerular diseases, also affected podocytes ( Figure 4 j). POSTN signaling is implicated in wound healing and fibrosis, 42 , 43 and POSTN-expressing fibroblasts were enriched within diseased glomeruli ( Figure 4 k). Their abundance was significantly associated with both proteinuria severity (R 2 = 0.29, P -value = 0.016) and the proportion of podocyte endocytosis (R 2 = 0.284, P -value = 0.019; Figure 4 l and m). These results indicate that myofibroblasts are common pathogenic cell types in glomerular disease and are associated with a decline in kidney function. Among them, POSTN-expressing myofibroblasts are additionally associated with proteinuria and appear to represent a key cellular component underlying glomerular disease manifestations. To identify potential therapeutic targets for myofibroblasts, we applied the Drug2Cell framework ( Supplementary Figure S5 G). 41 Among the top-ranked candidate compounds, cetirizine and olaratumab were identified as potential modulators of myofibroblast-associated programs. 44 These findings suggest that targeting myofibroblast activity may represent a potential therapeutic strategy for glomerular disease-associated fibrosis. TGF-β and Interferon Signaling in Endothelial Cells are Key to the Pathogenesis of Glomerular Diseases Endothelial cells were subclustered and annotated into 11 distinct cell types using known canonical markers ( Figure 5 a and b). DEGs revealed disease-associated transcriptional modules linked to vascular and immune signaling pathways (Module 2, Figure 5 c and d and Supplementary Table S9 ). Among these, endothelial cells from primary glomerular diseases showed enrichment of vasculogenesis-related programs, whereas disease-specific DEGs were particularly prominent in the MCD and MN groups ( Figure 5 e). Functional enrichment analysis indicated that these signatures were associated with TGF-β signaling and interferon responses, respectively ( Figure 5 f). Gene module scoring showed that TGF-β signaling was most strongly elevated in MN, followed by MCD and DKD ( Figure 5 g), whereas the interferon-α response score was the highest in the MCD group. Both pathways were consistently increased in disease groups compared with controls. When analyzed at the subcluster level, these signaling programs were enriched in glomerular endothelial-related subclusters, with the interferon-α response showing the highest expression in the degenerative endothelial cluster ( Figure 5 h), with interferon-stimulated genes showing particularly high expression in MCD ( Figure 5 i). Discussion This study presents a single-nucleus transcriptome analysis of human biopsy-confirmed glomerular diseases, comprising 333,938 nuclei obtained from 37 individuals, including 30 treatment-naïve patients with MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD and 7 controls. By profiling diverse kidney cell populations from diagnostic biopsy cores, our dataset provides a comprehensive view of early disease-associated transcriptional changes across glomerular diseases. Another strength of this study is the inclusion of subjects without substantial GFR reduction, which enabled us to compare cell type-specific transcriptomic alterations in relatively early disease states. Our transcriptome data may enhance the understanding of disease-specific pathophysiologic mechanisms of glomerular diseases, which may lead to the discovery of diagnostic or therapeutic biomarkers and common pathological pathways contributing to the progression of chronic kidney disease. This atlas therefore provides a framework for interpreting cell type–specific transcriptional alterations across major glomerular diseases. A notable observation from our analysis was the distinct pattern of transcriptional regulation across diseases and cell types. Upregulated genes tended to form disease-dominant modules, whereas downregulated genes were largely organized by cell type. This pattern suggests that disease-specific signaling programs activate distinct transcriptional responses, whereas functional impairment manifests through loss of cell type-specific gene expression. For example, the MN-dominant transcriptional signature was enriched for epithelial-mesenchymal transition and interferon-γ response pathways, consistent with immune-mediated injury associated with phospholipase A2 receptor autoimmunity 45 , 46 and IgAN modules with MAPK signaling, consistent with MAPK and/or extracellular signal-regulated kinase activation in mesangial injury. 47 Nevertheless, several upregulated modules also exhibited cell type-restricted patterns that complemented the corresponding downregulated programs within the same cell type. For example, proximal tubule modules paired upregulated transport programs with downregulated metabolic programs, suggesting adaptive tubular hypertrophy; endothelial modules paired vasculogenic activation with loss of MAPK negative regulators. We also identified a glomerular epithelial population exhibiting a hybrid transcriptional profile shared between podocytes and PECs. Podocytes are terminally differentiated cells that undergo structural injury and transcriptional remodeling under stress, whereas PECs retain proliferative potential and can respond dynamically to podocyte loss. The hybrid epithelial population was enriched in diseased glomeruli and showed activation of epithelial stress- and proliferation-associated programs, suggesting epithelial plasticity and remodeling within the injured glomerular compartment. This observation is consistent with previous studies showing that pathological activation of PEC signaling pathways can lead to abnormal PEC proliferation and contribute to glomerulosclerosis. Spatial transcriptomic analysis further supported the presence of these cells within diseased glomeruli. Although the lineage relationships of these cells cannot be resolved from cross-sectional human biopsy data alone, their shared transcriptional features and spatial localization support the existence of an injury-associated hybrid epithelial state in glomerular disease. Our study further identified a podocyte subpopulation characterized by expression of genes involved in protein endocytosis, including the cubilin and amnionless complex components LRP2 and CUBN . 38 , 48 , 49 , 50 , 51 Previous studies have suggested that podocytes may activate endocytic pathways under protein overload to maintain filtration barrier integrity. Consistent with this, the podocyte endocytosis program was associated with increased proteinuria and remained elevated in patients with persistent proteinuria after treatment. Recent work suggesting that antinephrin autoantibodies in podocytopathies induce nephrin internalization and glomerular endocytic activity provides a potential mechanistic framework, and the prominent MCD enrichment may reflect this adaptive or injury-associated response to slit diaphragm dysfunction. 52 The preferential enrichment of Bradykinin, complement, and interleukin17 signaling toward this population further suggests an injury-associated microenvironment, consistent with podocyte dedifferentiation features. These findings suggest that this transcriptional state may represent an adaptive but injury-associated podocyte response with potential relevance to disease severity and treatment response. In addition to epithelial injury programs, we observed consistent activation of stromal fibrotic pathways across glomerular diseases. Trajectory analysis suggested differentiation from fibroblasts to myofibroblasts, accompanied by enrichment of TGF-β signaling and extracellular matrix programs. Notably, the abundance of myofibroblasts correlated with declining kidney function even in patients without severe functional impairment at diagnosis, suggesting that fibrotic remodeling begins early in disease progression. Spatial transcriptomic data further revealed enrichment of POSTN-expressing fibroblasts within diseased glomeruli, supporting the existence of localized fibrotic microenvironments that may promote ongoing glomerular injury. Our data extend previous observations by demonstrating these fibrotic programs at single-cell resolution within human biopsy tissues. Drug2cell analysis further identified candidate compounds targeting disease-associated cellular states, providing a framework for future therapeutic hypothesis generation. The enrichment of distinct pathways in endothelial cells offers potential mechanistic insights into these diseases. For instance, the prominent TGF-β signaling in MN may contribute to the increased glomerular basement membrane thickness characteristic of the disease. 53 Furthermore, the upregulation of major histocompatibility complex molecules in both MCD and MN suggests that endothelial cells may activate antigen-experienced T-cells, implicating T-cell involvement in nephrotic syndrome. 54 , 55 Finally, the elevated interferon signature in MCD could help explain its characteristic steroid sensitivity. 56 There are several limitations in this study. First, glomerular cells comprised a relatively small proportion of total captured nuclei, reflecting the technical challenges of profiling human diagnostic biopsy tissue. Nevertheless, the absolute number of glomerular nuclei ( n = 13,475) was sufficient to identify multiple disease-associated cell states such as podocyte endocytosis. Second, the cohort is heterogeneous with limited samples per disease; however, the use of treatment-naïve diagnostic biopsies allowed us to capture early disease-associated transcriptional programs rarely accessible in human studies and was designed for shared rather than disease-specific classification. Third, our dataset mainly comprises transcriptomic information. Further enhancement by the inclusion of proteomic or epigenetic profiling could expand the insights related to pathophysiologic alterations in glomerular disease. 57 Lastly, control tissues were obtained from histologically normal cortex of nephrectomy specimens rather than healthy donor biopsies; subtle transcriptional alterations from tumor microenvironment effects cannot be fully excluded. To minimize these effects, control samples were collected by intraoperative biopsy-gun before renal artery clamping, mimicking native biopsy acquisition. Future validation with living donor or preimplantation biopsies may further confirm disease-associated programs. In conclusion, we report an extensive snRNA-seq dataset generated from rare and clinically valuable treatment-naïve human kidney biopsy tissues across MCD, MN, IgAN, and DKD. This dataset uniquely captures disease-relevant transcriptomic states of kidney-resident cells at the time of diagnosis, offering a snapshot that is difficult to obtain in other models or settings. Our findings provide novel insights into disease- and cell type-specific alterations in glomerular diseases. As a resource study, this work constitutes a foundational reference atlas that may support future investigations aiming to discover diagnostic markers, therapeutic targets, and mechanistic pathways in human kidney disease. Importantly, because the KORNERSTONE cohort is primarily composed of Korean patients, this dataset also expands the ethnic diversity of currently available kidney single-cell reference resources, which remain heavily weighted toward Western populations. title: Optimized Tissue Microarray for In Situ Characterization of Central Nervous System Tumors Using a Spatial Transcriptomics Platform.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Optimized Tissue Microarray for In Situ Characterization of Central Nervous System Tumors Using a Spatial Transcriptomics Platform. We present a standardized, end-to-end development and application of a Xenium tissue microarray (TMA) to profile glioblastoma, meningioma, schwannomas, and pituitary neuroendocrine tumors (PitNETs). The workflow covers: (i) pathology-guided selection of representative tumor regions (including tumor core and immune-rich interfaces when available); (ii) core extraction and array design to balance patient groups and clinical timepoints within each block; (iii) TMA embedding, sectioning, and slide preparation compatible with Xenium chemistry; (iv) assay execution, imaging, transcript decoding, and cell segmentation. This high-throughput workflow is specific for generating TMAs optimized for Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics for different central nervous system (CNS) tumor types. Spatial profiling of CNS tumors in focused studies (i.e., clinical trials) is often limited by scarce tissue, heterogeneity across tumor regions, and batch effects introduced by processing specimens across multiple runs. Building a Xenium-compatible TMA enables uniform handling of many patient samples and time points on a single slide, thereby improving cross-sample consistency while reducing reagent cost and turnaround time. We also highlight practical troubleshooting steps encountered in tumor sections, such as tissue loss and segmentation artifacts in highly cellular or necrotic regions. Representative results are summarized using key assay quality metrics to assess performance across cores, including usable tissue area, numbers of segmented cells/nuclei per core, decoded transcript yield, genes detected per cell, and the fraction of transcripts assigned to cells. This protocol yields reproducible, cell-resolved spatial gene expression maps across multiple tumor regions in parallel, enabling direct comparison of naïve and recurrent disease within a therapeutic context. This TMA approach is broadly applicable to both untreated and treated biospecimens, where standardized processing and scalable spatial profiling are essential for biomarker discovery and mechanistic insight.

title: Senescence-associated stromal remodeling in bone marrow aging and hematologic and bone-metastatic diseases
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Senescence-associated stromal remodeling in bone marrow aging and hematologic and bone-metastatic diseases Cellular senescence is implicated as a driver of age-related tissue dysfunction and chronic inflammation. However, no single marker defines a senescent cell, and distinguishing senescence from other stressors requires both experimental perturbation and comparison across contexts. As part of the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet), we generated a multimodal atlas integrating human bone marrow from 80 donors (54 assayed by single-cell RNA sequencing; 48 by Xenium spatial transcriptomics) with a 130 combined cases across four disease cohorts: breast and prostate cancer bone metastases (BCa/PCa; n=61), myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN; n=21), and multiple myeloma (MM; n=48). Human marrow aging was characterized by interferon and IL6/JAK/STAT3 activation in hematopoietic progenitors, myeloid-biased output, and progressive loss of naive CD4 T cell identity. Spatially, CDKN1A was concentrated in vascular stroma, and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) expression rose with age coordinately across stromal cell types within individual donors (mean pairwise rho = 0.46), consistent with shared influences on stromal aging. Malignancy was associated with distinct and disease-specific senescence-associated states rather than uniform amplification of aging programs. Senescent fibroblasts spatially adjacent to tumor in breast and prostate cancer bone metastases shared an upregulated secretory program comprising 148 genes encoding secreted proteins, alongside upregulated matrix-remodeling and cellular adhesion signatures. Osteolineage cells found in metastasis sites as well as in MPN marrow also displayed distinct senescence-associated phenotypes, including enlarged, multinucleated osteoclasts and CDKN1A+ osteoblasts with upregulated secretory programs. However, senescence-associated secretory programs and matrix dysregulation in stromal cells was not observed in MM, indicating that these features are not generic consequences of tumor burden within the bone marrow but rather arise from specific cancer-stromal interactions. Residual hematopoietic regions showed altered myeloid and erythroid composition and transcriptional states. To complement these human datasets, we used a mouse model in which doxorubicin-induced senescence reproduced molecular and compositional hallmarks of marrow aging that were selectively reversible with senolytic treatment. These data establish normal marrow as a quantitative baseline for senescence and separate shared from context-specific senescent states.

title: SpNeigh: spatial neighborhood and differential expression analysis for high-resolution spatial transcriptomics.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: SpNeigh: spatial neighborhood and differential expression analysis for high-resolution spatial transcriptomics. Spatial transcriptomics technologies such as Xenium, MERFISH, and Visium HD enable high-resolution profiling of gene expression while preserving tissue architecture. However, most computational methods for spatial analysis do not explicitly model local tissue context, such as boundaries, neighborhoods, or gradients. Here, we present SpNeigh (https://github.com/jinming-cheng/SpNeigh/), an R package for spatial neighborhood analysis and spatially aware differential expression modeling. SpNeigh includes tools for boundary detection, spatial neighborhood extraction, distance-based weighting, and gradient-based statistical testing. It supports both region-based differential expression and smooth spatial modeling using spline-based regression, along with a spatial enrichment index that identifies genes enriched near defined spatial features. We demonstrate the utility of SpNeigh across multiple platforms and tissues, including mouse brain, human breast cancer, and human liver, revealing intermediate populations at tissue interfaces, immune microenvironment differences, and spatially zonated gene expression patterns. SpNeigh offers a flexible and interpretable framework for dissecting spatial gene expression dynamics in complex tissues.

evidence_text:
Identification of high-risk cells in single-cell spatially resolved transcriptomics data using Diagnostic Evidence GAuge of Single-cells with spatial smoothing.

Summary

The examination of high-risk cells and regions in tissue samples from spatially resolved transcriptomics platforms offers meaningful insights into specific disease processes. For existing methods, while cell types or clusters can be identified and associated with disease attributes, individual cells are unable to be associated in the same manner.

Method

Diagnostic Evidence Gauge of Single-Cells and Spatial Transcriptomics (DEGAS) solves the above problem by employing latent representations of gene expression data and domain adaptation to transfer disease attributes from patients to individual cells from single-cell RNA sequencing datasets. In this research, we present and evaluate DEGAS's versatility in adapting to data arising from various single-cell spatially resolved transcriptomics (scSRT) platforms. DEGAS successfully identified high-risk cells and regions in liver hepatocellular carcinoma and skin cutaneous melanoma, which were validated through known markers. Additionally, DEGAS was applied to our newly generated Type II Diabetes Xenium dataset, revealing high-risk cells within the tissue samples.

Availability and implementation

The DEGAS software can be accessed at https://github.com/tsteelejohnson91/DEGAS. For the updated smoothing functions and associated codes, visit https://github.com/dchatter04/DEGAS-Spatial-Smoothing, which is archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18510221. Sources for the datasets reviewed are detailed in their respective sections. A description of some datasets, along with extra tables and figures, is provided in the Supplementary Materials file. Our newly generated Xenium data for Type II Diabetes can be found at https://doi.org/10.7303/syn68699752.

title: Evidence of off-target probe binding affecting 10x Genomics Xenium gene panels compromise accuracy of spatial transcriptomic profiling.
xenium_reason: New profiling/generation with Xenium is stated
evidence_text: Evidence of off-target probe binding affecting 10x Genomics Xenium gene panels compromise accuracy of spatial transcriptomic profiling. The accuracy of spatial gene expression profiles generated by probe-based in situ spatially resolved transcriptomic technologies depends on the specificity with which probes bind to their intended target gene. Off-target binding, defined as a probe binding to something other than the target gene, can distort a gene's true expression profile, making probe specificity essential for reliable transcriptomics. Here, we investigated off-target binding affecting the 10x Genomics Xenium technology. We developed a software tool, Off-target Probe Tracker (OPT), to identify putative off-target binding via alignment of probe target sequences and assessing whether mapped loci corresponded to the intended target gene across multiple reference annotations. Applying OPT to a Xenium human breast gene panel, we identified at least 14 out of the 313 genes in the panel potentially impacted by off-target binding to protein-coding genes. To substantiate our predictions, we leveraged a Xenium breast cancer dataset generated using this gene panel and compared results to orthogonal spatial and single-cell transcriptomic profiles from Visium CytAssist and 3' single-cell RNA-seq derived from the same tumor block. Our findings indicate that for some genes, the expression patterns detected by Xenium demonstrably reflect the aggregate expression of the target and predicted off-target genes based on Visium and single-cell RNA-seq, rather than the target gene alone. We further applied OPT to identify potential off-target binding in custom gene panels and integrate tissue-specific RNA-seq data to assess effects. Overall, this work enhances the biological interpretability of spatial transcriptomics data and improves reproducibility in spatial transcriptomics research.

title: Conserved minimal CD8 cytotoxic immune-state unit in an IL18R1-associated immune program in hepatocellular carcinoma.
xenium_reason: Xenium is explicitly used for validation
evidence_text:
Conserved minimal CD8 cytotoxic immune-state unit in an IL18R1-associated immune program in hepatocellular carcinoma.

Background and aims

The conserved human correlate of interleukin-18 receptor 1 (IL-18R1)-associated immune states in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains undefined. We aimed to identify a minimal, reproducible, immune-state component associated with IL18R1 across independent human HCC cohorts and evaluate its clinical relevance.

Methods

Publicly available single-cell RNA sequencing datasets from five independent HCC cohorts were analyzed using a unified framework. Paired tumor-adjacent cohorts were prioritized for primary analyses, whereas tumor-only cohorts served as supportive datasets. CD8 T cells were stratified by IL18R1 expression, and tumor-specific enrichment was quantified using difference-in-differences. We validated the spatial transcriptomics using a murine liver tumor Xenium dataset. Clinical relevance was evaluated using The Cancer Genome Atlas Liver Hepatocellular Carcinoma (TCGA-LIHC) bulk RNA-seq data.

Results

IL18R1-positive CD8 T cells exhibited a tumor-specific, C-C motif chemokine ligand 5 (CCL5)-centered cytotoxic transcriptional program, consistently enriched across datasets. Alternative IL18R1 stratification confirmed the identified immune program's robustness. Spatial transcriptomics localized this cytotoxic state in tumor-associated CD8 T cells and highlighted increased expression of Ccl5 and Cxcr3. Tumor-only cohorts demonstrated substantial heterogeneity, highlighting the importance of paired cohort design. In TCGA-LIHC, a composite CCL5-centered cytotoxic core score, not CCL5 alone, was associated with improved overall survival, although this attenuated after adjusting for clinical covariates.

Conclusions

The dominant human correlate of an IL18R1-associated immune state in HCC is a compact, CCL5-centered CD8 cytotoxic module, not a broad inflammatory response. This spatially validated unit provides a reproducible framework for HCC immune-state characterization and stratification.

evidence_text: Chromosome 6q mediated loss of LATS1 tumour suppression as a targetable mechanism of ultra-high-risk posterior fossa A ependymoma. Posterior Fossa A (PFA) is the most frequent and clinically aggressive ependymoma (EPN) subgroup, with relapse typically representing a terminal event despite intensive multimodal therapy. Ultra-high-risk PFA EPNs are characterised by chromosome 6q loss (6q-) with or without chromosome 1q gain (1q +). While the molecular mechanisms driving 1q+ have been elucidated, 6q- PFA pathobiology remains poorly understood. Here, we show that loss of 6q in PFA EPN results in deletion of LATS1 (Large Tumour Suppressor Kinase 1), thereby dysregulating the Hippo signalling pathway and enhancing YAP/TEAD activity. Integrated analyses of primary and recurrent PFA EPNs, incorporating clinical, multiomic, and functional assays, were performed to define the biology and therapeutic susceptibility of 6q- PFA EPNs. Cumulative 6q loss was associated with nearly half of PFA EPN-related deaths. Copy number profiling identified the LATS1 locus as recurrently deleted across all 6q- cases, including 10/60 with partial 6q deletions. Restoration of LATS1 expression in 6q- PFA cell lines re-established protein levels and suppressed proliferation. Tumour analyses showed marked Hippo pathway disruption with elevated YAP expression and TEAD2-related transcriptional activity. TEAD2 palmitoylation inhibitor VT107, and Proteolysis Targeted Chimera (PROTAC) degrader H122, exhibited PFA 6q- selective activity in vitro. TEAD2 upregulation was further observed in a previously described undifferentiated, progenitor-like population of PFA EPN cells. In conclusion, 6q loss defines an aggressive biological subset of PFA associated with dismal outcomes. Identification of LATS1 as a recurrently lost tumour suppressor implicates Hippo pathway dysregulation as a central driver of malignancy, and we identify YAP/TEAD signalling as a potential therapeutic target.
