Introduction  Ependymoma (EPN) is the second most common malignant brain tumour in childhood and comprises multiple molecular entities [ 32 ,  33 ]. Posterior fossa A (PFA) EPN is the most frequent subgroup, affects the youngest children, and carries the poorest outcomes [ 32 ,  40 ]. Despite modern therapy targeting maximal tumour resection followed by focal radiotherapy [ 42 ], relapse occurs in around 50% of cases, and only 25% of these children survive beyond 5 years [ 40 ,  56 ]. PFA EPNs showing chromosomal instability—typically gain of chromosome 1q (1q +) and/or loss of chromosome 6q (6q-) exhibit an especially dismal prognosis, forming an ultra-high-risk group for whom current standard-of-care interventions are rarely curative [ 5 ].  We previously hypothesised that certain molecularly defined EPN subgroups are destined to have poor outcomes [ 39 ]. Since then, we have presented evidence from a large, international cohort showing that 1q+ and 6q- increase in frequency during PFA EPN recurrence and progression. Up to two-thirds of patients acquire a high-risk copy number alteration by first relapse, compared to one-fifth at initial presentation [ 10 ]. This evolution of tumour biology may explain why recurrence is associated with such dismal outcomes.  Recent work into the biology of 1q+ in PFA progression has highlighted the role of  MDM4,  located on chromosome 1q, as a negative downstream regulator of P53, mimicking a P53 mutation [ 15 ]. In addition,  UCK2,  also on 1q, represents a potential therapeutic weakness that may render 1q+ PFA EPN sensitive to the chemotherapy agent 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU). This hypothesised therapeutic intervention is now a focus for the development of biology-driven clinical trials of 5-FU and radiotherapy in both North America (ACNS2422) and Europe.  In contrast, the biological basis for the poor prognosis associated with 6q- PFA EPN remains undefined. Here, we investigate the tumour biology of 6q- PFA EPN using an established international dataset. We hypothesise that the adverse outcome associated with 6q- results from the loss of the tumour-suppressor gene  LATS1 , leading to dysregulation of the Hippo pathway and offering a druggable target through inhibition of YAP/TEAD signalling.    Methods   Cohort details  Matched primary and recurrent tumour sample copy-number variation (CNV) data was previously obtained by DNA methylation profiling in our prior multi-institutional study [ 10 ]. This dataset included 101 children with recurrent, DNA methylation-classified PFA EPNs.  For additional experiments beyond the original multi-institutional cohort, immunohistochemistry was performed on archival FFPE material from 75 PFA EPNs (25 6q- and 50 wild type), which were obtained from Children’s Colorado Hospital. Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics was performed on 14 snap-frozen tumour samples from the Colorado paediatric neuro-oncology brain tumour bank. Bulk RNAseq, Immunohistochemistry and Xenium samples were obtained during routine surgery or autopsy respectively, with institutional approval and patient consent (COMIRB 95–500).    Bulk RNA sequencing analysis  Bulk RNA-seq analysis was performed on a dataset of primary and recurrent PFA ( GSE226961 ,  GSE243682 ,  GSE327676 )[ 10 ,  13 ]. RNA was isolated from snap-frozen material and sequenced on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Sequencing data were aligned using STAR [ 8 ], and transcript quantification (in fragments per kilobase per million reads, FPKM) was generated with Cufflinks [ 50 ]. Single-sample gene-set enrichment analysis (ssGSEA) was performed on individual RNA-seq FPKM data using the GenePattern portal [ 4 ,  45 ].    Survival analysis  Univariate analyses using the Kaplan–Meier method were employed to assess the effect of whole or partial loss of chromosome 6q on survival from both primary disease and recurrence. We also evaluated the impact of gene expression and transcription-factor target gene enrichment score (ssGSEA) on survival using the same method. Progression free survival was modelled as a time-dependent variable to capture the effect of CNV changes and associated biological effects at recurrence. This approach addresses the significant outcome impact of 1q gains and/or 6q losses at recurrence in PFA, which significantly confound overall survival analyses.    LATS1 knock-in experiments  LATS1 open reading frame (ORF) knock-in expression vector was designed and purchased through GeneCopia. Lentiviral LATS1 vector (hLATS1) and corresponding control vector (Ctl) were generated using the pLKO system, where LATS1 and control vectors are transfected into HEK293FT cells with psPAX and pMD2.G viral packaging plasmids and TransIT-LT1 Reagent (Mirus Bio). For in vitro assays, viral supernatant was collected in Opti-MEM with 15% FBS and 1% pen/strep. LATS1 ORF knock-in was performed in two PFA 6q- cell lines previously established and characterized in our laboratory (MAF-811; MAF-928)[ 1 ]. We used three comparator cell lines with PFA 6q WT: two supratentorial EPN ZFTA-fused cell lines (MAF-1329 [ 19 ] and DFKZ-EP1NS [ 30 ]) and a paediatric glioblastoma (GBM) cell line SF188 [ 9 ]. All cell lines were subjected to routine authentication by DNA fingerprinting and mycoplasma testing. For this study cell lines were propagated under standard tissue culture conditions and grown in fetal bovine serum (FBS)-supplemented media as monolayers, Cells used in in vitro experiments were transduced with viral supernatant using 8 μg/mL polybrene. LATS1 knock-in was confirmed by Western blot analysis.    In vitro comparative TEAD palmitoylation inhibitor VT107 and TEAD PROTAC degrader H122 drug screen  We screened the effect of TEAD palmitoylation inhibitor VT107 (MedChemExpress. Cat. no. HY-134957) [ 48 ] and TEAD PROTAC (proteolysis-targeting chimera) degrader H122 (MedChemExpress. Cat. no. HY-172113) [ 27 ] in PFA 6q- cell lines MAF-811 and MAF-928 and a panel of comparator paediatric brain tumour cell lines as previously described to identify ependymoma selective drug sensitivity [ 9 ]. These included EPN PFA 6q WT cell line DKFZ-BT232 [ 47 ], EPN ZFTA-fused cell lines MAF-1329 and DFKZ-EP1NS and non-EPN paediatric high-grade glioma (HGG) cell lines (diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas DIPG-IV and glioblastoma SF188) and medulloblastoma (MED) cell lines (DAOY, ONS76, FH-411and D458) that were maintained as described previously [ 9 ]. Cell lines were propagated as monolayers apart from semi-adherent suspension cell lines FH-411 and D458.  Cell lines were plated at ~50% confluence in 96-well plates and treated with a range of doses of VT107 (range = 10μM to 0.6 nM) and H122 (range = 1000 nM to 0.06 nM) for 72 h. Cell proliferation was measured using tritiated thymidine incorporation as previously described [ 9 ]. Treatment dose curves and associated IC-50 values were modelled using Prism statistical software (GraphPad Software, Inc., La Jolla, CA).  H122 PROTAC-specific degradation of TEAD was determined by Western blot analysis of protein extracted from PFA 6q- cell lines treated with a range of H122 doses (1000 nM to 8 nM) for 4 h. Determination of the baseline endogenous TEAD degradation rate in PFA 6q- cell lines was performed by extracting protein at 4 h and 24 h after treatment with protein translation inhibitor cycloheximide (100μγ/ml; Sigma Cat. no. C-6679).    Western blot  Western blots were performed as previously described [ 52 ]. Primary antibodies used were anti-LATS1 (1:1000, Proteintech #17,049–1-AP), anti-phospho-YAP (S127) (Cell Signaling, #4911), pan-TEAD (Cell-signaling #13,295), DNMT1 (Cell Signaling #5032) and anti-β-actin. Densitometry was performed using ImageJ software.    YAP immunohistochemistry  Standard immunohistochemistry was performed for YAP (1:200, antigen, Santa Cruz sc-101199) with antigen retrieval (10 mM Sodium Citrate pH 6.0, 110 °C, 10 min) and counterstained with hematoxylin, using techniques described previously [ 13 ]. Blinded scoring was performed using a subjective scoring scale (range 0–4) (AMD).    Xenium  in-situ  spatial transcriptomic analyses  The spatial expression of TEAD2 in PFA 6q- (n=5) and PFA WT (n=9) neoplastic subpopulations was performed using Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics (10X Genomics). Snap-frozen samples were embedded in Optimal Cutting Temperature (OCT) compound, cryosectioned at 10μM thickness (Leica CM1520 cryostat) and mounted onto Xenium Slides. Slides were processed on a Xenium Analyzer (Instrument software v3.3.0.0.; analysis v 3.3.0.1) following the manufacturer’s instructions. The Xenium Analyzer detected and amplified RNA, DNA, and protein probes in 15 serial decoding and imaging cycles whilst maintaining tissue integrity and producing images of whole tissue sections with single-cell and single-molecule resolution. A custom gene probe panel of 480 genes was synthesized that included marker genes of previously identified cellular subpopulations in ependymoma [ 13 – 15 ] and other paediatric brain tumour diagnoses [ 7 ,  37 ,  57 ] (Supplementary Table 1). RNA probes were hybridized overnight, ligated, and then amplified using rolling circle amplification according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10× Genomics  CG000578 ,  CG000580 ,  CG000613 ). All incubations were performed using reagents provided by 10× Genomics on an XT96 PCR machine (VWR). Autofluorescence was then quenched and morphology stains added for cell segmentation, either nuclear (DAPI) (samples 812–1, 821–1, 928–1, 723–1 and 723–2) or, cytoplasmic (18S RNA, alphaSMA and vimentin protein), and membrane (ATP1A1, CD45, E-cadherin) stain cell segmentation cocktail for improved cell segmentation (samples 928–2, 897–1, 897-X, 987–1, 911–1, 1536–1, 1536–2, 459–1 and 459–2). Slides were then loaded onto the Xenium Analyser for whole-slide tissue overview scanning and region selection. Tissue regions were denoted, and the onboard cyclic decoding and imaging occurred over a 20 – 48 h period. Data were analysed on the instrument after image acquisition, performing probe deconvolution, cell segmentation, and probe graph-based clustering. Quality control, image heatmaps and run data were reviewed in the Xenium Explorer (4.1.0) software. After Xenium analysis, H&E staining was performed on Xenium slides and whole-slide scans were performed (PhenoImager HT: 20× objective, 0.5 micron resolution). Images were converted to OME. TIFFs file using QuPath v0.5.1 and imported to Xenium Explorer and aligned with tissue images.  Cell cluster identities were assigned based on overlap with gene expression signatures from PFA neoplastic and non-neoplastic subpopulations identified by single-cell and single-nuclei RNAseq [ 10 ,  14 ] and Visium spatial transcriptomics [ 13 ] using hypergeometric analysis. For each sample, neoplastic clusters were then consolidated into five categories (ciliated (CEC), transportive (TEC), mesenchymal (MEC), undifferentiated-A (UEC) and proliferative undifferentiated-A (UECprolif.) EPN cells. Per cell TEAD2 and LATS1 transcript counts for each cluster were then extracted for comparative inter-sample and inter-subpopulation analyses. Xenium spatial transcriptomic data is available at GEO ( GSE327676 ).     Statistics  Statistical analyses were performed using R, GraphPad Prism, and Excel (Microsoft) software. Kaplan–Meier survival curves were compared with log-rank tests, and p<0.05 was considered statistically significant unless otherwise stated.    Results   Cumulative loss of chromosome 6q underlies almost 50% of PFA deaths  We re-analysed data from our previously published international cohort of primary and recurrent ependymomas [ 10 ] to provide a more detailed view of the high-risk copy-number changes, focusing on chromosome 6q- (Fig.  1 ). Compared with 1q+, 6q- was relatively uncommon at first diagnosis, occurring in 4% (3/75) of tumours in isolation, and 8% (6/75) when co-occurring with 1q+. The distribution was consistent with data from a large independent cohort [ 33 ] (Fig.  1 a). The proportion of tumours with 6q- increased progressively across recurrences, affecting 34% (25/73) at the first recurrence, 47% (8/17) of the cohort by the second recurrence, and 69% (9/13) of the third and later recurrences. Both isolated 6q- and 1q+/6q- co-occurrence rose over time (Fig.  1 a). In contrast, 1q+ appeared early – affecting 48% (36/75) of cases at first recurrence and then remained relatively stable, with 100% (5/5) of 1q+ co-occurring with 6q- by third and later recurrences (Fig.  1 b).    Fig. 1   Impact of 6q loss (6q-) in late recurrence and death in PFA. Cumulative acquisition of  a  6q- and  b  1q+ in successive PFA recurrences.  c  Proportion of acquired 6q-, 1q+ or 6q-/1q+ co-occurrence in PFA tumours at time of death. Abbr: P, presentation: R1; 1st recurrence; R2, 2nd recurrence; R3+, 3rd and subsequent recurrence and autopsy combined                   Consistent with prior studies delineating the high-risk behaviour of 1q+ in EPN [ 2 ,  5 ,  25 ,  29 ,  38 ], patients with 1q+, either alone or combined with 6q-, accounted for 55% (22/40) of all deaths. However, 6q- was also strongly associated with fatal outcomes; tumours harbouring 6q- (either alone or co-occurring with 1q +) also represented 45% (18/40) of all deaths, underscoring its major contribution to mortality in this cohort (Fig.  1 c).    The  LATS1  locus is lost in both whole and partial 6q- ependymoma, and outcome is poor irrespective of extent of loss  To explore the aggressive phenotype of 6q- PFA EPN, we sought to identify the gene or genes driving the 6q- phenotype. We first examined an autopsy sample (case−1), which showed a focal region of 6q loss spanning q23.3-q25.1, covering 13.6 megabases (Fig.  2 a). Among 60 genes in this region, eight were documented tumour suppressors [ 55 ]:  TNFAIP3 ,  PERP, HECA ,  PLAGL1 ,  SASH1 ,  SHPRH ,  LATS1 , and  ZC3H12D . Of these,  LATS1  and  PLAGL1  have been previously linked to EPN. Large Tumour Suppressor Kinase 1 ( LATS1 ) is an established tumour suppressor in a broad range of human malignancies [ 55 ] and, of the eight PFA 6q- minimal region of loss tumour suppressors, has the highest incidence of loss (1.5%) in a pan cancer study of tumour drivers [ 3 ]    Fig. 2   Candidate 6q tumour suppressor genes in the aggressive PFA 6q- phenotype.  a  PFA autopsy sample (case #1) showing a 60 Mb focal loss in 6q-, spanning 60 genes, including 8 tumour suppressor genes.  b  10 of 60 PFA 6q- cases examined had partial loss of 6q all of which encompassed the LATS1 locus.  c  PFS and  d  OS for partial loss versus complete loss of 6q in PFA.  e  LATS1 transcript in PFA 6q- (n=23), PFA 6q WT (n=60), a panel of other paediatric brain tumour types and normal cerebellum (ACP, adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma (n=9); ATRT, atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumour (n=13); HGG, high-grade glioma (n=25); MED, medulloblastoma (n=36); PA, pilocytic astrocytoma (n=21); normal cerebellum (n=5)). (f) LATS1 transcript expression decrease in successive recurrences in PFA (P=presentation; R1 = 1st recurrence; R2 = 2nd recurrence; R3+= 3rd and successive recurrences)                   This PFA 6q- focal region of loss also contained tumour suppressor  PLAGL1 , however  PLAGL1  has been reported as an oncogene in the context of EPN, therefore not consistent with the proposed loss of tumour suppressor function via 6q-. Specifically,  PLAGL1  fusions, resulting in high expression of  PLAGL1  transcripts, have been identified in a novel subset of paediatric supratentorial neuro-epithelial tumours, of which a high proportion were histopathologically diagnosed as EPN [ 44 ]. Additionally, a more recent study has shown that increased  PLAGL1  transcriptional activity is a result of ZFTA fusion in a subset of supratentorial EPN [ 24 ].  To understand the importance of this region, we reviewed the DNA-methylation-derived copy-number plots for all cases of 6q- in our cohort. Of 60 cases with 6q-, 10 (16.7%) demonstrated only partial deletions. Notably, all these areas of partial deletion encompassed the focal region of 6q loss as seen in case−1 that includes that  LATS1  locus (Fig.  2 b), implicating its role as the principal gene associated with the PFA 6q- phenotype in those cases with partial 6q loss.  We next compared survival between tumours with partial versus whole 6q loss. Progression-free survival from the time of 6q- acquisition showed no significant difference between these two groups (log-rank HR = 1.6, 95% CI 0.4–4.5; 26.65 months for partial loss and 18 months for whole loss; Fig.  2 c). Both exhibited poor overall survival, with median overall survival of around 50 months in either group (Fig.  2 d).  Analysis of bulk RNA-seq data confirmed markedly reduced  LATS1  transcript expression in 6q- (n=18) compared with 6q wild-type (n=58) PFA EPN (Fold change = 1.5; 2-tailed p=2×10 –5 ),  LATS1  in 6q- PFA EPN also had the lowest expression of any brain tumour type examined (Fig.  2 e). Mirroring the increased 6q loss seen in successive recurrences of PFA (Fig.  1 a) we observed a decrease in the expression of LATS1 transcript in successive recurrences (Fig.  2 f). Unlike 6q loss however, LATS1 transcript expression was not associated with progression free survival in our bulk RNAseq cohort where samples were dichotomized to higher or lower than median  LATS1  expression for progression free survival (PFS), either in all cases (n=88), or after exclusion of cases with confounding high-risk clinical variables (1q gain, 6q loss, infants under 1 year old)(n=40).    LATS1 knock-in restores protein expression and suppresses proliferation in 6q- PFA cell lines  To identify differences in cellular proliferation between 6q- and 6q wild-type PFA EPN, we reanalysed quantified Ki-67 proliferation indices by highest high-power field count from our prior study [ 10 ]. The 6q- tumours exhibited significantly increased Ki-67 levels (6q- n=17, 6q WT n=36, 2-tailed p = 0.0005), supporting the hypothesis that the 6q- PFA EPN cells have an intrinsically more proliferative phenotype (Fig.  3 a).    Fig. 3   Impact of LATS1 loss on PFA 6q- proliferation.  a  Ki-67 positive cell count per highest high power field (HPF) in individual patient samples grouped according to (i) 6q- and (ii) 6q WT (*** p<0.0001; Student’s t-test, 2-tailed).  b  LATS1 lentiviral knock-in increases protein expression of (i) LATS1 and (ii) phospho-YAP (pYAP)(S127), (iii) pan-TEAD and (iv) DNMT1 in PFA 6q- cell line MAF-811, and associated densitometric quantification of  c  LATS1 protein knock-in,  d  pYAP,  e  pan-TEAD, and (f) DNMT1. LATS1 lentiviral knock-in blocks proliferation in PFA 6q- cell lines  g  MAF-811 and  h  MAF-928 compared to empty vector controls. (i) LATS1 knock-in blocks growth in PFA 6q- compared to 6q WT ZFTA-fused EPN and pGBM cell lines (Student’s t-tests, 1-tailed) as measured by mCherry positive cell count                   Given the association between 6q-, increased Ki-67 indices, and poor prognosis [ 5 ], we investigated whether loss of  LATS1  contributes functionally to tumour growth. We performed  LATS1  lentiviral knock-in experiments and quantified LATS1 protein expression by western blot, normalised to beta-actin. In the 6q- PFA EPN cell line, MAF-811, LATS1 protein increased significantly at 24 h post-knock-in and continued rising through 72 h (Figs.  3 b and c), remaining persistently above control levels.  Furthermore,  LATS1  restoration resulted in markedly reduced proliferation in two independent 6q- PFA EPN lines (MAF-811 and MAF-928), compared to controls (Figs.  3 g,h). Moreover, compared with other established paediatric brain tumour lines (ZFTA-fused EPNs EP1NS and MAF-1329, and paediatric GBM line SF188),  LATS1- reconstituted 6q- EPN cells displayed the most restricted growth patterns with a rapid fall in cellular proliferation, whilst the 6q wildtype lines maintained steady proliferation (Fig.  3 i).    Loss of chromosome 6q suppresses  LATS1  and activates the Hippo pathway   LATS1  is a key negative regulator of the Hippo signalling pathway originally implicated in controlling organ size, cell fate, and proliferation, through S127 phosphorylation and subsequent degradation of YAP in the cytoplasm, preventing its transit to the nucleus where it binds and activates TEAD transcription factors [ 18 ,  28 ]. It acts as a tumour suppressor in multiple malignancies, including lung, breast, gastric, hepatic, renal, colorectal, and haematologic cancers [ 17 ,  34 ] .   Hippo dysregulation exists in several other EPN variants. A rare supratentorial EPN of childhood is driven by a Hippo pathway dysregulating YAP1-fusion [ 33 ]. NF2 mutant spinal ependymomas show Hippo dysregulation through the disrupted interaction of NF2 and LATS1 [ 36 ], and similarly, loss of chromosome 22 that includes the NF2 locus potentially disrupts LATS1 activity [ 23 ,  31 ,  36 ]. In addition to the formation of EPN-like tumours following LATS1 knockdown in neural progenitors in vivo, Eder et al. also showed YAP1 activation in this model produced EPN-like tumours [ 11 ]. We therefore hypothesised that  LATS1  loss in PFA 6q- deregulates Hippo signalling via release of YAP/TEAD activity and promotes their nuclear translocation.  To test this hypothesis, we performed immunohistochemistry for YAP expression on a cohort of 75 PFA EPNs (25 6q- and 50 wild type). Both nuclear and cytoplasmic YAP expression were significantly higher in 6q- tumours (p = 0.0081 and p = 0.0010, respectively; Fig.  4 ), consistent with Hippo pathway activation in those cases with reduced LATS1. We further hypothesise that increased nuclear YAP drives TEAD expression, whereas elevated cytoplasmic YAP likely reflects reduced LATS1-mediated degradation. The functional impact of LATS1 on the Hippo pathway in PFA is indicated by increased phospho-YAP (S127) upon LATS1 knock-in in PFA 6q- cell line MAF-811 (Fig.  3 b,d).    Fig. 4   Impact of LATS1 loss on YAP expression in situ. Representative  a  nuclear and  b  cytoplasmic YAP protein expression in PFA 6q-  c  Nuclear and  d  cytoplasmic YAP score in a cohort of 75 PFA EPN                     TEAD2 expression is upregulated in 6q- PFA EPN and predicts poor survival  We next examined the involvement of TEAD transcription factors, the primary effectors of the Hippo signalling cascade, in PFA 6q-. Reanalysis of bulk RNA-seq data revealed significantly higher  TEAD2  RNA expression in 6q- (n=23) versus 6q wild-type (n=60) PFA EPNs (FC=1.63; p=2.08×10 –6 )(Fig.  5 a). Consistent with this negative correlation between 6q- and increased TEAD2 RNA, we observed increased TEAD2 expression in successive PFA recurrence (Fig.  5 b) whereas 6q is increasingly lost (Fig.  1 a). TEAD4 was also significantly higher in PFA 6q- (FC=1.47; p=0.035), whereas TEAD1 and TEAD3 were not differentially expressed. Functionally, LATS1 knock-in did not significantly change pan-TEAD protein expression (Fig.  3 b,e), consistent with TEADs role as a transcription factor in the Hippo pathway that is activated once bound to nuclear YAP. No significant endogenous degradation of TEADs was observed up to 24 h after inhibition of protein synthesis (100 mg/ml cycloheximide treatment) (right)                   To determine the relative prognostic association of TEAD1-4 gene expression, we correlated all transcripts’ gene expression values with time to progression (TTP) in 79 recurrent PFA from any presentation.  TEAD2  ranked 45th out of a total of 28,595 transcripts negatively correlated with time to progression (Fig.  5 c). Higher than median  TEAD2  target-gene expression was associated with poor survival (HR = 3.2; p = 4×10 –7 )(Fig.  5 d). Similar trends were observed for  TEAD3  (HR = 1.8; p = 0.017) and  TEAD4  (HR = 1.9; p = 0.013), where high expression correlated with worse outcomes.  The Molecular Signatures Database (MSigDB; UC San Diego and Broad Institute) includes Transcription Factor Target (TFT) genesets (n=1066) of which TEAD2 is included, but not TEADs 1, 3 or 4.  TEAD2  TFT single sample gene set enrichment (ssGSE) scores were higher in 6q- cases (n=23) versus 6q wild-type (n=60) PFA EPNs (p = 3.44×10 –4 )(Fig.  5 e). The most significantly overexpressed TEAD2 TFTs in PFA 6q- cases included DNMT1 (DNA methyltransferase 1) (p=0.0013). DNMT1 is frequently overexpressed in cancers and drives silencing of tumor suppressor gene via promoter hypermethylation [ 41 ] and silencing of differentiation genes and maintenance of a stem-like state [ 35 ]. We examined the impact of LATS1 knock-in on TEAD2 transcriptional target DNMT1 (DNA methyltransferase 1)[ 22 ], which showed decreased protein expression 3 and 4 days post-LATS1 knock-in (Fig.  3 b,f).  As above for individual gene expression, we correlated all TFT geneset enrichments with TTP in recurrent PFA (n=79), which showed TEAD2 was the 65th most negatively correlated TFT geneset enrichment of all 1066 TFTs (Fig.  5 f). Kaplan–Meier analysis confirmed that high  TEAD2  target-gene expression enrichment (ssGSEA) was associated with poor survival (n=88) (HR = 2.80; p = 3.6×10 –6 ) (Fig.  5 g).    PFA 6q- cells are sensitive to TEAD palmitoylation inhibition and PROTAC-mediated TEAD degradation  We performed dose curve analysis of pan-TEAD palmitoylation inhibitor VT017 [ 48 ] in vitro in PFA 6q- cell lines MAF-811 and MAF-928 alongside PFA 6q WT cell line DKFZ-BT232, supratentorial ZFTA::RELA fusion ependymomas EP1NS and 1329 and a panel of comparator paediatric brain tumour cell lines as previously used to further determine PFA 6q- selective effects [ 9 ]. IC-50 values of VT107, as measured by  3 H-thymidine incorporation, showed sensitivity in both PFA 6q- cell lines, showing high nanomolar sensitivity (MAF-811 = 845 nM; MAF-928 = 420 nM) (Fig.  5 h). Comparator paediatric brain tumour cell lines showed variable sensitivity to VT107, with IC-50 doses not achieved in a number of cell lines at the broad dose range tested (0.61 nM to 10μM)(Figs.  5 h). PFA 6q WT cell line DKFZ-BT232 had a higher IC-50 value (1.36 μM) than PFA 6q- cell lines, although the IC-50 revealed a relatively high sensitivity to the drug compared to non-ependymoma high-grade glioma (HGG) and medulloblastoma (MED) pediatric comparator lines. Collectively, the sensitivity of BT232 and ZFTA::RELA fusion supratentorial ependymoma cell lines in addition to PFA 6q- suggest that ependymomas subtypes are broadly dependent on TEAD activity and implicate dysregulated Hippo signaling that is already known to drive YAP-fusion supratentorial EPN [ 33 ].  Proteolysis targeted chimeras (PROTACs) are in clinical trial in the oncology setting and represent a paradigm-shifting therapeutic approach to target transcription factors with several advantages over small molecule inhibitors, with improved efficiency at lower dosing and their ability to overcome drug resistance [ 46 ]. These compounds also provide a powerful laboratory tool for selective and rapid knock-down of target proteins. We tested a recently developed pan-TEAD-targeted PROTAC degrader H122 [ 27 ] in the PFA 6q- and comparator cell line panel as described above. PFA 6q- demonstrated the lowest IC-50 values for H122 (MAF-811 = 9.8 nM; MAF-928 = 4.5 nM) (Fig.  5 i), approximately 100-fold lower than those obtained using VT107. As for VT107, H122 IC-50 s were significantly higher for non-ependymoma HGG and MED cell lines. PFA 6q WT DKFZ-BT232 had a higher IC-50 (25.1 nM) than PFA 6q- cell lines, as did ZFTA::RELA fused supratentorial ependymoma cell lines, as seen using VT107 TEAD inhibition, again suggesting an underlying Hippo pathway dysregulation in EPN as a whole. Mechanistically, H122-treated PFA 6q- cell lines showed complete degradation of TEAD protein after 4 h and endogenous TEAD degradation was not seen up to 24 h post-protein translation inhibition (100μγ/ml cycloheximide) (Fig.  5 j), confirming H122 PROTAC on target effects and also demonstrating that PFA 6q- cell lines have an intact ubiquitination degradation pathway that is critical for PROTAC efficacy.    TEAD2 is enriched in undifferentiated ependymoma cell subpopulations (UEC-A)  Building on our prior work identifying intratumoural heterogeneity in PFA EPN [ 13 ,  14 ,  16 ], we examined  TEAD2  expression within distinct neoplastic subpopulations. In earlier single-cell analyses, we defined an Undifferentiated Ependymoma Cell type (UEC) population with neural stem-like features and progenitor potential [ 13 ].  Using Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics, we measured the expression of  TEAD2  and  LATS1  in individual cells in 14 PFA tissue sections (5 PFA 6q- and 9 PFA 6q WT patient samples) (1,096,706 total cells). Subcellular resolution in situ spatial transcriptomics was performed using a panel of 480 custom probes based on previously identified cellular subpopulations in EPN [ 13 – 15 ] and other paediatric brain tumour diagnoses [ 7 ,  37 ,  57 ] (Supplementary Table 1). Cell segmentation of tissue sections was combined with corresponding custom probe expression to identify cell types using graph-based clustering. Xenium clusters were annotated by comparison of marker genes with EPN single-cell RNAseq (scRNAseq) and Visium spatial transcriptomic neoplastic and non-neoplastic cell subpopulation markers [ 13 ,  14 ] and neoplastic cells were assigned to correspond with major PFA neoplastic subpopulations: undifferentiated EPN cell UEC-A (including a proliferative UEC-A subpopulation (UEC-A prolif.)), ependymally-differentiated transportive TEC and ciliated CEC EPN cells or and mesenchymally-differentiated MEC EPN cells. Significantly higher  TEAD2  expression was seen in UEC and UEC-A proliferative subpopulations than other neoplastic subpopulations (TEC, CEC and MEC) both in PFA 6q- and PFA 6q WT (Fig.  6 e). LATS1, was collectively lower in PFA 6q- than PFA 6q WT, but did not show differential expression between UEC and other populations (Supplementary Fig. 1). Gain-of-function activity of TEAD has previously been shown to drive expansion of the neural progenitor pool [ 6 ]. Consistent with this, our data indicate that TEADs—particularly TEAD2—underlie UEC-A proliferation, supporting our hypothesis that UEC-A cells represent a proliferative progenitor population contributing to the aggressive behaviour of PFA EPN. Abbreviations: UEC, undifferentiated EPN cell; TEC, transportive EPN cell, CEC, ciliated EPN cell; MEC, mesenchymal EPN cell                      Discussion  In this study, we show that 6q- is progressively accumulated at successive recurrences and is a prognostically adverse event in PFA EPN. 6q- at any recurrence is associated with shortened survival and accounts for nearly half of deaths. Through analysis of partial versus whole chromosome 6q loss, we demonstrate that  LATS1  deletion underlies this, leading to Hippo pathway dysregulation and downstream activation of TEAD family transcription factors – particularly  TEAD2 . Preclinical testing showed PFA 6q- cell lines were sensitive to TEAD inhibition. Spatial transcriptomics further localised  TEAD2  over-expression to undifferentiated, stem-like UEC-A progenitor cells. Our findings support a model in which chromosome 6q- leads to  LATS1  inactivation, thereby releasing  YAP , enhancing  TEAD2  transcriptional activity, and this stem-like tumour-cell population. Thus, Hippo pathway dysregulation emerges as a central feature of aggressive, recurrent PFA EPN.  Unlike 1q gain, which appears at presentation and earlier relapses, 6q loss emerges later and increases steadily across recurrences, indicating distinct evolutionary pressures and complementary mechanisms of aggressiveness. This may explain why tumours harbouring both 1q+ and 6q- exhibit the poorest outcomes [ 5 ,  15 ]. Previous research has focused mainly on 1q gain, which mimics p53 suppression through MDM4 overexpression and may be targetable with 5-FU [ 15 ]. Our data extend this paradigm by identifying 6q loss as an equally important later driver of rapid progression.  The Hippo pathway has been implicated in many malignancies and regulates cancer hallmarks, many of which have already been implicated in PFA EPN, including angiogenesis, proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, inflammation and immune evasion [ 13 ,  16 ,  28 ,  51 ,  53 ]. This work aligns with work in colorectal carcinoma, where rare “revival stem cells” emerge in response to cancer therapy and are regulated by Hippo pathway components [ 12 ,  49 ]. Similarly, our data provides initial work to identify TEAD2-high UEC-A cells as potential revival-like progenitors, consistent with prior observations of oncofetal reprogramming [ 10 ,  13 ,  16 ,  43 ]. Future studies should aim to further characterise the UEC-A population and improve understanding of its role in high-risk PFA EPN as a potential therapeutic target.  Loss of  LATS1  has previously been implicated as a potential tumorigenic mechanism in supratentorial EPN. Specifically, in the context of the exploration of  YAP1 -fused supratentorial disease. Eder and colleagues described a murine model in which deletion of YAP1's negative regulators LATS1 and LATS2 kinases in NEX-Cre lineage in double conditional knockout mice caused ependymoma-like tumours [ 11 ]. This experimental evidence strongly supports our conclusion that Hippo-pathway dysregulation represents a shared oncogenic mechanism in EPN, reinforcing the rationale for developing Hippo-targeted therapies.  Clinically, our findings carry important implications. The rarity of 6q- at PFA presentation means that its significance at that time point, as in the retrospective E-HIT2000 cohort is to be interpreted cautiously [ 21 ]. However, all studies on recurrent PFA should be stratified for 6q-. It does appear that PFA ependymoma treated with surgery ± radiation may sometimes be cured or go often years before another relapse while this is not the case in 6q- ependymoma. The ability to restore  LATS1  signalling in vitro suggests that targeting YAP/TEAD interactions or the wider Hippo pathway in 6q- PFA EPN may be feasible. Moreover, the enrichment of  TEAD2  in undifferentiated UEC-A cells raises the possibility of differentiation-based therapeutic strategies.  The current therapeutic landscape for Hippo pathway modulation is encouraging. Approaches include disrupting YAP-TEAD binding, suppressing  TEAD -regulated transcription, targeting transcriptional machinery, and blocking YAP-TEAD target genes [ 20 ]. Yap et al. reported a Phase1/2 trial of the Hippo agent VT3989 in mesothelioma, a high rate of partial responses and stable disease [ 54 ]. A Phase 3 trial is planned. VT3989 is an analogue of VT107 that demonstrated PFA 6q- specific anti-proliferative activity in our study. This approach, therefore, offers near-term translational potential for PFA 6q- and possibly YAP1-fused supratentorial disease. Over 40 PROTACs are currently in oncology clinical trials, marked by the recent FDA approval of vepdegestrant for advanced or metastatic breast cancer [ 26 ]. The high sensitivity of PFA 6q- cell lines to TEAD PROTAC H122 provide rationale for further preclinical testing of this breakthrough therapeutic strategy. Given the dismal prognosis of relapsed PFA EPN with 6q-, prioritising clinical translation of these findings is essential.  Future research should map the full spectrum of Hippo pathway dysregulation in all subtypes of EPN, including upstream regulators and other YAP/TEAD targets. Pre-clinical 6q-/LATS1 models will be crucial for evaluating candidate inhibitors, but we must simultaneously and urgently consider how we translate this new biological knowledge. However, we are confident that integrating 6q status into prospective clinical trials will refine risk stratification and guide therapy in recurrent disease.  In conclusion, loss of chromosome 6q, and consequent  LATS1  deletion emerge as a key molecular driver of recurrence and poor outcome in PFA EPN, acting through Hippo pathway dysregulation and  TEAD2 -mediated proliferative programs. These insights illuminate a new biological axis of ultra-high-risk ependymoma and provide a rationale for developing Hippo-targeted therapeutic approaches for affected children.    Key points  (1) Tumour suppressor  LATS1  is in the minimal region of chromosomal loss in PFA 6q-  (2)  LATS1  deletion drives Hippo pathway dysregulation and YAP/TEAD activation.  (3) Restoring  LATS1  expression or inhibiting TEAD suppresses growth in vitro, revealing a targetable pathway. evidence_text:
KLRB1 (CD161) as a context-dependent prognostic marker in breast cancer: An exploratory analysis of CD4+ memory T cell infiltration: a retrospective multi-cohort study. The prognostic value of KLRB1 (CD161) in breast cancer is debated, and whether CD4+ memory T cell abundance modulates it is unclear. In this retrospective multi-cohort study we integrated The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma (n = 1088) and Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium (METABRIC) (n = 1980) with investigator-generated single-cell RNA-sequencing from 3 patients, public single-cell RNA-sequencing validation (GSE176078), Xenium spatial transcriptomics (19 samples) and multiplex immunofluorescence of a paired primary tumor and metastatic lymph node. Cox regression tested whether xCell-estimated CD4+ memory T cell abundance modifies the KLRB1-overall survival association. Higher KLRB1 expression was associated with favorable overall survival (TCGA hazard ratio [HR] = 0.93, P = .001; METABRIC HR = 0.82, P < .001). The CD4+ memory T cell interaction was significant under median dichotomization (TCGA P = .043; METABRIC P = .014) and after adjustment for age and tumor stage in both cohorts (TCGA P = .033; METABRIC P = .026; pooled HR 1.20, P = .0025); full adjustment for grade and subtype preserved significance in METABRIC (P = .012) but not in TCGA (P = .205). Across 3 single-cell cases KLRB1 was enriched in CD4+ memory T cells; functional profiling identified a cytotoxicity-effector T/NK signature, and TIGIT+ KLRB1+ cells showed no clear evidence of a classical exhaustion transcriptional signature. In Xenium, KLRB1+ cells proximal to CD4+ memory T cells co-upregulated TIGIT (pooled OR = 2.98) and PRF1 (OR = 1.99); multiplex immunofluorescence showed no spatial mutual exclusion. CD4+ memory T cell abundance is a hypothesis-generating candidate context modifier of KLRB1-mediated prognosis. This finding requires external validation in a subtype-stratified cohort, and the present data do not support clinical use. 1. Introduction  Breast cancer is the most common malignancy among women worldwide, with approximately 2.3 million new cases and 670,000 deaths reported in 2022. [ 1 ]  Despite advances in multimodal therapy, a substantial proportion of patients develop recurrence and distant metastasis. The integration of immunotherapy, primarily PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors combined with chemotherapy, has improved outcomes for triple-negative breast cancer, but objective response rates remain limited to 20% to 30% and durable benefit is restricted to a subset of patients. [ 2 , 3 ]  This therapeutic gap underscores the urgent need for biomarkers that capture the functional state of the tumor immune microenvironment and enable more precise patient stratification.  Within the tumor immune microenvironment, natural killer (NK) cells and T lymphocytes constitute the principal effector populations mediating antitumor immunity. [ 4 ]  Among  CD4 + subsets, memory T cells confer durable immunosurveillance, and their intratumoral abundance has been associated with favorable prognosis across multiple cancer types. [ 5 , 6 ]  The balance between effector and exhausted T cell states, governed by transcriptional programs and differentiation trajectories, [ 7 , 8 ]  is increasingly recognized as a critical determinant of clinical outcome. Regulatory T cells (Tregs), characterized by  FOXP3  expression, accumulate within tumors and suppress effector cell functions through secretion of IL-10 and TGF-β, consumption of IL-2, and direct contact-mediated inhibition via immune checkpoint receptors including  CTLA-4 ,  LAG-3 , and  TIGIT . [ 9 ]    KLRB1  encodes cluster of differentiation 161 (encoded by  KLRB1 ) ( CD161 ), a type II transmembrane C-type lectin-like receptor belonging to the NK cell receptor complex on chromosome 12p13. [ 10 , 11 ] 
 CD161  is expressed on the majority of human NK cells, NKT cells, and subsets of  CD4 + and  CD8+  T cells, including tissue-resident memory populations. [ 12 ]  Upon engagement with its ligand  CLEC2D (LLT1 ),  CD161  can deliver both co-stimulatory and co-inhibitory signals depending on cellular context. The functional complexity of this receptor-ligand axis is reflected in contradictory prognostic associations reported across cancer types. Mathewson et al. [ 13 ]  identified  CD161  to  CLEC2D  as an inhibitory checkpoint in glioma, where  KLRB1  knockout in T cells enhanced antitumor immunity in vivo. In hepatocellular carcinoma, single-cell analysis revealed that  CD161 -high  CD8+  T cells exhibited an innate-like, low-cytotoxicity phenotype associated with early relapse, [ 14 ]  illustrating the context-dependent nature of the  KLRB1 / CD161  signal. Pan-cancer analyses have confirmed that  KLRB1  expression correlates with both favorable and unfavorable prognosis depending on tumor type. [ 15 ]   In breast cancer specifically, multiple studies have reported reduced  KLRB1  expression in tumor versus normal tissue, with low expression independently predicting poor survival and altered immune infiltration patterns. [ 16 – 18 ]  Machine-learning-based immune-related gene models have further established  KLRB1  as a prognostic and immune infiltration biomarker in breast cancer. [ 17 , 18 ]  However, whether the prognostic impact of  KLRB1  in breast cancer is modified by the composition of the surrounding immune microenvironment, particularly the abundance of  CD4 + memory T cells, has not been systematically investigated.  The recent development of spatial omics technologies has opened new avenues for interrogating immune cell organization within intact tissue architecture. Xenium in situ sequencing enables subcellular-resolution detection of hundreds of targeted genes. [ 19 ]  Multiplex immunofluorescence (mIHC) provides complementary protein level spatial information, enabling quantitative analysis of cell-to-cell distances, cellular neighborhoods, and their associations with clinical variables. [ 20 , 21 ]  Single-cell profiling of breast cancer has revealed tissue-resident memory subsets associated with improved prognosis [ 22 ]  and immune ecosystems that predict treatment response, [ 23 – 25 ]  while systematic evaluation of tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes supports their prognostic value across breast cancer subtypes. [ 26 – 28 ]   In the present study, we integrated large-scale transcriptomic cohorts (The Cancer Genome Atlas Breast Invasive Carcinoma [TCGA-BRCA] and Molecular Taxonomy of Breast Cancer International Consortium [METABRIC]) with investigator-generated single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) data (three investigator-generated cases: Cases A, B, and C; human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 ( HER2 )-enriched and Luminal B-like subtypes), publicly available scRNA validation, Xenium spatial transcriptomics (19 samples), and mIHC analysis of paired primary and metastatic breast cancer samples to address 3 interconnected questions: whether  CD4 + memory T cell abundance modifies the prognostic value of  KLRB1  in breast cancer; the spatial and single-cell functional states of  KLRB1+  cells; and how  KLRB1 -related immune cell organization differs between primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes. This is a retrospective, observational, multi-cohort study.    2. Materials and methods   2.1. Study design  The study comprised 5 interconnected analytical layers. First, we performed survival analyses in the TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC cohorts to test whether  CD4 + memory T cell abundance modifies the association between  KLRB1  expression and overall survival (OS). Second, we analyzed investigator-generated scRNA-seq data from 3 breast cancer patients (Cases A, B, and C; clinicopathologic details in Methods 2.4). Third, we validated the single-cell findings in a publicly available scRNA dataset ( GSE176078 ). Fourth, we performed a cross-sample meta-analysis of 19 breast cancer samples profiled by Xenium spatial transcriptomics ( GSE311609 ). Fifth, we performed mIHC on a paired primary tumor and metastatic lymph node from 1 breast cancer patient to characterize the spatial organization of  KLRB1+ ,  FOXP3 +,  GZMB +, and CD107A + cells.    2.2. TCGA-BRCA cohort  TCGA-BRCA transcriptomic data (TPM-normalized RNA-seq) and corresponding clinical annotations were downloaded from the NCI Genomic Data Commons (GDC) Data Portal ( https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov ). Gene identifiers were converted from Entrez ID to gene symbol using clusterProfiler::bitr. Immune cell abundance was estimated using the xCell algorithm [ 29 ]  with the rnaseq = TRUE parameter, generating enrichment scores for 64 immune and stromal cell types plus 3 composite scores (ImmuneScore, StromaScore and MicroenvironmentScore), i.e. 67 features in total. OS was derived from the GDC clinical record: patients recorded as deceased were assigned an event with time equal to demographic.days_to_death; all other patients were assigned a censored observation with time equal to the longest available follow-up among all recorded diagnosis records (diagnoses.N.days_to_last_follow_up). Times were converted from days to months (÷30.4375). The analysis set was defined identically for every survival analysis reported in this manuscript (Table  1  and  Supplementary Table S1 , Supplemental Digital Content 1) as: primary tumor samples with RNA-seq expression data, successful xCell deconvolution, derivable complete OS, and non-missing  KLRB1  expression and  CD4 + memory T cell score. The resulting participant flow was: 1097 expression samples, 1096 with successful xCell deconvolution, 1096 with derivable complete OS, 1089 primary tumor samples (7 metastatic samples excluded), yielding a final analysis set of 1088 patients (544  CD4 + memory T cell low, 544 high; 150 deaths). The nomogram complete-covariate subset comprised 1073 patients (150 deaths). The same definition applied to METABRIC yielded 1980 patients (990 low, 990 high; 1143 deaths). Subgroups are defined by the median xCell  CD4 + memory T cell score within each cohort. TCGA-BRCA: 150 deaths; METABRIC: 1143 deaths. The interaction  P  value was obtained from the  KLRB1  × group term of a Cox model. The age-adjusted value adds age at diagnosis as a covariate; the age- and stage-adjusted value additionally includes tumor stage; the fully adjusted METABRIC value further includes histological grade and molecular subtype. After adjustment for tumor stage the interaction was statistically significant in both cohorts (TCGA  P  = .033; METABRIC  P  = .026; fixed-effects meta-analysis HR 1.202, 95% CI 1.067–1.355,  P  = .0025,  I  2  = 0%).       2.3. METABRIC confirmatory cohort  METABRIC microarray expression data and clinical annotations were obtained from cBioPortal ( https://www.cbioportal.org ). Duplicate genes were resolved by retaining the probe with the highest median expression. After filtering for complete survival data, 1980 patients were included. Immune cell abundance was estimated using xCell with the rnaseq = FALSE parameter appropriate for microarray data. Because xCell applied to microarray data may underestimate low-abundance cell types, the METABRIC interaction analyses should be regarded as a confirmation of the TCGA discovery rather than as a fully independent validation.    2.4. Investigator-generated scRNA-seq (three validation cases: cases A, B, and C)  scRNA-seq was performed on tumor samples from 3 breast cancer patients (Cases A, B, and C), with matched peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples additionally profiled for Cases A and C. All 3 cases were profiled using the DNBelab C4 platform (MGI/BGI). Clinicopathologically, Case C had an invasive carcinoma of no special type (NST), histologic grade III, with a maximum tumor diameter of approximately 3.0 cm; no definite lymphovascular invasion or perineural invasion was identified. The nipple, skin, base, and surgical margins were free of carcinoma; the right axillary lymph nodes (0/18) showed no metastasis; the interpectoral region showed fibrofatty tissue without tumor involvement. immunohistochemistry (IHC) revealed estrogen receptor (ER) (moderate-strong positive, 80%), progesterone receptor (PR) (strong positive, 90%), AR (moderate-strong positive, 80%),  HER2  (1+, negative), CK14 (negative), P63 (negative),  TRPS1  (positive), P120 (membranous), E-cadherin (membranous), EGFR (negative), P53 (negative, nonsense-mutant pattern), Ki-67 (40%), S-100 (nerve-negative), TOPO-IIα (positive), CKpan (positive), and CD31 (delineating vasculature), consistent with an ER+/PR+,  HER2 -negative, Luminal B-like molecular subtype. Case A had an invasive ductal carcinoma of NST, histologic grade III, tumor size 5.8 × 3.2 × 2.2 cm, with perineural invasion and lymphovascular tumor thrombi; the carcinoma involved the nipple dermis; the right axillary lymph nodes were 6/21 positive for metastasis, and 2 satellite tumor nodules (0.5–0.7 cm) were present. IHC: ER negative, PR negative, AR 2+ (~90%),  HER2  3+, P120 membranous+, E-cadherin+, CK14 negative, P63 negative,  TRPS1 +, EGFR 1+, S–100 nerve+, P53+ (missense-mutant pattern), Ki-67 ~40%;  HER2 -enriched subtype. Case B had an invasive ductal carcinoma of NST, histologic grade II to III; axillary lymph nodes 0/18 and apical lymph nodes 0/2 were negative for metastasis. IHC: ER negative, PR negative, AR 2+ (~80%),  HER2  2 + (FISH-amplified), E-cadherin 2+, P120 membranous+, EGFR 1+, SOX-10 negative, CK14 negative, P53 2+, Ki-67 ~40%;  HER2 -enriched subtype (FISH-confirmed  HER2  amplification). From Case C, 3 libraries were generated. The total cell count of each library was verified from the primary sequencing data: a  CD4 5-unsorted tumor library (14,221 cells), a  CD4 5-sorted ( CD4 5+-enriched) tumor-infiltrating library from the primary tumor (referred to as the “tumor  CD4 5” library; 11,019 cells) and a matched PBMC library (referred to as the “PBMC” library; 5311 cells), enabling joint analysis of tumor-resident and circulating immune populations. The lymphoid-compartment analyses reported below aggregate the  CD4 5-sorted tumor and PBMC libraries. After quality control and removal of low-quality cells, the  CD4 5-sorted tumor and PBMC libraries comprised 16,330 cells, of which 4567 lymphoid cells (3822 T cells and 745 NK cells) were retained for the lymphoid-compartment analyses. Cell-type annotation was performed using canonical lineage markers: CD3E/CD3D for T cells; CD8A/CD8B for  CD8+  T cells;  CD4  for  CD4 + T cells;  FOXP3 /IL2RA/CTLA4 for Tregs; interleukin 7 receptor (IL7R) for memory T cells; NKG7/GNLY/KLRF1 for NK cells.  CD4 + memory T cells were defined as T cells that were  CD4 -positive, negative for CD8A/CD8B, negative for the Treg markers  FOXP3 /IL2RA/CTLA4, and positive for IL7R; this definition was applied identically to all 3 cases.  KLRB1 + cells were defined as cells with detectable  KLRB1  expression (counts > 0). Within  KLRB1 + lymphoid cells,  TIGIT -positive and  TIGIT -negative subsets were defined for stratified analysis. Per-gene odds ratios (ORs) for  KLRB1 + versus  KLRB1 − cells and for  TIGIT + versus  TIGIT − subsets were computed using Fisher exact test; depth-adjusted (sequencing depth) ORs were estimated using a logistic regression model adjusting for log10(total unique molecular identifier [UMIs]) per cell, identical to the main analyses described above. For Cases A and B, the same library preparation and quality control pipelines were applied. Data from the 3 cases were analyzed separately (per-case differential expression and OR estimation) and then summarized for cross-case concordance; no pooled integration of raw counts across cases was performed. Paired  CD4 5-sorted and  CD4 5-unsorted tumor libraries were generated for each of the 3 cases; matched PBMC libraries were additionally generated for Cases A and C, whereas Case B had no matched PBMC library. Across the 3 cases this yielded 8 libraries in total (three  CD4 5-sorted, 3  CD4 5-unsorted, and 2 PBMC libraries). For Cases A and B the paired tumor libraries were analyzed together, as the primary analysis focused on intratumoral T cell states.    2.5. Public scRNA validation ( GSE176078 )  The publicly available breast cancer scRNA-seq dataset  GSE176078  (10x Genomics) was used as an independent validation cohort. [ 30 ] 
 KLRB1 + cell definition and functional gene analysis followed the same principles as for the investigator-generated data; cell-type annotation was taken from the annotation supplied with  GSE176078 .    2.6. Xenium spatial transcriptomics  Nineteen breast cancer samples profiled by Xenium In Situ gene expression (10x Genomics) were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus (accession  GSE311609 ). [ 19 , 31 , 32 ]  For each sample, gene expression counts and spatial coordinates were read using scanpy.  KLRB1 + cells were defined as cells with detectable  KLRB1  expression.  CD4 + memory T cells were defined as cells simultaneously positive for  CD4 , CD3E, and IL7R. Because some effector memory T cells may express low levels of IL7R, this definition may preferentially capture central memory  CD4  + T cells. A  KLRB1  + cell that is itself a  CD4  + memory T cell has a distance of zero to the nearest  CD4  + memory T cell and would therefore be classified as proximal irrespective of its spatial context; in the primary analysis the distance from each  KLRB1  + cell to the nearest  CD4  + memory T cell was therefore computed with the cell itself excluded, using the second-nearest  CD4  + memory T cell for cells that were themselves  CD4  + memory T cells. The complete 19-sample analysis performed with the cell included is reported as a sensitivity analysis.  KLRB1  + cells within 30 µm were classified as proximal; those beyond 50 µm were classified as distal. After random downsampling of the distal group to at most the proximal cell count (all distal cells are used when they are fewer than the proximal cells), positivity rates of  TIGIT , PRF1, FCGR3A, LAG3, and HAVCR2 were compared between proximal and distal  KLRB1  + cells using Fisher exact test. Cross-sample meta-analysis was performed using a DerSimonian-Laird random-effects model on log(OR) effect sizes, pooled across samples in which the gene was detectable; the pooled effect sizes reported in the text are back-transformed to ORs for interpretability.    2.7. mIHC and spatial analysis  Formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue blocks of a primary breast tumor and its paired metastatic axillary lymph node were obtained from 1 female patient who underwent surgical resection at the Affiliated Taizhou People’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University. Four-marker Opal multiplex fluorescence IHC was performed using the following primary antibodies: anti- KLRB1  (clone HP-3G10, 1:200), anti- FOXP3  (clone 236A/E7, 1:100), anti- GZMB  (clone GB11, 1:500), and anti-CD107A (clone H4A3, 1:200). DAPI was used for nuclear counterstaining. Whole-slide scanning was performed on a Vectra Polaris automated quantitative pathology imaging system at 20 × magnification. Cell detection and classification were performed in QuPath, and the centroid coordinates of each classified cell were exported. For each pairwise combination, the observed statistic was the mean nearest-neighbor Euclidean distance from each source cell to the nearest target cell. Two null models that preserve the marginal distribution of the target cells were used, each with 1000 permutations: (i) complete spatial randomness (CSR), in which the target cells were placed uniformly at random within the convex hull of all detected cells; and (ii) a toroidal-shift, in which the target point pattern was translated by a random vector with wrap-around, thereby preserving the internal clustering of the target cells while breaking any source–target association. A two-sided permutation  P  value was computed as twice the smaller tail proportion. The effect size was defined as the ratio of the observed mean distance to the mean of the null distribution, where 1.0 denotes no spatial association, values > 1 mutual exclusion, and values < 1 co-localization.    2.8. Statistical analysis  All statistical analyses were performed in R version 4.5.3 and Python (scanpy 1.12.4). Continuous variables are presented as median with range or mean with standard deviation. Cox proportional hazards regression results are reported as hazard ratios [HRs] with 95% confidence interval (CIs). To further control for potential confounding, we fitted Cox models with progressive adjustment for clinical covariates (age at diagnosis, tumor stage [early vs late], histological grade [grade 1–2 vs grade 3] and molecular subtype [Prediction Analysis of Microarray 50/Claudin-low]) where available in each cohort; cases with missing covariate values were excluded from the corresponding adjusted model. Fixed-effects meta-analysis of the age- and stage-adjusted interaction across the 2 cohorts was performed on the log HR scale. This study is reported in accordance with the STROBE statement for observational studies. Unit of inference for single-cell analyses: all single-cell comparisons were performed between cells within an individual case; cells from different patients were never pooled into a single test. Results are therefore reported as per-case (i.e. patient-level) estimates, and the evidence for generalisability is the directional concordance of these estimates across the 3 cases. Depth-adjusted ORs were estimated using logistic regression with log10 UMI per cell as a covariate. Between-study heterogeneity in meta-analysis was quantified using the I 2  statistic. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) was applied to control for multiple hypothesis testing where applicable. All hypothesis tests were two-sided. Statistical significance was defined as  P  < .05.    2.9. Data availability TCGA-BRCA and METABRIC data are publicly available from the NCI GDC and cBioPortal, respectively. Xenium data are publicly available from Gene Expression Omnibus under accession number  GSE311609 . The investigator-generated scRNA-seq datasets (Cases A, B and C;  CD4 5-sorted and  CD4 5-unsorted tumor libraries, and matched PBMC libraries where applicable) are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request. All custom scripts used for the data analyses reported in the manuscript are provided as Supplementary Code S1–S4; the numerical supplementary tables are provided as  Supplementary Tables S1–S6 , Supplemental Digital Content 1 (each table in its own Word file, with its table title) and, in machine-readable form, as Supplementary Data (one Excel workbook). Purely figure-production and manuscript-assembly utilities are not included.

evidence_text:
GxP-Ready Single-Cell RNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics End-to-End Pipeline for Clinical Research. Single-cell/nucleus RNA-sequencing and Spatial Transcriptomics are powerful tools for investigating cellular heterogeneity and tissue architecture that have deepened our disease understanding. Their broader adoption in clinical and regulated settings, however, is hindered by regulatory requirements related to data integrity, regulatory compliance, reproducibility, and scalability. To address this gap, we developed NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)-a modular, GxP-ready end-to-end computational pipeline that combines established single-cell workflows with a new Nextflow pipeline for Spatial Transcriptomics. NNclinSSOAP transforms RNA sequencing and Xenium spatial data into integrated, annotated single-cell objects and spatially resolved tissue maps. Designed to support mechanistic studies and clinical endpoint generation, it enables traceable and reproducible processing of large-scale datasets, scalable for use in HPC environments. Here, we provide a step-by-step demo case for using NNclinSSOAP that can be executed within 1.5 h on a standard laptop. All code and data are available open-source. Introduction  Single-cell/single-nucleus RNA sequencing (sc/snRNA-seq) has revolutionized biological research by enabling the study of gene expression at the resolution of individual cells and nuclei. The technology allows for the identification of cell types, the characterization of cellular heterogeneity within tissues, underlying cell–cell communication, and the understanding of complex biological processes at an unprecedented level of detail [ 1 ]. This granularity can uncover rare cell populations, specific gene expression profiles, and dynamic changes over time [ 2 ]. However, it inherently lacks spatial [ 3 ] information, which is critical for understanding the tissue architecture and the local microenvironment in which the cells reside [ 4 ]. Conversely, Spatial Transcriptomics retains high-resolution spatial information but often lacks the single-cell resolution necessary to discern the complexity of cellular interactions and the interplay of different cell types within tissues [ 5 ].  The multimodal omics approach of combining scRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics addresses their respective limitations and provides a more comprehensive overview of cellular mechanisms in tissue contexts. This enables cellular identity and spatial organization to be established concurrently, which can aid in revealing the mechanisms of action of drugs and understanding disease pathology [ 6 – 8 ].  The use of these technologies and the large data handling requirements that come with them pose challenges for use in clinical settings. Ideally, such data need to be stored and handled in a Good Experimental Practice (GxP)-compliant way and compute resources need to be large enough to handle the data volumes.  This paper addresses these critical challenges, describing the implementation and usage instructions for NNclinSSOAP (Novo Nordisk Clinical Single-cell Spatial Omics Analytical Pipeline)—a GxP-ready pipeline for running sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics together. Our approach ensures data integrity and facilitates the translation of findings into robust and reliable conclusions for downstream applications, contributing to the standardization and quality control necessary for wider application of sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics in regulated environments and clinical trial settings. Unlike applications aimed primarily at interactive exploration, NNclinSSOAP is designed as an open-source, configurable pipeline that users can adapt to their own study designs, analysis needs, and compute environments.    Pipeline Overview  The development of this paper was motivated by the need for a combined sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Transcriptomics workflow in a clinical research and trial endpoint analysis context. While single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics technologies have become widely used for tissue and disease understanding for hypothesis generation, their application in regulated environments such as clinical trials presents specific challenges related to GxP requirements. Existing workflows, although effective in research settings, often do not address these requirements in a systematic way.  To meet these needs, we designed an end-to-end pipeline that integrates established methods and best practices from the broader community, with adaptations that ensure GxP-readiness and scalability. It was developed to ingest, process, and analyze sc/snRNA-seq and spatial data to generate clinical endpoints and run predefined analysis as per trial analysis plans, while providing a transparent and auditable framework suitable for clinical studies. Because of the number of samples set to be collected from multiple omics modalities, it was clear that the workflow would need to handle large data volumes and support execution in a high-performance computing (HPC) environment. To address these points, we adopted a modular, containerized architecture, enabling compliant storage and processing environments to be connected to the NNclinSSOAP pipeline.  The development process was iterative and collaborative, involving and building on cross-departmental expertise in computational biology, cloud engineering, statistics, and regulatory science. To address diverse data types and evolving analytical requirements, NNclinSSOAP was designed in a modular fashion that allows for straightforward adaptation to new datasets, data modalities, and requirements, providing flexibility and scalability for future research requirements and analyses. It is composed of 3 main components, connected as illustrated in Fig.  1  and described below:    1.  sc/snRNA-seq workflow: Handles the preprocessing, alignment, and quantification of single-nucleus RNA-seq data, leveraging nf-core/scrnaseq [ 9 ] for standardized and scalable data processing.    2.  R library/scripts: Enables advanced postprocessing, quality control, annotation, and statistical analyses of the output from the sc/snRNA-seq pipelines, ensuring robust downstream interpretation.    3.  SpatialXenium: A new Nextflow pipeline developed by us, designed to analyze multimodal data from the Spatial Transcriptomics platform Xenium [ 10 ], and optimized to run on HPCs ensuring efficient handling of large datasets. It ingests spatially resolved gene expression data and performs quality control, normalization, clustering, and spatial niche construction. The pipeline outputs processed Seurat objects (RDS), cluster/niche compositions, top marker genes, and visualizations (Principal Component Analysis [PCA], Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection [UMAP], and spatial plots). Optionally, it performs label transfer, adding cell-type annotation to the visualizations. The submodules that make up SpatialXenium are described in further detail in Box  1 .      Fig. 1.
