GxP-readiness  In this manuscript, GxP-readiness refers to the ability of a computational workflow to be deployed within a regulated clinical-research environment in a way that supports data integrity, traceability, reproducibility, auditability, and controlled change management. The term does not imply that the pipeline alone makes an analysis fully GxP compliant. Rather, NNclinSSOAP provides pipeline-level controls that can be combined with an institution’s validated infrastructure, standard operating procedures, access controls, and documentation practices. Relevant expectations for clinical computerized systems and analysis planning include principles described in ICH E6(R3) [ 11 ], ICH E9 [ 12 ], and FDA 21 CFR Part 11 [ 13 ].  NNclinSSOAP implements these pipeline-level controls through a modular architecture, containerized execution environments, and automatic provenance capture. The whirl package provides the functionality of executing scripts in batch and simultaneously getting a log from the individual execution [ 14 ]. Nextflow, an open-source workflow management system [ 15 ], allows each workflow step to be run as a specified module with captured parameters and process metadata, while containers help control software versions and dependencies. The entire workflow is documented automatically in BioCompute Objects (BCOs). They document the intended purpose, inputs, software and version identity, parameter settings, execution details, provenance, and output locations of an analysis, providing a standardized record that can be reviewed, repeated, and archived [ 16 , 17 ]. BioCompute is an FDA-supported standard for regulatory submissions, and can be used during regulated activities and communication with the agency [ 18 ].  In clinical use, the GxP-ready pipeline is intended to be executed after the analysis has been specified in the clinical study analysis plan. Input data, configuration files, and output objects are treated as controlled analysis artifacts. Sample metadata and QC thresholds are defined before execution where possible, the run is executed in a validated or otherwise qualified compute environment, and generated reports, logs, BCOs, and Seurat objects are retained as evidence of what was run.  In our implementation, clinical data storage and access are handled by a compliant Amazon Web Services (AWS) storage service with separate input and output locations and role-based access. For data processing, analyses were performed within a dedicated, GxP-validated compute environment developed in-house as part of the Novo Nordisk secure analytics platform. This environment operates within a cloud-based infrastructure to provide both scalability and regulatory compliance throughout the data life cycle. The flow of inputs and outputs and the environments used is shown in Fig.  1 . Other institutions can reuse the open-source code, containers, and provenance mechanisms that NNclinSSOAP provides, connecting the workflow to their own validated compute, storage, access-control, retention, audit-trail, and electronic-signature processes.  The scope of readiness is therefore layered. Elements that transfer directly with the pipeline include modular workflow definitions, container manifests, configurable analysis parameters, BCO generation, execution logs, and standard outputs for review. Elements that remain institution-specific include formal software validation or verification, training, role-based review and approval of BCOs, controlled versioning and change management of the validated pipeline, secure data retention, audit trails, and any electronic-signature practices. This distinction is important because BioCompute primarily defines what is documented. It does not replace local validation, governance, or standard operating procedures required for full GxP compliance.  Within the pipeline, GxP-readiness is also reflected in how analysis decisions are exposed rather than hidden. QC filters and label-transfer probability thresholds are explicit user-configurable parameters. Cells failing QC are excluded from downstream analysis according to documented thresholds, and low-probability labels are not silently converted into confident cell types. Instead, they are flagged as “Ambiguous” in the labeled Seurat metadata and visualizations and are accompanied by prediction files. This allows downstream users and reviewers to distinguish confident annotations from those requiring caution or manual review.    Applications  NNclinSSOAP was specifically developed for clinical trials incorporating transcriptomics as study endpoints, including sc/snRNA-seq and Spatial Xenium. As a pioneering framework in the pharmaceutical industry, particularly for cardiometabolic diseases, NNclinSSOAP has already been used in 2 mechanism-of-action trials. The first trial, focused on Alzheimer’s disease, incorporated scRNA-seq data as a primary endpoint [ 19 ], and therefore utilized only Procedure 1, which is tailored for single-cell transcriptomics. In contrast, the second trial, a clinical study in kidney disease [ 20 , 21 ], employed both Procedures 1 and 2 as it included both snRNA-seq and Xenium Spatial Transcriptomics data.  By enabling rapid and GxP-aligned data processing, this workflow sets a new standard for transcriptomic analysis in clinical trials. Looking ahead, it is broadly applicable to trials in other therapeutic areas, provided that compatible input data are available. Thanks to Nextflow’s modular architecture, the workflow can be easily adapted to accommodate additional analytical modules in the future.  Notably, the SpatialXenium Nextflow pipeline described in this paper is publicly available as part of the repository and can be integrated into new or existing Nextflow workflows, independently of the broader workflow described in the paper.    Comparison to other methods  There are numerous tools and packages available to facilitate sc/snRNA Transcriptomics data preprocessing [ 22 ]. For sc/snRNA-seq, we used the established nf-core pipeline scrnaseq as part of Procedure 1. Beyond the initial preprocessing steps, downstream processing and analysis of sc/snRNA-seq data commonly leverage widely used packages such as Seurat [ 23 ] that we use as part of our R library. Our SpatialXenium pipeline is wrapped around the Seurat suite relevant for Spatial Transcriptomics data QC, preprocessing, and analytics.  Integrated platforms for combining single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics exist [ 24 ], but not as workflows aligned with GxP requirements. The purpose of this section is to contextualize NNclinSSOAP rather than to provide a formal benchmarking study. NNclinSSOAP builds on established community methods and combines them into a documented, containerized, and provenance-aware workflow for regulated clinical research settings. The points below therefore focus on workflow structure, traceability, reproducibility, and deployment considerations. Six main features make NNclinSSOAP different to other methods:    1.  Modularity. NNclinSSOAP not only makes it possible to run the underlying sc/snRNA-seq and SpatialXenium workflows separately, but the workflows themselves build on Nextflow modules. This simplifies both using the workflows and adapting them to future needs as well as making them scalable, a key factor in data heavy settings.    2.  GxP-readiness. Using Nextflow for building our workflows enables NNclinSSOAP to be both scalable and reproducible. Combined with BCO-based provenance capture, this supports selected GxP-relevant expectations, particularly traceability, reproducibility, and reviewability. It allows users to connect to a compute environment of choice, without compromising reproducibility, enabling analysis of data volumes at a much greater scale than in the demo case described in this paper. Full GxP compliance ultimately depends on deployment within an appropriate governed environment.    3.  The SpatialXenium pipeline. There is a publicly available pipeline, nf-core/spatialxe, currently under development. It is a flexible image- and coordinate-based reanalysis framework, focused on controlling and improving Xenium data quality through multiple segmentation and spatial-data methods. SpatialXenium differs from this, instead focusing on postprocessing and analysis of Xenium data. It provides users a fully specified, protocol-locked, and easily reproducible end-to-end pipeline, implementing Spatial Transcriptomics analysis from Seurat for Xenium data.    4.  We provide an R library capable of processing outputs generated by nf-core/scrnaseq, supporting standard Seurat workflows and downstream annotation. These scripts offer flexibility, incorporating tools such as Harmony [ 25 ] and RPCA [ 26 ] for multisample integration. For cell-type annotation, automated approaches like Azimuth [ 27 ] or SingleR [ 28 ] are supported, and user-defined reference datasets can be added. For differential treatment effect analysis, we use a pseudobulk [ 29 ] approach by aggregating counts per sample and cell type, followed by statistical assessment using edgeR [ 30 ], which enables robust testing of group-level differences while accounting for biological variability. Alternatively, other statistical methods can be integrated as needed. An overview of this workflow is illustrated in Fig.  1 .    5.  By leveraging the whirl package [ 14 ] to execute the R library, the pipeline produces a BCO along with multiple log files—one corresponding to each R script. The package offers the flexibility to modify certain domains within the BCO and to select specific scripts to run as needed.    6.  The R environment required for running these procedures is provided as a Docker container, ensuring that all necessary packages and dependencies are included and eliminating compatibility issues for the user. This approach allows the entire environment to be reliably loaded and the workflow to be executed as intended. However, one limitation is that package versions within the container may become outdated as new releases are made. Users also have the flexibility to set up and use their own custom environments if preferred.       Experimental Design   Expertise needed for implementation and interpretation  NNclinSSOAP was developed to be used by computational biologists, producing results (e.g., tables and figures) that can be interpreted and understood by medical or biological experts without a data science background. For users following the procedures step-by-step, no expertise is needed and none of the topics below need to be considered. However, some familiarity with single-cell transcriptomics and relevant training in statistical analysis of high-dimensional omics data and running analytics scripts is advisable for a smooth experience and ability to understand the outputs scientifically.  If the workflow outlined in this paper is adapted to another dataset different from the demo, carefully consider the points below. It is also recommended to read the extensive information and instructions provided in the code repository  README.md  and .md files in  /docs . For this, a broad understanding of R, Nextflow, cloud computing, containerization, and single-cell transcriptomics is needed.    Sampling strategy-dependent analysis  The datasets used in Procedure 2 contain a single sample each, one with healthy kidney tissue and the other with cancerous kidney tissue. This case facilitates analysis from the perspective of seeing differences in cell types and gene expression. Depending on a dataset’s sampling strategy, experimental design, and analysis plans, as often preregistered in a clinical trial setting, other relevant analyses and visualizations are possible, e.g., mitochondrial genes, cell cycle genes, biological sex-related genes, batch effect contribution from metadata, etc. For samples taken from the same subject at multiple time points (longitudinal data), it is possible to analyze changes over time. For samples taken at a single time point for multiple subjects (cross-sectional data), it is possible to analyze the homo-/heterogeneity within a population. Combining these 2 strategies creates a clinical trial scenario where NNclinSSOAP can be used to analyze subjects’ tissue characteristics over time as a response to treatment, comparing to a placebo group or among groups at a single time point for disease understanding.    Optional settings and configurations  Beyond the default settings and basic configurations required to run the demo case in the “Methods” section, NNclinSSOAP can be customized through various command line flags and configuration files. Figure  2  provides a high-level overview of these options.  For the sc/snRNA-seq workflow, users can customize the metadata and configuration files to use with their own data, according to the nf-core/scrnaseq documentation:  https://nf-co.re/scrnaseq/4.0.0/docs/usage/ . For improved version control and streamlined collaboration, it is highly recommended to maintain a dedicated Git repository containing all related metadata and configuration files.  Once the nf-core/scrnaseq pipeline has completed, NNclinSSOAP provides users with tools to further analyze and explore their data. Specifically, 3 main R scripts are included for downstream analysis (see Fig.  3 ), each designed with flexibility in both parameters and methods. To customize or modify the pipeline execution, users can edit the associated config file  preprocessing_workflow.yml . These options provide users with extensive flexibility for preprocessing, integrating, and annotating single-cell data within the NNclinSSOAP framework. Note that the RPCA integration method is computationally intensive and may not be suitable for local execution.    Fig. 3.   Summary of sc/snRNA-seq data analysis workflow and results. To load their own data into the pipeline, users must modify the  configs/read_samples.txt  file, ensuring it accurately lists each sample along with its corresponding metadata. Column names as well as visit and treatment arm values can be set from  configs/preprocessing_workflow.yml . All columns are intended to populate the Seurat object’s metadata, but if your dataset lacks certain variables (arm and visit), populate them with an NA and scripts 1 ( preprocessing_workflow.R ) and 2 ( cell_annotation.R ) will still function, allowing you to generate an integrated and annotated Seurat object.  Script 3 ( de_analysis.R ), designed for differential gene expression analysis in clinical settings to assess treatment response, specifically calculates treatment effects, which assumes the data are longitudinal, with 2 time points (a baseline and follow-up visit) and 2 distinct treatment arms (e.g., drug A and placebo), as is the case in the demo data (see Fig.  3 ). Since the pipeline is run using the whirl wrapper, users can also adjust the  whirl/_whirl_preprocessing.yml  and  whirl/_whirl_analysis.yml  config files to edit BCO domains or exclude scripts, such as  de_analysis.R , from execution as needed.  For SpatialXenium, the genes shown in the UMAP and spatial feature plots are read from  assets/genes.txt  in the Spatial Transcriptomics workflow. By default, this file contains the genes needed to reproduce our results on the demo case data. Users should adapt this file if using other datasets, to reflect their genes of interest. Multiple command line options control which cells and genes are included in the UMAP and spatial feature plots, and how strict the filtering is.    Quality control  QC thresholds should be reviewed in the context of each dataset and, where applicable, defined before downstream biological or clinical interpretation. For Xenium data, the relationship between read counts, gene detection, and QV score provides a practical check of assay quality (see Fig.  4 ). A high-quality dataset is expected to retain most informative cells and genes after filtering, with low-quality or control-probe-rich observations limited to a minority of the data. In contrast, a problematic dataset may show a large fraction of observations with low read counts, low QV scores, unusually high read-count outliers, or high control-probe proportions. The selected thresholds are captured in configuration files and execution outputs (see Fig.  2 ), supporting reproducibility and review of the filtering decisions.    Fig. 4. Seurat Spatial Transcriptomics visualization options  The tissue visualizations overlaid with gene expression and cell types generated from running SpatialXenium utilize the Seurat v5 package’s functions  ImageDimPlot() and  ImageFeaturePlot() . These offer a wide range of options beyond what is covered by default in SpatialXenium, enabling extensive control over plot aesthetics and content, including color scales, transparency, cell border properties, molecule overlays, coexpression blending for pairs of genes and grouping cell types. For advanced users wanting to tailor SpatialXenium visualizations to their specific biological questions,  ImageDimPlot()  is called from  label_transfers.r  and  ImageFeaturePlot()  is called from  plot_features.r . We strongly recommend familiarity with R, Seurat, and Nextflow for doing this, as making changes may result in errors downstream. From a development and maintenance point of view, the open-source strategy invites users to contribute to the project as well as report any issues they encounter. Expected Results  The result of following both procedures is a transformation of raw sc/snRNA-seq data into an integrated and annotated Seurat object, and raw Xenium data into a spatially resolved cell object and map. This can aid in answering clinical questions, giving the user a deeper understanding of the analyzed tissues both at a cellular expression and a structural level, as is the case in the demo case data in this paper, highlighting differences between healthy and cancer kidney tissue.  When the procedures are executed with the supplied demo data using the specified software versions, parameters and settings, deterministic tables and files are expected to be reproducible. Stochastic visualization steps such as UMAP may show minor layout differences while preserving the same biological topology and interpretation. If the paper is followed using a personal dataset, the same types of outputs are expected, but results will differ according to the input data.   Sc/snRNA-seq (procedure 1)  Executing the sc/snRNA-seq workflow (Procedure 1, step 2) generates an nf-core results folder. The demo case dataset has been run with the cellranger aligner [ 31 ], so the results are the standard cellranger outputs. The special addition is the BCO object that has been generated since the plugin is included when running the nextflow pipeline.  In the second part of the workflow (Procedure 1, steps 4 and 5), each script produces a variety of plots and output files, which are organized into dedicated folders—see Box  2  for a summary of the results file structure.    •  Quality Control (QC): QC plots document the standard Seurat workflow, starting from reading the counts matrix and progressing through to the creation of the final Seurat object (see Fig.  3 A to D). A separate folder is generated for each sample’s QC outputs, while the integrated Seurat object is stored in the parent directory.    •  Cell Annotation: This step generates visualizations such as UMAPs displaying annotated clusters and violin plot displaying the annotation scores, along with an updated Seurat object that contains cell type assignments (see Fig.  3 E and F).    •  Differential Expression analysis: For each cell type, the pipeline outputs a normalized counts CSV file, a CSV file with differential expression results, and a volcano and line plot summarizing key findings (see Fig.  3 G and H).      Box 2.   Example file structure from Procedure 1.5   
     
     SpatialXenium (procedure 2)  Executing the SpatialXenium workflow (Procedure 2, step 4) produces several key outputs that can be used for clinical interpretation of the tissues analyzed, shown in Fig.  4 . By using Nextflow, reports covering errors, timing and resource usage have automatically been created. An example results file structure is shown in Box  3 . To aid with technical and clinical interpretation, key outputs from Quality Control (QC), gene expression and cell type analysis are described in further detail below:    •  Quality Control: The QC plots (see Fig.  4 A and B) summarize how many genes and reads are captured per cell and how these values are distributed across the dataset. This allows users to identify low-quality cells, technical outliers, or regions with suboptimal capture efficiency before drawing any biological or clinical conclusion, ensuring that downstream patterns (e.g. “immune poor” areas) are not artifacts of poor data quality.    •  Gene Expression: The gene expression visualizations (see Fig.  4 C and D) show how the selected markers from  assets/genes.txt  are distributed both in UMAP space and across the tissue. Clinically, these plots help confirm that canonical markers (for example, tumor, immune, or stromal genes) are expressed in the expected tissue compartments and spatial niches, supporting interpretations such as tumor–stroma interactions, immune infiltration patterns, or localization of specific disease-relevant pathways.    •  Cell Type: The cell-type plots (see Fig.  4 E and F) resulting from the label transfer display the predicted cell types in UMAP space projected back onto the tissue, with cells below the chosen probability threshold set to “Ambiguous”. This makes it clear which assignments are robust enough to support biological or clinical interpretation, which should be treated with caution. In a clinical context, these maps can be used to explore how specific cell types (e.g., cytotoxic T cells, fibroblasts, and endothelial cells) are spatially organized within lesions, margins, or normal tissue, and how this architecture might relate to disease severity or therapeutic response.      Box 3.   Example file structure. Full sample file structure only shown for sample 1 for simplicity.   
     
      Conclusion  NNclinSSOAP offers a GxP-ready framework for scalable processing and analysis of single-cell and Spatial Transcriptomics data for clinical research and trials. Its modular design and automated provenance capture ensure transparent, reproducible, auditable, and fully traceable analyses suitable for regulated environments, e.g., clinical trials. Together, these features provide a practical, unique, and extensible foundation for deploying multimodal transcriptomics across mechanistic studies and clinical trials. Spatial Mapping of the Precancer-to-Cancer Transition in Breast and Prostate. Breast and prostate cancers are both hormone-driven adenocarcinomas that undergo analogous invasion programs. Using lightsheet microscopy on intact tumors, we identified transitional junctions between precancerous and invasive regions. We then developed a multimodal serial-section workflow integrating volumetric reconstruction with spatial transcriptomics. Analysis of 319 spatial assays from 51 cases revealed gene expression features and novel structural insights defining the shift from precancer to invasive disease. In breast cancer, loss of MGP and PLAT was associated with invasive transition and promoted tumorigenesis in functional assays. In prostate cancer, GDF15, ALDH1A3, ANPEP, and FASN were upregulated along invasive progression, and their knockdown in PC-3 cells suppressed proliferation and migration. Enrichment of tumor-associated macrophages (SPP1+ and MS4A6A+) along non-triple-negative breast cancer breast cancer transitions highlights immune involvement as a potential driver of invasiveness.

Significance

Our method of defining precise spatial locations of invasive transition allows for the direct interrogation of transition drivers, presenting new therapeutic targets for the two most prevalent cancers and providing a framework for studying spatially defined mechanisms of tumor progression. See related commentary by Jing and Li, p. 1720. Although they originate in distinct organs, there are notable similarities in their development, progression, and underlying biological mechanisms ( Fig. 1A ; ref. 1 ). Both cancers rely on steroid hormones for growth and development, leading to similar therapeutic strategies targeting hormone signaling ( 2 – 4 ). They also share underlying hereditary genetic mechanisms for cancer initiation, such as alterations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 ( 5 , 6 ), and morphologic similarities, particularly in the organization of their epithelial structures. Both tissues are composed of glandular structures with two primary cell layers, an inner luminal cell layer and an outer basal cell layer, and are responsible for secretory functions (production of milk in the breast and prostatic fluid in the prostate; refs. 7 , 8 ). Figure 1. 3D spatial omic cohort for epithelial transition in breast and prostate cancers. A, Similarities between breast and prostate cancers in terms of sex hormone regulation, genetic predisposition, developmental processes, tissue architecture, physiologic functions, and disease progression timelines. B, Composition of the breast-and-prostate cancer transition cohort analyzed in this study, encompassing stacked 3D and native 3D and 2D cohorts. Left, breakdown of each cohort. Right, assay and case counts for each assay. Stacked 3D cohort: samples with serial sections reconstructed into 3D tumor volumes. This cohort utilizes Xenium, Visium HD, Visium, CosMx, CODEX, and H&E imaging. Native 3D cohort: samples processed with lightsheet microscopy to capture intact 3D structures. 2D cohort: individual sample sections without serial sections. These tissues also share a similar path to tumorigenesis, in which carcinoma typically arises from luminal cells. The surrounding basal layer remains intact during early precancer states, those being ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) in the breast and high-grade prostatic intraepithelial neoplasia (HGPIN) in the prostate ( 9 , 10 ). Luminal cells in both cancers also typically express hormone receptors, such as estrogen receptor (ER) and progesterone receptor (PR) in the breast and androgen receptor (AR) in the prostate. During the transition from precancer to malignancy in both tumor types, the basal cell layer is broken, and neoplastic cells spread into the surrounding environment ( 11 , 12 ). As such, precancerous lesions often have an attenuated basal layer, indicating progression toward loss of this barrier. Additionally, DCIS and HGPIN can both display similar epithelial cell patterns, such as cribriform architecture ( 13 ). Despite the clinical importance of tumor progression, the spatial and molecular dynamics of these transitions, particularly in breast and prostate cancers, remain poorly understood. This is, in part, due to the inability of conventional two-dimensional (2D) single-modality approaches to capture the full complexity of tumor topology and tumor–microenvironment interactions in situ . In this study, we developed a new volumetric approach that combines native three-dimensional (3D) and vertically reconstructed 2D data modalities to investigate malignant transition in breast and prostate tissues. We first imaged 14 tissue blocks from four cases with 3D lightsheet microscopy, providing high-resolution 3D immunofluorescence (IF) data for tissue blocks in their entirety. We report differences between the 3D morphologies of precancerous lesions and invasive carcinoma in both cancer types. To investigate the molecular signatures associated with these transitions, we developed a multimodal 3D serial sectioning approach, combining spatial transcriptomics (ST), multiplex imaging, and histologic staining. We assembled a cohort of 319 assays spanning 51 cases, nine of which were serially sectioned, and imaged with a variety of spatial data types ( Fig. 1B ; Supplementary Tables S1–S3). Additionally, we supplemented our 3D serial section cohort with 69 nonserial sections of Xenium, CosMx, CODEX, Visium, and Visium HD data. This 3D serial section approach enables reconstruction of 3D tissue structures from 2D sections, providing a unified framework for analyzing molecular and morphologic changes across 3D space. By leveraging Xenium, CosMx, Visium, Visium HD, and CODEX platforms, we interweave data at varying resolutions and biomarker coverage depth, overcoming important limitations inherent to single-platform analyses. Using this new approach, we reveal mechanisms underlying the progression of DCIS to intraductal carcinoma (IDC) in breast cancer and the transition from normal glands to Gleason pattern 3 (GP3) in prostate cancer. We have identified differentially expressed genes (DEG), spatial relationships, and tumor microenvironment (TME) features integral to epithelial cell state transitions. Furthermore, we have provided functional and mechanistic insights into the potential involvement of some of these genes in the key transitions. In addition to technical pipelines relevant to other cancer types, this study offers a blueprint for understanding breast and prostate cancer progression and suggests potential processes for therapeutic intervention. Results Breast and Prostate Cancer Transition Study Cohort Overview We profiled 319 tumor and normal sections (2D) and blocks (3D) from 51 cases, encompassing breast cancer (112 assays, 21 cases) and prostate cancer (207 assays, 30 cases) as part of the NCI Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN; Fig. 1B ; Supplementary Tables S1–S3). The samples were divided into three cohorts based on the assay method and analysis strategy: stacked 3D, native 3D, and 2D cohorts. The stacked 3D cohort comprised 233 assays, including 76 assays from breast cancer and 157 from prostate cancer. Five spatial omics platforms (Xenium, CosMx, Visium, Visium HD, and CODEX), together with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) imaging, were used to reconstruct 3D tumor structures and investigate molecular markers associated with the transition from noninvasive to invasive states (Supplementary Tables S2–S5). We also added additional 2D sections to form a nonserial 2D analysis cohort to increase sample size for DEG analyses, which included a total of 305 sections from 47 cases. Additionally, we performed native 3D assays using fluorescent lightsheet microscopy (FLSM) to trace the glandular structures in 3D and directly observe the transition from noninvasive to invasive states in both breast and prostate cancers. Volumetric Lightsheet Microscopy Reveals Tumor Architecture To investigate the architecture of precancerous and invasive tumor volumes within intact samples, we utilized FLSM to image cleared and immunostained tumor tissues ( Fig. 2A and B ). This analysis included five samples from two patients with breast cancer and nine samples from two patients with prostate cancer ( Fig. 2A , “Methods”). Cytokeratin-5 (CK5) and pan-cytokeratin (PanCK) were used to label basal cells and epithelial cells, respectively, enabling the delineation of normal, precancerous, and invasive lesions in both breast and prostate cancer tissues ( Fig. 2C and D ). Figure 2. Volumetric lightsheet microscopy reveals 3D tumor architecture. A, Lightsheet cohort information. Samples used for the following detailed analysis were highlighted in pink and blue for breast and prostate tumors, respectively. B, Schematic of the experimental workflow for lightsheet microscopy. Tumor samples (“Methods”) were tissue-cleared and antibody-labeled before imaging by lightsheet microscopy. C, 3D view of the breast cancer sample HT944B1. D, 3D view of the prostate cancer sample HT957Z1. E, Two representative regions of DCIS were observed in a given breast cancer sample, surrounded by IDC and normal ductal structures. Regions are indicated in C . Scale bars, 100 μm. F, Fraction of PanCK-positive regions that are IDC (yellow) vs. DCIS (blue) across the whole structure in ROI1. This 7 mm by 2.5 mm by 1 mm sample (Supplementary Mov. S1) was filled with large but scattered regions positive with PanCK staining but little to no CK5 staining on the periphery, indicative of IDC and a discontinuous or absent basal layer ( Fig. 2C , yellow arrowhead in E ; Supplementary Mov. S2 and S3). Although IDC regions seem separated and scattered on a 2D section, they are interconnected throughout the tumor sample and can span large volumes (Supplementary Mov. S1, S2, and S4; Supplementary Fig. 1A), consistent with a pattern of invasion and uncontrolled growth in the 3D space. There are also six distinct PanCK-positive areas with CK5 staining surrounding their periphery. Some regions feature a thin layer of PanCK staining within the CK5 boundary, indicative of normal ductal structures in which a single layer of basal epithelial layer surrounds a single layer of luminal epithelial layer ( Fig. 2E , green dashed line). Others feature an enlarged PanCK patch inside of the CK5 boundary, indicative of DCIS regions in which malignant luminal cells in the breast duct start to proliferate but the basal layer is still intact ( Fig. 2E , blue dashed line). DCIS morphology either resembles a large homogeneous mass [ Fig. 2E , region-of-interest (ROI)1] or an enlarged ductal structure ( Fig. 2E , ROI2). For example, the DCIS structure highlighted in ROI1 spans more than 750 μm in the z-dimension, which is the direction perpendicular to the sections ( Fig. 2F ). The regions with intact CK5 + basal layers seem to retain the CK5 layer throughout the volume we observed, which leads us to hypothesize that the invasive lesion exists outside of the sampled region. Nonetheless, DCIS regions can be embedded within IDC regions ( Fig. 2G ; Supplementary Mov. S4). Lastly, we observed one region with multiple DCIS-like areas nested into a single larger structure, with strong CK5 staining interwoven with PanCK-stained precancer cells (Supplementary Fig. S1B and S1C; Supplementary Mov. S5). We propose that the observed structure is a breast lobule filled with neoplastic cells. As lobular carcinoma in situ was not indicated by our pathologist, we hypothesize that the cancer cells originated from DCIS regions outside of the sample but invaded through the ductal system. To investigate differences between high-grade PIN and invasive prostate tumor structures, we focused our detailed analysis on HT957Z1 that has coexisting normal glandular structures, high-grade PIN, and invasive adenocarcinoma. The pathology report of this patient indicates prostatic acinar adenocarcinoma with a Gleason score of 4 + 3. We observe bright but unspecific staining of spherical structures throughout many prostate samples, which we suspect originate from antibodies trapped by corpora amylacea ( Fig. 2D ; Supplementary Fig. S1D and S1E; Supplementary Mov. S6). We postulate that this reflects the overall inflammatory status of the patient. Similar to breast cancer samples, normal prostate ducts and acini are marked by an outer layer of CK5 and a thin inner layer of PanCK (Supplementary Fig. S1E). Some ductal structures feature an enlarged inner PanCK layer (25–50 µm thick rather than the typical ∼10 μm thick) with an intact CK5 boundary, suggestive of high-grade PIN structures ( Fig. 2H , blue dashed line). These high-grade PIN structures are adjacent to, and seemingly connected to, disordered PanCK+ branching structures without CK5 on the periphery, consistent with the invasive pattern of Gleason score 4 ( Fig. 2H , yellow dashed line, and Supplementary Mov. S7). Indeed, the CK5 to PanCK ratio decreased with the transition from 0.4 to 0.1 ( Fig. 2I ). This observed transition offers a detailed view of the architectural changes during the neoplastic transition ( Fig. 2J ; Supplementary Mov. S8). In addition, we observed ductal structures with strong CK5 staining on the basal layer and a lumen filled with PanCK-positive cells, similar to the DCIS morphology observed in breast cancer. These could be IDC of the prostate ( Fig. 2H ; Supplementary Fig. S1F orange dashed line). In summary, FLSM of intact breast and prostate tumors revealed that regions appearing disconnected in 2D are in fact highly interconnected in 3D, with DCIS and high-grade PIN lesions embedded within and/or transitioning into invasive carcinoma. These analyses highlight how basal layer integrity and epithelial expansion define architectural shifts, providing a direct volumetric view of noninvasive and invasive morphology. Gene Discovery Serial Section Workflow and Computational Framework To understand the molecular drivers associated with the structural transition, we devised a multimodal workflow integrating spatial assays across different platforms. Although the archetypical 2D section is blind to transition dynamics in the third dimension, it does provide large amounts of data, thanks to lower imaging costs. With a view to optimizing 2D tradeoffs of cost versus the limited field-of-view provided by 2D spatial assays, we developed an experimental and computational framework for volumetric integration of 2D sections from a tissue block using five platforms, namely H&E, Xenium, CosMx, CODEX, and the Visium family (Supplementary Fig. S2A). The data from the intermingled sections are computationally combined, furnishing a comprehensive view of spatial and structural variations (Supplementary Fig. S2B). Briefly, sections are cut at specific intervals and optimally arranged on slides according to the respective imaging area of each platform. Following imaging, sections are spatially registered using a keypoint workflow, enabling precise computational alignment across sections (arXiv:1511.01154), and the resulting data are annotated for gene discovery (“Methods”). The product is a block-specific atlas of computationally registered sections that can be examined for precancer-to-cancer transitions and interconnected tumor volumes. Single-platform 2D sections are generally unable to fully characterize transitions, unless the transition region is both sufficiently linear and there is a serendipitous match between it and the section orientation (Supplementary Fig. S2B). The computationally registered multisections in our method capture both linear and nonlinear transition regions within the section area, leaving no topologically disconnected image fragments of the transition region. The integration of platform data and the respective genes they cover support further computational inferences of the transition continuum by proximal correlations of expression (Supplementary Fig. S2C). The approach is used here for finding ROI level DEGs associated with cancer transition in volumetric tumor blocks. Effectively, this allows regions, for example, DCIS, microinvasion (MI), and IDC in breast cancer, to be examined holistically along a spatial continuum. We developed two methods to discover genes associated with these interconnected transition regions: path-based and morphology-based (“Methods”). Briefly, in the path-based method, we calculated a single correlation value across multiple spatial platforms within each interconnected 3D volume. The regression was run on expression values for each region along the path of the transitioning epithelial structure. In the morphology-based method, all regions morphologically annotated as noninvasive (e.g., DCIS) were compared WITH the all invasive regions (e.g., IDC) within the same platform. We also supplement these 3D ROI-level DEGs with 2D approaches that involve assessing regions’ myoepithelial intensity using basal layer markers. Using these markers, we are able to assign each region an invasiveness score, which is an indication of the basal layer marker gene abundance for the region and serves as a continuous metric reflecting the degree of morphologic and molecular progression along the transition axis within each ROI. This score was then correlated with gene expression, allowing the identification of cohort-level genes associated with myoepithelial integrity (“Methods”). Transitionary regions in all ROIs were reviewed and validated by board-certified pathologists. Biomarkers for DCIS-to-IDC Transition in Breast Cancer First, we applied our methodology to ascertain biomarkers correlated to the DCIS-to-IDC transition in breast cancer. Nine tissue samples were serially sectioned (“Methods”). Two samples having greater sectioning depths (460 and 120 µm) were selected for ROI-based analysis, as their increased depths enabled visualization of more pronounced morphologic changes along the Z-dimension of the tissue blocks. HT704B1, a 450-µm deep breast carcinoma specimen with regions of DCIS and IDC, was analyzed using five spatial platforms: Xenium ( n = 6), CODEX ( n = 12), H&E ( n = 20), CosMx ( n = 4), and Visium HD ( n = 2; Fig. 3A ; Supplementary Mov. S9 and S10). The 3D analysis of these sections revealed that regions separated in 2D space by more than 5 mm were in fact interconnected in the Z plane ( Fig. 3B ; Supplementary Table S6), underscoring the value of serial sectioning for understanding true morphologic relationships. We analyzed two regions of interest, ROI1 and ROI2, and identified common metabolic, epithelial integrity, and proliferation modules associated with the transition from DCIS to MI and to IDC ( Fig. 3C–E ; Supplementary Mov. S11 and S12). For example, DCIS in ROI1 demonstrated sustained expression of HMGCS2 (R 2 = 0.79, P = 0.003: path-based) and TFF1 (R 2 = 0.82, P = 0.002: path-based), which was lost in the interconnected IDC volume ( Fig. 3D ). Additionally, DCIS in ROI2 demonstrated strong expression of PLAT that significantly decreased at the site of MI ( Fig. 3E ). Both TFF1 and PLAT may play a role in maintaining epithelial integrity, potentially limiting neoplastic cell migration and invasiveness ( 14 – 18 ). HMGCS2 facilitates ketogenesis, enabling the production of lipid-derived energy ( 19 ), possibly enhancing precancerous cells' survival under hypoxic conditions often present in DCIS regions ( 20 ). In IDC, we observed upregulation of two genes involved in cell proliferation, TCIM (FC = 0.60: morphology-based on Xenium; ref. 21 ) and MKI67 (FC = 0.47: morphology-based on Xenium), in ROI1, and angiogenic factor VEGFA (R 2 = 0.74, P ≤ 0.001; path-based; ref. 22 ) in ROI2 ( Fig. 3D and E ). TCIM , acting through the activation of Wnt/β-catenin pathway ( 21 ), may play a role in inducing invasive cancer cell proliferation marked by MKI67 . In HT891Z1, we analyzed two ROIs, ROI1 and ROI2, that capture the transition from a normal gland, through HGPIN, to GP3 morphology (Supplementary Mov. S17 and S18). In HT891Z1 ROI1, the transition showed distinct differences in gene expression along the normal–HGPIN–GP3 axis ( Fig. 4C ). In less invasive and normal regions, we observed higher expression of FAS (R 2 = 0.53, P = 0.026; path-based). FAS , encoding the Fas cell surface death receptor that promotes apoptosis via the formation of the death-inducing signaling complex, initiates a cascade of caspases, culminating in programmed cell death ( Fig. 4D and E ; refs. 35 , 36 ). Conversely, along the normal to GP3 transition, we observed upregulation of GDF15 (R 2 = 0.68, P = 0.006; path-based) and MYC (R 2 = 0.58, P = 0.016, path-based) , whose expression also goes up as breast cancer progresses ( Fig. 4E ). GDF15 , a member of the TGF-β superfamily, has been implicated in bone metastasis and progression to castration-resistant prostate cancer ( 37 ) but not in earlier stages of prostate cancer. Notably, in section Z290 of ROI1, we observed a striking dichotomy between normal and HGPIN expression patterns on the same section. On the right side of the gland, FAS was detected, whereas the left side exhibited elevated expressions of MYC and GDF15 . Subsequent Z-sections revealed these two sides diverging into distinct morphologies, with the right retaining normal features of the prostatic gland and the left progressing toward HGPIN morphology. In HT913Z1, ROI1 shows a normal duct transitioning into GP3 morphology (Supplementary Fig. S5A and S5B; Supplementary Mov. S19). In the normal axis, we observed elevated expression of SORL1 across multiple sections with Xenium (Supplementary Fig. S5C), a gene not previously described in prostate cancer but which plays a role in lipid metabolism and trafficking through interactions with receptors like low-density lipoprotein receptor ( 38 ). In the invasive axis of HT913Z1, we observed upregulation of SERPINA3 , with a distinct expression pattern localized only to specific GP3 areas. SERPINA3 has been implicated in a variety of processes, including mediating apoptosis, autophagy, and aerobic glycolysis, thereby affecting cell survival and metabolic pathways ( 39 ). Additionally, in melanoma, high SERPINA3 expression has been associated with extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, increased invasion, metastasis, and poorer overall survival, suggesting a similar proinvasive role ( 40 ). Finally, we identified pathways shared across multiple ROIs that may help to drive the normal-to-GP3 transition ( Fig. 4F ; Supplementary Fig. S4 and S5C). In areas having essentially normal glandular morphology, we observed upregulation of genes associated with gland differentiation and hormone signaling ( FHL2 and SOX9 ; refs. 41 , 42 ), inhibition of epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT; SORL1 , NTN4 , and FLRT3 ; refs. 43 – 45 ), tissue integrity ( UPK1A ; ref. 46 ), survival ( FAS ; ref. 35 ), and metabolism ( SLC40A1 ; ref. 47 ). In contrast, regions with more aggressive HGPIN and GP3 morphology displayed increased expression of genes involved in migration and angiogenesis ( GDF15 , MYC , and EPHA6 ; refs. 37 , 48 , 49 ), metabolism and cell–cell communication ( ALDH1A3 ; ref. 50 ), tissue integrity ( SCIN ; refs. 51 , 52 ), survival ( SERPINA3 ; ref. 39 ), and cell proliferation and differentiation ( NPDCD1 ; ref. 53 ). In all, changes in the expression of these genes reflect biological transformations that occur from noninvasive to invasive transition in prostate cancer. Impact of the TME on Malignant Transition in Breast and Prostate Cancers In addition to epithelial cell markers, we explored changes in the TME that might facilitate the transition from normal to more invasive epithelial cells. We identified two TME cell types potentially involved in this transition: tumor-associated macrophages (TAM) and cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAF). Using our 2D automated gene discovery workflow ( Fig. 5A ), we identified two markers, SPP1 and MS4A6A , that distinguish TAM populations across different morphologic regions in non-TNBC breast cancer ( Fig. 5B ). In HT704B1 ROI1, we analyzed the expression of SPP1 and MS4A6A throughout the z-dimensional section stack, in which there is a clear association of MS4A6A + TAMs infiltrating DCIS regions, whereas SPP1 + TAMs are more prevalent within IDC regions ( Fig. 5C and D ; Supplementary Fig. S6A and S6B). Interestingly, only luminal cell-of-origin breast tumors displayed this relationship, whereas sections from basal tumors differed in that their SPP1 + and MS4A6A + TME expression was associated with noninvasive morphology. Similarly to TNBC, in prostate cancer, we observed localization of MS4A6A + TAMs with noninvasive morphology. To further evaluate this association in three dimensions, we performed an analysis using all Xenium sections from HT704B1. For each TAM, we computed the shortest 3D distance to the nearest epithelial region. We then quantified the basal-layer intensity score of the corresponding epithelial region as a measure of invasiveness. Across five of the six sections analyzed, SPP1 + TAMs were preferentially associated with more invasive epithelial regions characterized by lower basal-layer integrity scores, whereas MS4A6A + TAMs were more frequently localized near less invasive regions with higher basal-layer integrity scores (Supplementary Fig. S6C). In non-TNBC breast sections, we observed upregulation of key stromal genes around invasive regions— MFAP5 and ASPN —that contribute to tumor progression ( Fig. 5B and E ). MFAP5 , a fibroblast-secreted ECM glycoprotein, facilitates cancer cell invasion by remodeling the ECM and activating PI3K/AKT and TGF-β signaling pathways, which drive the EMT ( 54 – 56 ). It also enhances angiogenesis by upregulating VEGF , promoting tumor vascularization ( 57 ). The juxtaposition of these immune and stromal programs with transitioning epithelial cells suggests that malignant invasion arises from coordinated epithelial–microenvironmental interactions. However, our analyses highlight several patterns of gene expression associated with the transition from noninvasive to invasive states in breast and prostate cancers ( Fig. 6A ; Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). In breast cancer, genes linked to tissue integrity and remodeling—including MGP and PLAT —were consistently enriched in noninvasive states (DCIS) across multiple samples ( Fig. 6A ; Supplementary Fig. S7A and S7B). Additional markers such as KIT and CA9 also localized to DCIS regions at the ROI-level in HT206B1 (Supplementary Fig. 3). In contrast, IDC was marked by angiogenesis-related genes, with KRT8 and VEGFA enriched at the cohort level and CP enriched within ROI analyses (Figs. 3F , 6A and B ). IF validation further confirmed that MGP protein was significantly upregulated in DCIS relative to IDC (normal vs. IDC: P = 1.29e−4, DCIS vs. IDC: P = 3.81e−8; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6B ; Supplementary Fig. S8A; Supplementary Mov. S20). MGP , a γ-carboxyglutamic domain containing protein, plays a critical role in inhibiting soft tissue calcification and maintaining ECM integrity by preventing inappropriate calcium deposition, ensuring ECM flexibility and function ( 62 ). In premalignant states, maintaining ECM organization is essential, as dysregulation—such as increased stiffness from mineralization—may facilitate tumor invasion and progression by altering ECM composition and structure ( 28 , 63 ). Similarly, PLAT protein was significantly enriched in noninvasive breast regions (normal vs. IDC: P = 3.81e−4; DCIS vs. IDC: P = 0.009; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6C ; Supplementary Fig. S8B). In prostate cancer, noninvasive regions expressed ECM-related genes such as UPK1A and FLRT3 . ANPEP and ALDH1A3 , linked to cell–cell communications and metabolism ( 64 , 65 ), were upregulated in invasive prostate cancer regions but downregulated in invasive breast cancer areas. We also validated some invasive drivers by IF, including GDF15 ( P = 0.031; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6D ; Supplementary Fig. S8C) and ALDH1A3 ( P = 3.46e−6; Student t test; two-sided. Fig. 6E ; Supplementary Fig. S8D), both of which were significantly upregulated in invasive lesions compared with normal glands. GDF15 , a stress-induced cytokine in the TGF-β family, is known to promote EMT and tumor progression ( 37 , 66 , 67 ). Finally, several genes were consistently enriched across both cancer types, including FASN (Supplementary Fig. S8E and F; fatty acid synthase), which promotes tumor progression by supplying lipids necessary for the energy demands of rapidly proliferating cells ( 68 ), and EPHA6 (Supplementary Fig. S8G), a member of the Eph receptor tyrosine kinase family that is involved in cell–cell communications and has been indicated as a metastasis-associated gene in prostate cancer ( 49 ). We then selected candidate transition markers, including those showing consistent trends both at the transcriptional and protein levels, for functional validation in patient-derived cell lines. In breast cancer, we used short hairpin RNA (shRNA)-mediated knockdown of noninvasive enriched tissue remodeling-related genes MGP and PLAT in patient-derived DCIS cell lines ETCC-006 and ETCC-010 ( 69 ). Real-time quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR) confirmed significant transcript reduction ( P < 0.005), and functional assays showed significant effects associated with the gene knockdowns ( Fig. 7A ). CCK-8 assays showed that silencing either gene enhanced proliferation across 24- to 120-hour time points after transfection, and wound-healing assays demonstrated accelerated migration, as reflected by greater wound closure at 24 hours ( Fig. 7B–D ; Supplementary Fig. S9). These results indicate that loss of MGP or PLAT promotes proliferative and migratory behaviors, consistent with their protective roles in maintaining DCIS. Figure 7.
