                     Mural cells lose vasoprotective programs in RV failure  Mural snRNA-seq subclustering (Extended Data Fig.  3n ) separates pericytes from smooth muscle. Pericytes undergo phase 1 loss of vascular-protective programs spanning metabolic, homeostatic, anti-protease, anti-inflammatory and anti-oxidant functions (gene lists in Extended Data Fig.  3o  and Supplementary Data  8  and  9 ), concordant across bulk, snRNA-seq and Xenium pseudobulk. The loss is largely pericyte restricted. Pericyte snRNA-seq additionally showed downregulation of the TGFβ co-receptor  TGFBR3  and the hypoxia pathway gene  HIF3A . We quantify the protective program loss by a curated pseudobulk module score ( TIMP3 ,  IL1RL1 ,  GPX3 ,  ELN ; Extended Data Fig.  3p ), whose NF/pRV/RVF trajectory parallelled the fibroblast module. At the lineage level, mural cells did not demonstrate significant phase 2 changes, whereas sublineage analyses by snRNA-seq pseudobulk reveal IEG/AP-1 stress and partial contractile reversion as the dominant gene groupings (heatmap in Extended Data Fig.  3q ). Xenium subtype resolution (Extended Data Fig.  3r ) resolves focal subset-restricted hits:  MYH11  loss in Pericyte_KCNJ8, Pericyte_THBS4 and VSMC_Inflamed;  CNN1  induction in VSMC_Arterial; and  NR4A3  induction in VSMC_Inflamed (cross-platform concordance in Extended Data Fig.  3s ), supporting a focal phase 2 program rather than a pan-mural shift.    The immune compartment remodels in RV failure with resident macrophage identity loss and cumulative inflammatory transition  Myeloid subclustering yielded six snRNA-seq populations (Fig.  6a–c  and Supplementary Data  7 ): CCR2 −  resident macrophage, inflammatory macrophage (iMac), monocyte/monocyte-derived, TREM2 + , dendritic and proliferating; mast cells were only identified by Xenium. CCR2 −  resident macrophages expressed the conserved TLF framework ( TIMD4 ,  LYVE1 ,  FOLR2 )  36  . iMac cells retained resident markers while strongly expressing immediate-early genes ( NR4A1/  NR4A2/NR4A3 ,  FOS ,  EGR1 ) and, more modestly, NF-κB target cytokines ( CCL3 ,  CCL4 ,  IL1B ) while also lacking monocyte lineage markers, reflecting an activated-resident rather than a recruited-monocyte state. TREM2 +  cells expressed a lipid-associated signature  37   implicated in phagocytosis of cardiomyocyte-ejected dysfunctional mitochondria  38 , 39  .  Pseudobulk DESeq2 identified CCR2 −  resident macrophages as the most responsive myeloid population (169 pRV versus NF snRNA-seq DEGs; 10 Xenium). Phase 1 featured cross-platform loss of resident/scavenger markers ( VSIG4 ,  CD163 ). No individual significant DEG emerged from snRNAseq analysis of pRV → RVF, but the inflammatory transition appeared cumulative from NF → pRV → RVF. From NF → RVF, resident macrophages induced the NR4A immediate-early family, the activation marker  CD83  and coordinated MHC-II induction ( HLA-DRB1  significant), supporting increased antigen presentation capacity. Myeloid WGCNA (Fig.  6d–f ) recapitulated this pattern: RVF-upregulated M8 enriched for MHC-II master  CIITA   40  , whereas the RVF-downregulated  NR3C1  target-enriched M1 module captured the same coordinated resident identity loss. After co-embedding RV and LV (from Koenig et al.  10  ) myeloid cells (Extended Data Fig.  4e,f ), the same resident/scavenger markers,  VSIG4  and  CD163 , fell in both ventricles (Extended Data Fig.  4g,h ), identifying erosion of resident macrophage identity as a shared, chamber-independent feature of heart failure.  Within the myeloid compartment, the dominant transcriptional change was a coordinated, pan-myeloid downregulation of GR transactivation targets. The canonical GR transactivation targets  FKBP5 ,  TSC22D3 ,  ZBTB16  and  KLF9 — together with  ANGPTL4 —were concordantly downregulated as an early stepwise shift  23  , established at the pre-failure (pRV) stage and sustained in RVF (Fig.  6g,h  and Supplementary Data  17 ), and this decline was consistent across myeloid subtypes rather than confined to a single population. In parallel, MHC-II/antigen presentation genes, led by the master regulator  CIITA , were induced with the same early kinetics. Critically, this rewiring was program specific rather than a generalized inflammatory activation, and two innate immune axes that commonly accompany myocardial stress were explicitly unchanged across disease stage. The NLRP3 inflammasome, a canonical driver of heart failure inflammation, showed minimal induction of its sensors, adaptor, caspases or effector cytokines ( IL1B ,  IL18 )  41 , 42  . Likewise, the type I IFN/antiviral ISG response, increasingly reported in failing and inflamed myocardium, remained flat, arguing against an IFN-driven component to the myeloid response  43 , 44  . Thus, the failing RV myeloid compartment shows a focused, coordinated shift in GR target gene expression, in the absence of inflammasome or type I IFN activation. Comparison with failing LV (dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM)) myeloid cells shows that this configuration is only partly conserved across ventricles: MHC-II/antigen presentation induction is shared, and the type I IFN response stays low in both, whereas the loss of GR target gene expression and the absence of inflammasome activation are RV specific. LV DCM myeloid cells instead retain GR target expression and show inflammasome induction (Extended Data Fig.  4i ).  Spatial Xenium refined myeloid taxonomy into eight subpopulations, adding Mac C1q and Mast Cell. Residents distributed broadly, and iMacs co-localized with monocytes at the tissue periphery—a spatial pattern that cannot by itself distinguish phenotypic transition of resident macrophages from monocyte-derived recruitment (Fig.  6i ). TLF marker retention in iMacs, iMac non-expansion (not significant by Kruskal−Wallis) and CCR2 −  contraction are consistent with phenotypic transition, but the iMac/monocyte spatial co-occurrence and absence of imaging-based lineage tracing leave the relative contribution of resident cell transition versus monocyte recruitment unresolved.    ECs suppress anti-oxidant programs and activate in RV failure  EC snRNA-seq subclustering yielded five clusters (Fig.  7a,b  and Supplementary Data  7 ), including an endocardial population ( LEPR ,  NPR3 ). snRNA-seq showed EC expansion in pRV/RVF driven by capillary and arterial ECs, with relative contraction of endocardial and lymphatic ECs (Fig.  7c ). Xenium favored arterial expansion with stable capillary proportions, reflecting platform-specific recovery biases. High-dimensional WGCNA (hdWGCNA)  45   resolved seven EC modules (catalog in  Methods  and Supplementary Data  18 ), with ecM1/ecM4/ecM7 (capillary/arterial/venous EC programs) being upregulated in RVF (Fig.  7d–g ).  Phase 1 EC resolved into two cross-platform programs (Fig.  4a,b ). Phase 1 loss of homeostatic features included suppression of vasoprotective genes ( IL1RL1 , the dominant anti-oxidant  GPX3 ,  ACE2  and  EDN1 ). ISGs rose in parallel, with concordant induction of  IFI44L ,  RSAD2 ,  IFI44 ,  OAS1 / OAS2 / OAS3 ,  MX1 , and  STAT1  by snRNA-seq and bulk (not included in the Xenium 477-gene panel). We curated 13 phase 2 EC candidate genes spanning five functional programs: angiogenic destabilization ( ANGPT2 ,  MYC ,  ADAMTS1 ), EC stress ( STC1 ,  NR4A1 ,  NR4A3 ), EC activation ( ACKR1 ,  PLA2G2A ), mesenchymal ( SNAI1 ), and EC identity ( VWF ,  PECAM1 ,  MECOM ,  CA4 ), and we tested cross-platform concordance in EC pan-pseudobulk (RVF versus pRV; Fig.  7h,i ). The functional phase 2 program validated cleanly: angiogenic destabilization (3/3 Xenium-sig + sn-concordant), the isolated  SNAI1  event,  ACKR1  biphasic reduction in phase 1 and recovery in phase 2 and  CA4  capillary identity erosion; EC stress IFN effector genes (IEGs) were direction concordant but false discovery rate (FDR) modest at the lineage level. Three EC identity/activation candidates ( VWF ,  MECOM ,  PLA2G2A ) showed Xenium signal without snRNA-seq direction concordance.  At the sublineage level, cardioprotective  NRG1  was strongly induced in endocardial ECs in phase 1 (Fig.  7j ). The arterial specifier  MECOM   46 , 47   visually trended up in arterial ECs snRNA-seq in phase 1 (Fig.  7k ; notably, phase 2 in Xenium); because  MECOM  regulates arteriovenous specification in human cardiac endothelium, adult  MECOM  induction may explain capillary/arterial-biased expansion.    A mouse PAB model recapitulates some but not all aspects of human RVF  PAB isolates the RV-specific consequence of sustained pressure overload, the hemodynamic insult shared with pulmonary hypertension and other right-sided afterload diseases, in the absence of pulmonary vascular and systemic confounders or LV failure. We profiled snRNA-seq of sham ( n  = 3) and PAB with mild or severe RVF ( n  = 3,  n  = 4; stratified by RV dilation (RV end-diastolic area); Supplementary Table  7 , Extended Data Fig.  5a,b  and Supplementary Data  19 ). Most cell populations were recovered except adipocytes  48  , with EC expansion and cardiomyocyte contraction across disease states paralleling the human dataset (Extended Data Fig.  5c ). EC expansion was largely arterial in mice versus capillary/arterial in humans (Extended Data Fig.  5d,e ), and human EC hdWGCNA modules embedded consistently. Myeloid cells (<2% of total cells) separated into MHC-II - high and resident macrophages. PAB-induced shifts in RV myeloid cells were broadly discordant with human RVF. Across single-nucleus myeloid cells, PAB did not reproduce the human antigen presentation response: the M8 antigen-presenting module was not induced (Extended Data Fig.  5f ), and the pooled MHC-II module score was unchanged across severity (Extended Data Fig.  5g ). Also,  NR3C1  (GR) target genes showed no repression (Extended Data Fig.  5g ). Because antigen-presenting macrophages are a minor fraction of RV myeloid cells, we tested MHC-II directly in residents with two orthogonal assays, both of which showed active suppression in PAB RV resident macrophages. Flow cytometry showed that surface MHC-II (I-A/I-E geometric mean fluorescence intensity) on CCR2 −  resident macrophages declined in a severity-dependent manner ( P  = 0.013) even as leukocyte, myeloid, macrophage and resident macrophage frequencies remained unchanged across severity (Extended Data Fig.  5h ). Genetic pulse−chase fate mapping ( Cx3cr1 -CreER; Rosa26 -tdTomato) with flow-sorted bulk RNA-seq of long-lived resident macrophages confirmed MHC-II suppression in PAB RV resident macrophages (Extended Data Fig.  5i  and Supplementary Data  20 )  49  . Thus, the antigen presentation/MHC-II program induced in human RVF resident macrophages is instead suppressed in the mouse PAB RV, establishing inter-species divergence of the RVF myeloid signature. Consistent with a decreased transcriptional level of mitochondrial genes, respirometry (Fig.  5i  and Supplementary Data  15 ) showed reduced respiratory capacity at both timepoints: at 2 weeks, the deficit was concentrated in severely affected mice (severe-RVF, approximately 35% reduction in coupled complex I + complex II + FAO respiration versus sham); by 2 months, it penetrated mild-RVF and intensified in severe-RVF (approximately 50−60% reduction). In summary, comparing human adult RVF to mouse PAB-induced RVF, we found:    Conservation of cardiac cell types, with the notable absence of adipose cells in mice    Concordant expansion of ECs with RVF, largely arterial in mice versus capillary in humans    Discordance in MHC-II downregulation in mouse myeloid cells versus induction in human RVF    Concordant cardiomyocyte mitochondrial transcript suppression in both species (significant by gene set enrichment but more modest in mouse than the clear suppression in human RVF)    Markedly reduced mitochondrial respiratory capacity, with the functional deficit exceeding the transcriptional change      Pediatric RVF shows similar transcriptional responses as adult RVF  We also profiled RVs from patients with HLHS after single-ventricle palliation ( n  = 5 Fontan without RVF;  n  = 4 Fontan with RVF;  n  = 1 Glenn with RVF; palliated without RVF called ped-HLHS and with RVF called ped-RVF) plus pediatric controls ( n  = 4; ped-NF). Details of this pediatric dataset can be found in Lavine et al.  50  . Single-nucleus RNA-seq recovered similar cell populations as in adults, with concordant EC expansion and cardiomyocyte contraction in ped-HLHS/RVF (Fig.  8a,b  and Supplementary Data  21 ). Cross-age WGCNA modules and global RVF transcriptional changes correlated well (Fig.  8c,d  and Supplementary Data  22 ). At the mitochondrial level, however, the pediatric RV diverged from the adult and PAB cohorts: cardiomyocyte mitochondrial modules were not clearly induced (Fig.  8e ), and mitochondrial transcripts showed only modest, non‑significant downregulation (Fig.  8f ), directionally consistent with, but far milder than, the coordinated nuclear‑encoded mitochondrial gene loss of adult RVF. Concordantly, within‑pediatric respirometry (ped‑NF versus ped‑RVF; Fig.  5h ) revealed no significant deficit in ETC complex activity (complex I −9.7%, complex I + II −2.3%, complex II +4.1%, complex IV +42.4%; all Mann−Whitney not significant), unlike the marked complex‑level deficits of adult RVF and PAB. Notably, preserved maximal ETC capacity does not exclude the substrate‑level bioenergetic impairment, reduced carnitine palmitoyltransferase (CPT) activity and altered TCA cycle flux, reported in explanted failing single‑ventricle hearts by Garcia et al.  51  , who also found that NF single‑ventricle hearts already adopt an intermediate metabolic phenotype. Our data, therefore, indicate that the severe, coordinated ETC transcriptional and functional collapse characteristic of adult RVF is attenuated in pediatric HLHS‑palliated RVs rather than implying globally normal pediatric mitochondrial metabolism.                    In summary, comparing pediatric to adult RVF, we found that:    Gene expression modules are largely concordant between adult and pediatric RVs.    Overall, there is substantial, but not perfect, concordance in the transcriptional changes during RVF.    Endothelial expansion is seen in both cases of RVF, although it appears driven by venous ECs in pediatric hearts versus capillary ECs in adult hearts.    Mitochondrial gene expression is mostly unchanged in pediatric RVF, unlike adult RVF. Consistent with this, mitochondrial respiration also appears unchanged.    Myeloid MHC-II expression is induced in both cases.      RVF and LVF share core transcriptional programs  Cell-type-resolved LV concordances have already emerged from the fibroblast (Extended Data Fig.  4a–c ) and myeloid (Extended Data Fig.  4d–i ) analyses above. To consolidate that picture and extend it to the bulk module and transcriptome scale, we leveraged the same Koenig et al.  10   human LV snRNA-seq dataset across the full RV WGCNA module set, which showed that RV modules were broadly conserved in LV with concordant NF-versus-DCM trends (Fig.  8g ). Findings that were common to RVF and LVF included induction of the contractile/cytoskeletal/focal adhesion module M2 (Fig.  8h ); repression of the nuclear-encoded ETC mitochondrial modules M10, M25, M26 and M28 (Fig.  8i ); and NF-versus-failing pseudobulk cardiomyocyte FCs (Fig.  8j ). One chamber-specific divergence emerged from the myeloid comparison: the RV iMac population uniquely retained TLF residency markers that were not reported in the Koenig et al. LV inflammatory macrophages. This is consistent with, although it does not prove, an RV iMac hybrid resident-like state.  Thus, the core heart failure programs (mitochondrial suppression, inflammatory activation and myofibroblast activation) are shared between RVF and LVF.     Discussion  We integrated bulk, single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics with orthogonal mitochondrial respirometry, flow cytometry and histology to construct a multi-lineage atlas of human RVF, from which a two-phase model emerges. Phase 1 (NF → pRV) carries the dominant transcriptional burden in bulk and snRNA-seq pseudobulk and features tissue-wide erosion of protective programs, resident macrophage identity loss, fibroblast activation, endothelial expansion and anti-oxidant suppression and pan-tissue  FKBP5  loss. The compensated-to-decompensated (pRV → RVF) transition is best framed as a transcriptional set-point shift in phase 1 (approximately 95% of platform-resolved DEGs) followed by qualitatively distinct, lineage-specific phase 2 programs that include cardiomyocyte oxidative stress, EC  ANGPT2 / ADAMTS1  induction consistent with vascular remodeling and fibroblast matricellular activation.  A central and unanticipated finding is that the pediatric single-ventricle RV resists the mitochondrial failure that characterizes adult and mouse pressure overload. In adult RVF, a coordinated decline in nuclear-encoded mitochondrial transcripts, accompanied by suppression of the ERRα/PGC-1α biogenesis program, parallel impaired complex I + II respiratory function. The mouse PAB RV showed the same concordant decline: cardiomyocyte mitochondrial transcripts were coordinately downregulated (gene set enrichment, consistent with the decreased ETC gene expression reported by Hwang et al.  53  ) alongside reduced respiratory capacity, although the per-animal transcriptional effect was modest relative to the functional deficit. By contrast, pediatric HLHS-palliated failing RVs were metabolically spared. Mitochondrial transcripts were neither induced nor significantly suppressed, and respiratory capacity was preserved (Fig.  5h ). The cross-cohort respiratory pattern (Fig.  5j ), with deficits in adult and mouse but not pediatric single-ventricle RVF, together with the transcriptional data, suggests that the adult and mouse pressure-overloaded RVs undergo coupled mitochondrial transcriptional and functional decline. Conversely, the developing single-ventricle heart sustains respiratory function.  A notable feature of the RV myeloid compartment was a macrophage population marked by an immediate-early gene program, including  NR4A1 ,  NR4A3 ,  DUSP2 ,  FOS  and  JUN , which we designate as iMac. Because induction of these transcription factors is a recognized consequence of enzymatic tissue dissociation in single-cell RNA-seq, such signatures are often dismissed as technical artifact  54  . Several lines of evidence argue against that interpretation here. The program was defined in snRNA-seq, which omits the warm enzymatic dissociation step responsible for the artifact, and was independently recovered by in situ spatial transcriptomics (Xenium), in which transcripts are detected on fixed tissue without any dissociation. Furthermore, the signature was confined to a single macrophage subset and showed reproducible spatial organization, co-localizing with monocytes within discrete tissue foci—a distribution incompatible with a uniform, handling-induced stress response, which would be expected across all cell types irrespective of identity. The iMacs additionally retained resident macrophage markers that were not observed in the inflammatory macrophages of the Koenig et al.  10   left ventricular atlas, suggesting that the RV harbors an activated, resident-like macrophage state localized to sites of monocyte accrual. Whether this state reflects local activation of resident macrophages or in situ adaptation of recruited cells cannot be resolved from cross-sectional human data and will require lineage-resolved models. Regardless of origin, its presence points to a chamber-specific organization of the myeloid response in right ventricular failure.  We found evidence for disruption in GR signaling, with tissue-wide loss of the GR co-chaperone  FKBP5  and a coordinated, pan-myeloid suppression of  NR3C1  transactivation targets, although this evidence is limited to transcriptional state. Because the GR can bind both positive and negative glucocorticoid response elements (GREs) and drive either induction or repression accordingly, downregulation of GRE-associated transcripts does not by itself imply reduced GR activity. Therefore, the direction of GR signaling cannot be inferred from target gene expression alone, and functional validation of altered glucocorticoid signaling will require dedicated studies. However, the PAB model only partially reproduces this human signature ( NR3C1  targets unchanged), limiting its utility for studying RV glucocorticoid biology. Because  FKBP5  loss is observed across both tissue-resident and circulating-origin lineages, the underlying signal could reflect either local microenvironmental modulation of glucocorticoid responsiveness or systemic axis perturbation. Distinguishing these possibilities will require dedicated experimental designs.  The endothelial expansion seen in pRV/RVF across adult human, pediatric human and mice is somewhat unusual among heart failure transcriptomic studies but has been reported in the context of ischemic left ventricular cardiomyopathy  11  . We hypothesize that this reflects coronary microvascular adaptation to RV-specific hemodynamics (a thin-walled chamber perfused throughout systole as well as diastole), driving compensatory capillary/arterial expansion to maintain oxygen delivery in the setting of pressure loading, with adult  MECOM  +  arterial induction and pediatric venous-dominated expansion reflecting different developmental contexts. Phase 2 angiopoietin axis destabilization ( ANGPT2 ,  MYC ,  ADAMTS1 ) suggests that this initially compensatory vascular response transitions toward destabilization at decompensation. Functional validation will require perfusion imaging, vascular casting or interventional EC studies.  More broadly, mouse PAB reproduces the hemodynamic burden of human RVF and converges with human RVF in terms of metabolic and structural programs: suppression of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes, reduced respiratory capacity, cardiomyocyte fetal gene reactivation, endothelial expansion and progressive fibrosis. However, it diverges in immune and hormonal programs, most notably myeloid antigen presentation (MHC-II/ CIITA ) and glucocorticoid signaling and in finer features such as the arterial-biased endothelial expansion seen in mice. The model is, therefore, well suited to studying RV metabolic and fibrotic remodeling but should be applied cautiously to immune or glucocorticoid pathways.  Our atlas can be placed directly against previous cross-chamber and cross-etiology studies. In the NF human heart, the right and left ventricles are nearly transcriptionally identical. The four-chamber atlas of Tucker et al.  16   reported only approximately 24 genes differentially expressed between the ventricles, versus more than 1,000 for each atrial−ventricular contrast, implying that the RV-specific programs we resolve in failure are disease emergent rather than reflections of baseline chamber identity. Against the matched failing-LV/DCM atlas of Koenig et al.  10  , the failing RV and LV share a substantial core transcriptional program (mitochondrial suppression, cytoskeletal remodeling and immune activation)  10 , 12 , 15   with RV-specific divergence in focal programs such as glucocorticoid axis loss and reduced inflammasome induction. A rat pulmonary-artery-banding (RV) versus aortic-banding (LV) model likewise shows broadly overlapping ventricular transcriptomes at baseline (approximately 91% shared) but a distinct, stronger RV disease response, together with a conserved secreted/matrix right-heart-failure signature of approximately 50 genes spanning rat PAB and human chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH)  55  . Notably, isolated afterload modeling argues that RVF and LVF are largely distinct: only 2.2% of human LVF genes overlap the rat PAB regulated set  55  . Our predominantly LVF secondary cohort is the informative exception: its RVF shares the broad cardiomyopathic core of the failing LV, which we attribute to the common myocardial and systemic substrate of LVF-associated RVF rather than to the isolated afterload that drives the RV-versus-LV divergence seen in the banding model.  These comparisons carry translational implications. The shared core molecular pathology between LVF-associated RVF and LVF suggests that the clinical failure of LV-directed guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in isolated RVF  9   reflects engagement of non-cardiac targets, biomechanical context, chamber geometry or upstream hemodynamic triggers rather than fundamentally divergent molecular pathways. Combined with a parallel plasma LTBP-2 biomarker study  56  , the fibrosis-related RV transcripts identified here may eventually serve as biomarkers of RV remodeling. Overall, the multi-lineage microenvironmental remodeling that we identify nominates anti-fibrotic strategies (notably, TGFBR3), immunomodulatory approaches and direct mitochondrial functional support as plausible RV-specific therapeutic avenues.  Our study has limitations. The snRNA-seq cohort ( n  = 11), although among the largest for human RV, remains modest. We address this through the larger bulk cohort ( n  = 142) and cross-platform concordance for key claims. Xenium was available for  n  = 3 per group, limiting CellChat inference, and is restricted to the 477-gene panel, so off-panel claims (notably,  POSTN ,  FKBP5 ,  TGFBR3  and  MLIP ) rest on bulk and snRNA-seq alone. Also, the phase 2 signal is quantitatively limited across platforms. Endothelial EndoMT and cardiomyocyte reactivation programs will require targeted functional validation.    Methods   Ethical compliance  This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations. Studies involving human tissue were approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board (study number 802781), the Childrenʼs Hospital of Philadelphia Institutional Review Board (study number 22-020464) and the Gift-of-Life Donor Program. Experimental model and subject details   Mouse models  All animal studies were approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocols 805255 and 805309). Mice were housed in the University of Pennsylvania vivarium on a 12-hour light/dark cycle (lights on 07:00, off 19:00), at an ambient temperature of 20−23 °C and 30−70% relative humidity, with constant access to normal chow and water. Experiments were initiated on mice 6−10 weeks (typically 7−8 weeks) of age, unless otherwise stated. All experiments were performed with littermate controls. Only male mice were used in order to remove sex as a biological variable. PAB and sham surgery were performed on 9-week-old male C57BL/6J mice (The Jackson Laboratory, 000664); resident macrophage bulk RNA-seq used 8-week-old male heterozygous  Cx3cr1 -CreER; Rosa26 -tdTomato mice. Per-experiment group sizes are given in Supplementary Tables  7  and  8 . The mouse studies described here involved heterozygous  Cx3cr1 -CreER; Rosa26 -tdTomato mice, which were bred from  Cx3cr1 -CreER (The Jackson Laboratory, 020940) and  Rosa26 -tdTomato (The Jackson Laboratory, 007914) mice.     Method details   Statement on human specimens  This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations and was approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board (study number 802781), the Childrenʼs Hospital of Philadelphia Institutional Review Board (study number 22-020464) and the Gift-of-Life Donor Program. Prospective informed and written consent for research use of surgically explanted tissue was obtained from the transplant recipients or from the next-of-kin in the case of deceased organ donors. The consent obtained covers publication of the resulting data: participants, or next-of-kin for deceased organ donors, were informed that the results of the research may be presented at scientific meetings or in publications, with identity not disclosed and only coded identifiers used. No compensation was provided for participation  57  . All sequencing data were deidentified prior to deposition. Heart tissue was procured according to a previously described standard protocol  57  . In brief, all hearts underwent in situ cardioplegia and were kept in cold cardioplegia or saline until transmural samples were snap frozen in liquid nitrogen (within 4 hours) and stored at −80 °C until processing for mRNA analysis.      Participant demographics  Bulk RNA-seq included 142 participants: NF  n  = 29 (11 male, 18 female; mean age 51.8 ± 16.1 years, range 18−75), pressure-loaded  n  = 78 (61 male, 17 female; mean age 53.6 ± 11.0 years, range 20−69) and RV failure  n  = 35 (21 male, 14 female; mean age 55.0 ± 8.7 years, range 27−69). Single-nucleus RNA-seq included 11 participants: NF  n  = 4 (two male, two female; mean age 55.5 ± 12.1 years, range 39−65), pressure-loaded  n  = 4 (two male, two female; mean age 54.2 ± 1.3 years, range 53−56) and RV failure  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 47.7 ± 20.0 years, range 27−67). Xenium spatial transcriptomics included nine participants: NF  n  = 3 (one male, two female; mean age 61.0 ± 6.1 years, range 54−65), pressure-loaded  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 54.3 ± 1.5 years, range 53−56) and RV failure  n  = 3 (two male, one female; mean age 47.7 ± 20.0 years, range 27−67). Per-participant sex, age and underlying diagnosis are given in Supplementary Tables  1 ,  4  and  6 . The pediatric single-nucleus cohort comprised 14 participants from two institutions (Colorado  n  = 9, Washington University in St. Louis  n  = 5): NF donors  n  = 4 (two male, two female; mean age 4.9 ± 3.3 years, range 1.3−8.0), single-ventricle participants with protein-losing enteropathy or plastic bronchitis  n  = 5 (three male, two female; mean age 9.6 ± 5.1 years, range 4.8−16.0) and single-ventricle participants with systolic heart failure  n  = 5 (four male, one female; mean age 10.5 ± 8.3 years, range 3.8−23.0). One participant in the systolic heart failure group was 23 years old at collection. All others were under 18.    Bulk RNA-seq: sample stratification  Diseased RVs were stratified into two groups: pRV (right atrial pressure and right atrial to pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ratio—that is, RA ≤ 8 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≤ 0.37) and RVF (RA ≥ 9 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≥ 0.63) based on validated clinical predictors of RVF or death after left ventricular assist device placement  17 , 18  .    Bulk RNA-seq: human sample preparation  Snap-frozen cardiac tissues from the RVs of explanted donors were pulverized in a liquid nitrogen-cooled cryomill. Total RNA extraction was performed using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen) with poly(A) selection. RNA quality was assessed using RNA 6000 Nano Kit (Agilent Technologies) and 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies), targeting an RNA integrity number (RIN) score >7.0. RNA-seq libraries were prepared using TruSeq mRNA Stranded Kit (Illumina) according to the manufacturerʼs recommended protocol.    Bulk RNA-seq: transcriptome pseudo-alignment  Libraries were sequenced to a depth of more than 20 million reads per sample. Reads were trimmed using Trimmomatic  58  . Trimmed reads were pseudo-aligned to the human transcriptome (GRCh38) using Kallisto  59  . Transcript-level abundances were converted to gene-level counts with tximport, which weights transcripts by length to correct for the length dependence of read counts under the 2 × 150 sequencing configuration  60  . The resultant gene-level count matrices were then used for downstream analysis.    Bulk RNA-seq: differential gene expression  DEGs were detected using DESeq2 (ref.   61  ). To account for inter-subject differences including sex, race, other clinical variables and batch effects, SVA  62   was used to estimate 21 surrogate variables and remove sequencing batch effects—that is, with the model Expression ~ Group + SV1 +…+ SV21, where the tilde represents ‘distributed as’. A joint model was fit over all contrasts, and then pairwise comparisons (for example, NF versus pRV) were conducted for disease states using the Wald test at an  α  value of 0.1. The surrogate variables were fit from demographic and clinical covariates (sex, age, race, body surface area, height, weight, body mass index, thyroid disease, pacemaker status and sequencing and library preparation batch). Those covariates are not released, as they are indirect identifiers. The fitted surrogate variables are deposited with the count matrix so that the published models can be reproduced without patient-level characteristics.    Bulk RNA-seq: WGCNA  The R packages WGCNA  20   and hdWGCNA  45   were used for all WGCNA analysis. Only genes expressed in more than 5% of subjects (or nuclei for EC snRNA-seq) were retained for analysis. For bulk analysis, WGCNA was run on DESeq2 normalized counts and was used to identify gene modules that co-varied among subjects, agnostic of disease state.  The key of EC hdWGCNA module identities is as follows: ecM1 core/capillary identity ( n  = 1,139 genes); ecM2 sarcomeric/cardiomyocyte ambient signature ( n  = 836); ecM3 constitutive RNA splicing/processing ( n  = 647); ecM4 arterial identity ( n  = 125); ecM5 AP-1/NR4A immediate-early stress ( n  = 120); ecM6 peri-vascular/mural-like ECM ( n  = 115); ecM7 venous/inflamed program ( n  = 91). Hubs are in Supplementary Data  18 .  For the bulk WGCNA module catalog (nomenclature), the module identities used were as follows (29 in total; full hub gene lists in Supplementary Data  4 ): M1 resident-macrophage identity (hubs  VSIG4 ,  CD163 ,  MRC1 ,  LAPTM5 ,  HCLS1 ,  FCN3 ); M2 cytoskeletal/focal adhesion + structural/ECM (contractile, multi-lineage); M3 late chromatin/epitranscriptomic ( METTL3 ,  INO80 ,  KANSL1 ,  PHF8 ,  MBD1 ); M4 myeloid/T cell antigen presentation; M7 polycomb/developmental ( EZH2 ,  HOXB8 ,  ITGA4 ,  POLE2 ); M8 MHC-II master,  CIITA -enriched; M10/M25/M26 nuclear-encoded ETC/OXPHOS (M10/M26 also complex III/ATP synthase/ MCUR1 ); M12 cardiomyocyte ( TNNI3 ,  TNNI3K ,  BMPR2 ,  MYH7 ); M13 immunoglobulin repertoire ( IGHG/IGKC ); M14 cardiac transcriptional regulators ( CASZ1 ,  RARA ,  KDM5A ,  MED13L ,  TLE4 ,  DDR1 ); M15 endothelial activation (95 genes, chemokine signaling); M21 TGFβ/Notch/Wnt suppressors ( SKI ,  AXIN1 ,  MIB2 ,  CTBP1 ,  MTA1 ,  ALKBH5 ); M24 complex I/IV hubs; M27 splicing/RNA processing ( SRSF7 ,  SF3B1 ); and M28 mtDNA-encoded ETC ( MT-ATP6 ,  MT-CO2 ,  MT-CO3 ,  MT-CYB ,  SOD1 ). Modules M5, M6 and M16 are referenced descriptively without standalone identities.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sample selection  Diseased hearts were selected from patients with DCM who had no high-impact variants identified on whole-exome sequencing. To maximize the probability of capturing transcriptional changes, the RVF samples were enriched for severity, possessing decreased diastolic function (RA ≥ 14 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≥ 0.7), decreased systolic function (TAPSE ≤ 1.7) and at least moderate tricuspid regurgitation; pRV samples were comparatively enriched for normal diastolic function (RA ≤ 4 mmHg, RA:PCWP ≤ 0.33), systolic function (TAPSE ≥ 2.2) and trivial or less tricuspid regurgitation. RVF and pRV samples were otherwise well balanced for other clinical and demographic variables (Supplementary Tables  4  and  5 ). For the pediatric HLHS cohort, Fontan/Glenn single-ventricle physiology differs fundamentally from adult LVF secondary pressure overload in onset timing, ventricular morphology and load history; pediatric comparisons, therefore, test molecular convergence rather than direct replication.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: human sample preparation  Samples were prepared as described previously  12  . In brief, frozen cardiac tissues from the RV of explanted donors (approximately 100 mg) were sectioned to 100 µm (Leica, CM1950 cryostat) and then transferred into a 2-ml Dounce homogenizer containing 1 ml of chilled lysis buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 250 mM sucrose, 25 mM KCl, 3 mM MgCl 2 , 1 µM DTT and 0.05% IGEPAL-630 in nuclease-free water). Samples were homogenized with 10 passes of a coarse pestle and then 10 passes of a fine pestle and then incubated on ice for 15 minutes. Large debris was removed by centrifugation at 40 g  for 1 minute (Beckman Coulter, Allegra X-15R swinging bucket centrifuge) before sequentially being filtered through a 50-µm and then a 10-µm filter (puriSelect Life Science) into a 50-ml conical tube. The filters were washed with 6 ml of wash buffer (0.01% BSA, 5 mM MgCl 2 , PBS), and the resultant suspension was pelleted at 550 g  for 5 minutes at 4 °C. The pelleted nuclei were resuspended in 150 µl of cold nuclei resuspension buffer (0.01% BSA, 5 mM MgCl 2 , 0.4 U µl −1  murine RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs), PBS) and counted on a hemocytometer before dilution to 1,000 nuclei per microliter.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: mouse sample preparation  Samples were prepared similarly as above for the human samples, with the notable exception of an additional fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) step at the end. DAPI (1 µg ml −1 ) was added into the lysis buffer. Instead of resuspension in nuclei resuspension buffer, nuclei were resuspended in FACS buffer (1% BSA, 0.4 U µl −1  murine RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs), PBS). Nuclei were flowed at the lowest flow rate on a FACSAria III (BD Biosciences) with a 100-µm nozzle. In total, 100,000 DAPI +  singlets were collected. Nuclei were recovered by spinning at 500 g  for 5 minutes and then resuspended in nuclei resuspension buffer before quantification and dilution to 1,000 nuclei per microliter.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: 10x Chromium single-cell gene expression  Nuclei were loaded onto the 10x Genomics Chromium microfluidic platform (Single Cell 3′ solution, v3) for an estimated recovery of 6,000 cells per device. Processing of libraries was performed according to the manufacturerʼs instructions.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sequencing and alignment  Complementary DNA libraries were multiplexed and sequenced on a NovaSeq 6000 S4 chip (Azenta) to a goal of approximately 75,000−100,000 reads per nucleus. Raw base call files for each sample were demultiplexed and converted to FASTQ files using the 10x Genomics toolkit Cell Ranger 7.1.0 (cellranger mkfastq)  63  . FASTQ files were then uploaded to the 10x Genomic Cloud where Cell Ranger Count 7.1.0 was run on each sample to map them to the human (GRCh38) 2020-A transcriptome or the mouse (GRCm39) 2020-A transcriptome with the include-introns flag set to true. Resultant raw feature matrices were then used for downstream analysis.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: ambient RNA and noise removal  To remove ambient and background RNA contamination, we used CellBender  64  , running remove-background with hyperparameter tuning (primarily of learning rate) to ensure smooth convergence during model training. CellBender-denoised count matrices were then further processed with DecontX  65   to estimate and subtract residual per-cell ambient contamination, and the DecontX-corrected counts were carried forward for all downstream analyses. Some residual cytoplasmic RNA contamination during nuclear isolation can nevertheless produce low-level off-target detection of canonical cell type markers (for example,  RYR2  in non-cardiomyocyte populations); cell type assignment, therefore, relies on relative enrichment over a panel of cluster-defining markers rather than presence/absence of any single gene.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: filtering and quality control  All further analysis was conducted in Seurat  66  . Nuclei with more than 5% mitochondrial transcripts, with fewer than 200 transcripts or with more than 100,000 transcripts were discarded. For each nucleus, the entropy (using the Python package ndd and its entropy function) and the exonic percentage (using scR-Invex) were calculated. Nuclei with entropy below Q1 − 1.5×IQR (first quartile (Q1), interquartile range (IQR)), exon percentage above Q3 + 1.5×IQR (third quartile (Q3)) or mitochondrial read percentage above Q3 + 1.5×IQR were flagged as outliers and removed. For secondary outlier detection, nuclei were then clustered using Seuratʼs built-in graph-based clustering approach (FindNeighbors and FindClusters). Each cluster was fit with an ellipsoid using the sklearn EllipticEnvelope function, and the 5% of nuclei farthest from the cluster centroid were labeled as outliers and also removed. For doublet removal, we elected to utilize a semi-supervised approach, as has been done previously  11  , which was based upon identifying nuclei that simultaneously had gene expression signatures consistent with two (or more) cell populations  11  . Practically, this was done by iteratively clustering nuclei at high resolution, generating  z -score expression profiles for each expected cell population and visualizing the nuclei clusters colored by  z -score using uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) embedding. Clusters that demonstrated high expression profiles for multiple cell types were deleted, and then the entire above process was repeated until no further clusters were removed (six rounds).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: myeloid subtype marker rationale  Myeloid subtype assignments were supported by markers with established functional roles:  F13A1  (coagulation factor XIII) is required for post-infarction cardiac integrity  67  .  MARCO  and  HPGDS  define scavenger populations implicated in non-inflammatory clearance of damage-associated molecular patterns and prostaglandin D 2 -mediated inflammation resolution, respectively  36  .  VSIG4 ,  CD163  and  LYVE1  mark self-renewing tissue-resident macrophage subsets associated with complement-mediated immune quiescence  36   and hyaluronan-dependent maintenance of arterial tone  68  . Initial high-resolution subclustering of CCR2 −  resident macrophages identified three transcriptionally distinguishable subsets (enriched for  HPGDS , a broader  F13A1 / CD209 / VSIG4  signature or  RBPJ ), but these subsets showed no disease-specific expansion (all differences <10% of total resident macrophages) and were combined into a single CCR2 −  resident macrophage population for downstream analyses.  CCR2  transcript itself is sparsely detected in droplet-based snRNA-seq of human heart  10  , a well-described dropout effect that disproportionately affects modestly expressed transcripts. Populations were, therefore, defined by combinatorial marker expression rather than by  CCR2  expression alone.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: sample integration  The 11 single-nucleus datasets were integrated using the R Harmony package  69  . Specifically, the 11 preprocessed (as above) and normalized/scaled (via SCTransform) datasets were first combined via Seurat merge, and then the RunHarmony command was utilized to generate batch-corrected PCA components (50 dimensions). These Harmony-corrected dimensions (rather than raw PCA) were used for all downstream neighbor graph construction (FindNeighbors), clustering (FindClusters) and UMAP embedding (RunUMAP).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: reference mapping  Reference mapping was conducted using the Seurat version 4 reference mapping pipeline. In brief, both the reference and query datasets were initially preprocessed via SCTransform. The reference dataset was then integrated using canonical correlation analysis (CCA) integration rather than Harmony integration as used elsewhere. Anchors between the reference and query dataset were then identified and used to map query data to the integrated reference dataset.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: differential gene expression  Differential gene expression at the single-nucleus level was performed using the FindMarkers function. The default Wilcoxon rank-sum method was used for statistical testing. Only genes with log 2 FC > 0.1 were retained, and those with adjusted  P  < 0.05 were considered significant.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: pseudobulk differential gene expression  Pseudobulk dataset generation was done by summing counts (from the ‘counts’ slot of the SCTransform assay) for each major cell type using the AggregateExpression function. Differential gene expression analysis was then conducted via DESeq2. For both snRNA-seq and Xenium pseudobulk analyses, multiple-testing correction was performed using Benjamini−Hochberg FDR within each DESeq2 run (per subtype × contrast); no global correction was applied across the full subtype × contrast matrix, in keeping with standard pseudobulk practice where each cell type is treated as a distinct experiment. DEG counts reported throughout this paper use the unified threshold adjusted  P  < 0.05, |log 2 FC| > 0.5 and baseMean > 50 unless otherwise stated.    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: enrichment analysis  Pathway enrichment analysis was conducted using the web interface for Enrichr  70   and the R enrichR package. Inputs were genes upregulated or downregulated in the cluster of interest (log 2 FC > 0.1, adjusted  P  < 0.05). Combined score was calculated as  c  = log( p ) ×  z , where  c  is the combined score,  p  is Fisherʼs exact test  P  value and  z  is  z -score for deviation from expected rank.    Bulk RNA-seq: PAH comparison  To compare RVF transcriptional programs across etiologies, we reanalyzed the published PAH RV bulk RNA-seq dataset from Khassafi et al.  19  . Raw count matrices were obtained from the Gene Expression Omnibus ( GSE240941 ) and processed using the same DESeq2 pipeline as our adult RV bulk data. DEGs from PAH RVF versus PAH NF were compared with our RVF versus NF DEGs to identify concordant and discordant genes. Pathway enrichment analysis (EnrichR) was performed separately on concordant genes (same direction in both datasets) and discordant genes (opposite direction).    Single-nucleus RNA-seq: mitochondrial transcription factor analysis  We assessed mitochondrial biogenesis transcriptional regulators across three analytic axes (per-patient pseudobulk DESeq2 expression, CollecTRI/decoupleR  71   transcription factor activity inference and MitoCarta3.0 (ref.   72  ) module scoring) to disentangle transcription factor transcript level, downstream regulon activity and aggregate mitochondrial program output.   Mitochondrial transcription factor panel  A literature-curated panel of nine mitochondrial biogenesis regulators was analyzed:  ESRRA ,  ESRRG ,  PPARA ,  PPARGC1A  (PGC-1α),  NRF1 ,  NFE2L2  (NRF2),  TFAM ,  POLRMT  and  TFB2M , covering the PGC-1α/ERR/PPAR/ NRF1 / TFAM  axis governing nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene expression and mtDNA transcription.    Per-patient pseudobulk expression  For each subtype and lineage, raw RNA counts were aggregated per patient × disease state with Seurat AggregateExpression; counts were then modeled by DESeq2 (design = ~group) with apeglm log 2 FC shrinkage and Benjamini−Hochberg correction. Pairwise contrasts (NF versus pRV, pRV versus RVF, NF versus RVF) used the Wald test. Per-patient violin plots show pseudobulk variance-stabilized transformation (VST) expression, with pairwise Wilcoxon rank-sum  P  values reported between disease states. Pseudobulk treats each patient as the unit of replication, avoiding the inflated significance produced by treating individual nuclei as independent observations.    Transcription factor activity inference via CollecTRI/decoupleR  Transcription factor activities were inferred from the cardiomyocyte snRNA-seq using the decoupleR R package with the CollecTRI regulon network (decoupleR::get_collectri, organism = ‘human’, split_complexes = FALSE). Per-cell transcription factor activity was estimated by univariate linear modeling (decoupleR::run_ulm) on SCTransform-normalized expression with default minimum regulon size. Per-patient mean activity per disease group was computed and visualized as a heatmap for the curated mitochondrial transcription factor panel; this approach captures downstream regulon-level activation independent of transcription factor transcript abundance. Pairwise group differences were tested by Wilcoxon rank-sum on per-patient mean activities.    MitoCarta3.0 module score  The MitoCarta3.0 inventory of human mitochondrial-localized genes was used to score aggregate mitochondrial program output. Seurat AddModuleScore was applied to the full MitoCarta3.0 gene set on the SCTransform-normalized snRNA-seq cardiomyocyte data; per-cell scores were aggregated per cardiomyocyte subcluster × disease state.    Bulk RNA-seq cross-validation  DESeq2-VST expression values for the same nine-transcription-factor panel were extracted from the bulk RNA-seq cohort ( n  = 142 patients). Disease-state differences were tested by Wilcoxon rank-sum.     Spatial transcriptomics: 10x Xenium  The Xenium protocol was completed using the Xenium Slides and Sample Prep Reagents Kit (10x Genomics, PN-1000460) and associated consumables. The procedure itself was done using the manufacturerʼs suggested protocol ( CG000578 ; 10x Genomics) without modifications. In brief, 5-µm sections of formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) RV samples were mounted onto a Xenium slide (10x Genomics) prior to deparaffinization, decrosslinking, fixation and permeabilization. We specifically chose nine RV samples (three NF, three pRV and three RVF) based on RNA quality and sample geometry (variable sizes but typically 10 × 10 mm) for Xenium analysis. Probes were hybridized, washed, ligated and amplified prior to autofluorescence quenching and nuclei staining. Custom probes were designed based on a manually curated list of 100 cluster-specific marker genes from the snRNA-seq data (using the Seurat FindAllMarkers function). The prepared slides were then loaded onto the Xenium Analyzer (10x Genomics), which was run following the recommended protocol. A total of 477 target genes (377 predesigned from the Human Multi-Tissue and Cancer Panel and 100 custom genes) plus 64 negative control probes (541 total) were included on the panel (design ID: 44Z7X8; Supplementary Data  10 ). Output was visualized via Xenium Explorer (10x Genomics). Default Xenium segmentation recovered fewer cells than transcript-level methods, and Baysor  73   produced visually apparent over-segmentation of large cardiomyocytes. Proseg  74   (version 0.3.0) was, therefore, used for resegmentation with the ‘–xenium’ preset, which leverages nucleus boundary overlap for transcript-to-cell assignment. Transcripts with quality value <20 were excluded prior to resegmentation. Each tissue section was divided into overlapping spatial patches using SpatialData/Sopa  75  , and Proseg was run independently on each patch with default parameters (10 components, initial voxel size 10 µm). Patch-level results were merged with global cell ID remapping to avoid collisions across patches. Cell type annotation was performed using RCTD  76   (spacexr R package) in full mode, using our snRNA-seq dataset as the reference. The snRNA-seq reference was constructed from the 12 major cell type annotations with downsampling to a maximum of 500 nuclei per cell type. RCTD was run with UMI_min = 10 and UMI_min_sigma = 100. RCTD weights were used to assign each spatially resolved cell to its most likely cell type. SPLIT  77   ambient RNA correction was applied to the Proseg-resegmented count matrices. To validate cell type frequency estimates against segmentation-dependent cell size variation, nucleus-level proportions were computed by mapping Xenium DAPI nucleus boundaries to Proseg cell boundaries using polygon intersection, with each nucleus inheriting the RCTD annotation of its maximally overlapping Proseg cell. This provides an orthogonal frequency estimate where each nucleus counts as one unit regardless of cell body size. SpaGE  21   imputation was used to impute the expression of genes not included in the Xenium panel but present in the snRNA-seq reference. Subclustering of spatially resolved cells was performed within each of the 12 major cell types using Seurat (version 5). For each cell type, the SPLIT-corrected count matrix (supplemented with SpaGE-imputed genes) was normalized via SCTransform, reduced to 30 principal components and clustered using the Louvain algorithm at a resolution selected to maximize biological interpretability while minimizing over-splitting. Subtype annotations were manually assigned based on marker gene expression and concordance with snRNA-seq subtypes. Pseudobulk differential gene expression analysis was performed within each spatial cell type using DESeq2. To preserve biologically meaningful transcript abundance differences that SPLIT over-corrects, pseudobulk aggregation was performed on the raw, uncorrected Proseg-resegmented count matrix. Genes with |log 2 FC| > 0.5 and adjusted  P  < 0.05 were considered significant. Spatial niche identification was performed using Seurat’s BuildNicheAssay function with  k  = 100 nearest spatial neighbors. To prevent patient-specific cardiomyocyte subtype variation from dominating niche definitions, all cardiomyocyte subtypes were collapsed into a single label prior to niche computation. Centered log ratio (CLR) transformation was applied to niche proportion vectors to amplify differences in rare cell type fractions, followed by  z -scoring. Mini-batch  k -means clustering ( k  = 15) was performed on the CLR-transformed vectors. Clusters sharing similar compositions were merged into 14 final niches. Niche proportions were compared across disease groups (NF, pRV, RVF;  n  = 3 per group) using Kruskal−Wallis tests with Benjamini−Hochberg correction.    Spatial transcriptomics: CellChat cell−cell communication analysis  To infer intercellular signaling within RV myocardium while retaining spatial context, we combined single-nucleus expression with Xenium spatial coordinates. Because the Xenium panel measured only 477 genes, single-nucleus expression was first imputed onto Xenium cells per patient, using each patientʼs own matched snRNA-seq dataset as the reference, so no expression information was shared across individuals. Cell type annotations were consolidated into 13 broad groups from subclustered labels: ECs, cardiomyocytes, fibroblasts, macrophages, pericytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, lymphocytes, myeloid cells (monocytes, dendritic cells and proliferating myeloid cells), adipocytes, epicardial cells, neural cells, lymphatic endothelial cells and mast cells. CellChat  29   was run separately for each patient. For each sample, the imputed expression matrix, lineage annotations and Xenium cell centroids were used to construct a spatial CellChat object with spatial scale factors derived from the Xenium coordinate system. Ligand−receptor interactions were drawn from CellChatDB.human. Overexpressed genes and interactions were identified, and communication probabilities were computed under spatial constraints using the truncated mean method (trim = 0.25). Interactions supported by fewer than five cells were removed. Pathway-level probabilities were aggregated across constituent ligand−receptor pairs. For aggregate network visualization, per-patient CellChat objects restricted to the myocardium niche were averaged across patients within each condition (NF,  n  = 3; pRV,  n  = 3; RVF,  n  = 3) to prevent dominance by any single individual. Edge weights were normalized by the product of sender and receiver cell type proportions to control for compositional differences across conditions. For pathway ranking, summed communication probability across all ligand−receptor pairs was computed per pathway per condition and normalized to sum to 1 within each condition. Analyses were performed in R with CellChat version 3.    PAB procedure  All animal studies were approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (protocols 805255 and 805309). Mice were housed on a normal light/dark cycle (light on from 7:00 to 19:00) with constant access to normal chow and water. PAB was performed in 9-week-old C57BL/6J mice. The anesthetic procedure included induction with ketamine (100 mg kg −1  body weight) and xylazine (10 mg kg −1  body weight) cocktail (intraperitoneal injection), tracheal intubation with a 20-gauge needle and ventilation with a Harvard rodent ventilator (Harvard Apparatus) at a rate of 120−180 breaths per minute and tidal volume of 10 µl g −1  body weight. The main pulmonary artery trunk was dissected from surrounding tissues and constricted with a 7-0 suture tied against a 25-gauge needle to generate a severe RVF. The same procedure including dissection was performed for sham mice apart from pulmonary artery ligature. Close monitoring was performed during procedure and recovery. Meloxicam was administered preoperatively and postoperatively for 48 hours for analgesia, and mice were evaluated daily for 3 days after surgery. The skin sutures were removed 7−10 days postoperatively to avoid irritation and infection. RV remodeling was confirmed by echocardiography at 2-week and 2-month post-surgery timepoints (Supplementary Table  8 ).    PAB resident macrophage bulk RNA-seq  Heterozygous  Cx3cr1 -CreER; Rosa26 -tdTomato mice were fed tamoxifen chow (Inotiv, TD.130856) starting at 3 weeks of age for 1 week. At 8 weeks of age, mice underwent PAB (or sham surgery). Two weeks after surgery, mice were anesthetized with isoflurane inhalation, and their hearts were perfused with 20 ml of cold PBS. The hearts were then dissected, atria were removed and the left and right ventricles were harvested for single-cell isolation. The ventricles were digested as previously described to generate a single-cell suspension  78 , 79  . In brief, ventricles were finely minced in ice-cold PBS until a smooth consistency was achieved. Minced tissues were transferred to Eppendorf tubes containing digestion buffer (RPMI supplemented with 450 U ml −1  Collagenase I, 60 U ml −1  DNase I and 60 U ml −1  hyaluronidase enzymes) and digested at 37 °C on a shaker for 45 minutes. After digestion, samples were briefly vortexed and immediately placed on ice to stop the reaction. Then, the cell suspensions were mechanistically dissociated by pipetting with a 1,000-µl pipettor. The digested solution was filtered through a 40-µm cell strainer and rinsed with neutralization buffer (HBSS without Ca 2+ /Mg 2+ , 2% heat-inactivated bovine serum and 0.2% BSA) to obtain a single-cell suspension. Red blood cells were lysed using ACK lysis buffer. Single-cell suspensions were stained for  CD45  (clone 30-F11; BioLegend, 103132), CD11b (clone M1/70; BioLegend, 101223) and  CD64  (clone X54-5/7.1; BioLegend, 139323). Resident macrophages (CD45 + CD11b + CD64 + tdTomato + ) were sorted by FACS, pelleted and then sent to Azenta for ultra-low-input RNA-seq.    Right ventricular cardiomyocyte mitochondrial isolation from frozen tissue  Mitochondria were isolated from flash-frozen tissue as done previously with modifications  80 , 81  . In brief, frozen right ventricular cardiac muscle was thawed on ice in mitochondrial isolation medium (Buffer A, 50 mM MOPS, 100 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgSO 4 , pH 7.1) for 10 minutes. Thereafter, the cardiac tissue was minced on ice for 3 minutes and then subjected to a 15-minute digestion in Buffer A supplemented with 0.25 mg ml −1  Collagenase II (Worthington,  LS004176 ) while rocking at room temperature. After collagenase digestion, cardiac tissue was centrifuged at 300 g  for 5 minutes at 4 °C. The pellet was then resuspended in Buffer B (50 mM MOPS, 100 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 5 mM MgSO 4 , 2 g l −1  BSA, pH 7.1) and homogenized via a glass-Teflon homogenizer (Wheaton) for approximately five passes and subsequently centrifuged at 800 g  for 10 minutes at 4 °C. The resulting supernatant containing the mitochondrial fraction was collected in a separate pre-chilled tube and centrifuged at 10,000 g  for 10 minutes at 4 °C to pellet mitochondria. The final mitochondrial pellet was washed with Buffer A to remove damaged mitochondria on the exterior of the pellet and then was resuspended in Buffer A. Protein concentration was determined using a bicinchoninic acid protein assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225). For mouse PAB and pediatric human samples, mitochondria were similarly isolated from flash-frozen RV tissue using the protocol described above. Pediatric samples were obtained from pediatric patients with HLHS (with and without RVF) and from non-diseased pediatric donors with normal cardiac anatomy.    Assessment of mitochondrial electron transport capacity using high-resolution respirometry  Mitochondria isolated from freeze/thawed tissue are fully uncoupled and have been suggested to lose components of the TCA cycle throughout processing; however, they still maintain electron transport capacity  80  . Using high-resolution respirometry (Oroboros O2K), oxygen consumption (     J      O    2       ) was measured in isolated mitochondria from human right ventricular muscle in Buffer D (105 mM K-MES, 30 mM KCl, 1 mM EGTA, 10 mM K 2 HPO 4 , 5 mM MgCl 2 -6H 2 O, 2.5 mg ml −1  BSA, pH 7.2) supplemented with 20 mM creatine at 37 °C. Alamethicin (10 µg ml −1 ) was supplemented to Buffer D during the experiment to ensure complete membrane permeabilization and access to substrates. Then, 5−15 mg of right ventricular tissue homogenate was added to the respiratory chambers at an oxygen concentration of approximately 200 µM. Once a baseline steady-state rate was established, substrates were injected as follows: NADH (1 mM) and cytochrome c (Cyt C) (5 µM), succinate (10 mM), rotenone (5 µM), antimycin A (5 µM), N,N,N′,N′-tetramethyl- p -phenylenediamine (TMPD, 0.5 mM) and ascorbate (1 mM). The mean      J      O    2        after each injection was measured and obtained once a steady-state flux was maintained for 5 minutes. Primary measurements included complex I (NADH + Cyt C), complex I + II (after succinate addition; coupled maximal OXPHOS capacity), complex II (rotenone-resistant respiration; succinate-driven with complex I inhibited) and complex IV (ascorbate + TMPD) maximal electron transfer capacity. Residual oxygen consumption (ROX) was defined as the      J      O    2        remaining after antimycin A addition (complex III inhibitor) and was subtracted from each preceding respiratory state to yield mitochondrial-specific values, in keeping with MITOEAGLE consortium conventions. All respiratory rates were normalized to the mass of starting mitochondrial protein (pmol O 2  s −1  mg −1  mitochondrial protein) for cross-cohort consistency. Inter-group differences were assessed by Kruskal−Wallis test with Mann−Whitney pairwise post hoc comparisons (NF versus pRV, NF versus RVF, pRV versus RVF). Non-mitochondrial respiration (ROX) was independently tested across groups to confirm that observed mitochondrial deficits were not confounded by NADPH oxidase (NOX)-mediated changes in non-mitochondrial O 2  consumption. The same O2K inhibitor titration protocol was applied to pediatric human samples. The pediatric respirometry cohort consisted of pediatric NF controls (non-diseased pediatric donors with normal cardiac anatomy,  n  = 7) and pediatric HLHS-palliated failing RVs ( n  = 9), forming a within-pediatric NF-versus-failing comparison matched for age, ventricular morphology (single-ventricle physiology in the failing arm) and load history.  Mouse PAB respirometry used a different, FAO-focused protocol on intact RV tissue fiber bundle preparations (rather than freeze/thaw-isolated mitochondria), reflecting the smaller available tissue mass and the goal of profiling β-oxidation capacity in the same run. Substrate addition was sequential: pyruvate + malate (complex I leak respiration in the absence of adenosine diphosphate (ADP)), ADP (complex I-driven coupled phosphorylating respiration), Cyt C (outer mitochondrial membrane integrity check; intact outer membrane defined as Cyt C / ADP ratio < 1.10), octanoyl-carnitine (complex I + FAO substrates) and succinate (complex I + II + FAO maximal coupled capacity). Respiratory control ratio (RCR) was calculated as ADP/pyruvate + malate. Inter-group differences (sham versus PAB-mild-RVF versus PAB-severe-RVF) at each timepoint (2 weeks, 2 months) were assessed by Kruskal−Wallis test with Mann−Whitney pairwise post hoc comparisons, in keeping with the adult and pediatric statistical framework.    Immune repertoire profiling  Mouse RV cardiac single-cell suspensions were stained with the following anti-mouse antibodies: CD45-BUV395 (clone 30-F11; BioLegend, 103191), CCR2-BV421 (SA203G11; BioLegend, 150605), Ly-6G − PerCP-Cy5.5 (1A8; BioLegend, 127615), CD11b-PE (M1/70; BioLegend, 101207), CD64-PE-Cy7 (X54-5/7.1; BioLegend, 139313), TREM2-APC (237920; R&D Systems, FAB17291A) and I-A/I-E (MHC-II)-APC-Cy7 (M5/114.15.2; BioLegend, 107627). Antibodies were used at the manufacturer-recommended amounts in a 100-µl staining volume: CD45-BUV395, CD11b-PE and I-A/I-E (MHC-II)-APC-Cy7 at 0.25 µg per 10 6  cells; CCR2-BV421, Ly-6G − PerCP-Cy5.5 and CD64-PE-Cy7 at 0.5 µg per 10 6  cells; and TREM2 − APC at 10 µl per 10 6  cells. Samples were acquired on an LSRFortessa (five-laser: 355 nm, 405 nm, 488 nm, 561 nm and 640 nm) using FACSDiva version 9.1 (BD Biosciences) and were analysed in FlowJo. Compensation was calculated from single-stain controls acquired in the same run. After exclusion of doublets (forward scatter area (FSC-A)/forward scatter height (FSC-H)), populations were gated as follows: leukocytes (CD45 + ); myeloid cells (CD45 + CD11b + Ly-6G − ; Ly-6G −  excluding neutrophils); and macrophages (CD64 +  within the myeloid gate). Macrophage residency was defined by CCR2 alone: CCR2 −  cells as resident macrophages and CCR2 +  cells as recruited and monocyte derived. TREM2 +  macrophages were gated within the macrophage gate. Surface MHC-II was quantified as the geometric mean fluorescence intensity (gMFI) of I-A / I-E on the CCR2 −  resident gate. MHC-II gMFI was analyzed on a log scale (fluorescence intensity is log distributed). Trends across sham, mild-RVF and severe-RVF groups were tested with a batch-adjusted linear model on the per-animal (log transformed for gMFI) values. One sham was excluded for quality control. Gates were drawn separately for each of the two staining cohorts, on the internal negative population of each bivariate plot, and applied identically to every sample within a cohort. The complete gating cascade for a representative animal from each cohort is shown in Extended Data Fig.  9 .                      Histology  Full-thickness human RV and mouse hearts were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde, serially dehydrated in ethanol and paraffin embedded (FFPE). FFPE blocks were sectioned at 10 μm, mounted onto slides and stained with either trichrome or Sirius Red according to the manufacturerʼs instructions. Widefield brightfield microscopy was performed on a Keyence BZ-X810 microscope at ×10 with image stitching using BZ-X800 software. Image processing was performed in Fiji. For mouse slides, a region of interest (ROI) was manually drawn to isolate the RV free wall from the septum. Tissue borders and fibrosis-positive regions were identified using color deconvolution to generate binary masks. Statistical analysis was performed in Prism using Kruskal−Wallis with two-stage linear step-up Benjamini−Krieger−Yekutieli correction for pairwise comparisons.  For cardiomyocyte cross-sectional analyses, slides were stained with Alexa Fluor 488 WGA (Cell Signaling Technology, 1:100) and α-actinin (Abcam, ab68167, 1:200) and DAPI. Donkey anti-rabbit IgG Alexa Fluor 568 was used as secondary antibody (Invitrogen/Thermo Fisher Scientific, A10042, 1:500). Three representative stitched ×40 tile-scan images were acquired per subject in RV regions where cardiomyocytes were predominantly oriented in cross-section. Regions containing predominantly longitudinally oriented cardiomyocytes were manually excluded. Cellpose  82   was used for cell segmentation on processed WGA images using the following settings: diameter 100, flow threshold 0.5, cell probability threshold 0.0, normalization percentiles 1.0−99.0 and dynamic Niter iterations 200. Generated images were subsequently analyzed in CellProfiler  83  . Cardiomyocytes were identified by filtering segmented objects based on α-actinin intensity, size and eccentricity to exclude non-cardiomyocytes, cell aggregates and obliquely sectioned cells. Minimum Feret diameter (MinFerDia) was extracted for each cardiomyocyte as a proxy for cross-sectional cell size (17,864 cardiomyocytes total across the 12 patients). For visualization (Extended Data Fig.  2i ), per-patient median minimum Feret diameter was used. The full per-cell dataset is provided in Supplementary Data  16 .  Statistical analyses were performed in R using linear mixed-effects models to account for the hierarchical structure of the data. Experimental group (NF/pRV/RVF for human studies and sham/mild-RVF/severe-RVF for mouse studies) was modeled as a fixed effect. Subject identity was included as a random intercept for all analyses, and slide was additionally included as a random intercept for mouse studies to account for repeated measurements obtained from the same specimen and histologic section. Pairwise group comparisons were performed using estimated marginal means with Benjamini−Hochberg correction for multiple testing.    Clustering parameters  All clustering analyses used the following parameters unless otherwise specified. For bulk RNA-seq WGCNA, a soft-thresholding power was selected using the pickSoftThreshold function to achieve approximate scale-free topology. For snRNA-seq analysis, SCTransform normalization was applied with mitochondrial read percentage regressed out. PCA was computed using the top 3,000 variable features, and 50 principal components were retained for downstream analysis. Nearest neighbor graphs were constructed using FindNeighbors with  k  = 20. Clustering was performed using FindClusters with the Louvain algorithm. Clustering resolution was selected in a semi-supervised manner: nuclei were clustered at a range of resolutions (0.1−2.0), and the resolution yielding biologically interpretable clusters with distinct marker genes was selected. For the 12 major cell types, the default Seurat resolution of 0.8 was used. For subclustering, a resolution of 0.5 was used for fibroblast, endothelial, myeloid, mural and natural killer/T lineages. Cardiomyocyte subclustering used a resolution of 0.3. For EC hdWGCNA, seven modules were identified using a soft-thresholding power automatically selected via the pickSoftThreshold function to approximate scale-free topology. For Xenium subclustering, 30 principal components were used with resolutions of 0.3 (cardiomyocytes) to 0.5 (all other cell types). UMAP was computed using RunUMAP with n.neighbors = 30 and min.dist = 0.3.   Quantification and statistical analysis  Details of specific statistical analyses for each section, sample sizes and statistical tests used are given in the  Methods  and in the corresponding figure legends. All analysis was done in R using primarily custom-written scripts, which are available with deposited data, and the Seurat package. For pseudobulk DE, DESeq2 was run independently for each cell subtype, and pairwise disease comparison and  P  values were adjusted for multiple testing within each analysis using the Benjamini−Hochberg procedure. Cross-subtype correction was not applied, as each subtype−comparison pair tests an independent biological question.     Software and versions  Analyses were performed in R version 4.3.3. Bulk RNA-seq processing used Trimmomatic version 0.39, kallisto version 0.51.1, tximport version 1.30.0, DESeq2 version 1.42.1 with apeglm version 1.24.0 shrinkage, sva version 3.50.0, edgeR version 4.0.16 and WGCNA version 1.73. Xenium data were processed with Proseg version 1.1.9 and Sopa version 2.2.10 and analyzed with spacexr (RCTD) version 2.2.1, SPLIT version 0.1.3, SpaGE (GitHub commit edd0fb70; no tagged releases) and CellChat version 3. Histology was analyzed in Fiji/ImageJ version 1.54p, Cellpose version 3.1.1.2 and CellProfiler version 4.2.8. Flow cytometry was acquired with FACSDiva version 9.1, gated in FlowJo version 11.1.0 and reanalyzed with flowWorkspace version 4.14.3 and ggcyto version 1.30.2. Genotype-driven tumor ecosystems drive immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in melanoma.

Background

Genetic and transcriptional alterations in cancer cells shape their interactions with immune and stromal compartments, thereby influencing tumor progression, immune evasion, and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Yet, how these interactions are spatially organized within melanoma and how they relate to clinical outcome remains incompletely understood.

Methods

We used spatial multi-omic profiling on melanoma tissues from patients, compared those with loss-of-function mutations in the Neurofibromin 1 (NF1) tumor suppressor gene to those with intact NF1, and integrated these results with functional studies and subsequent gene expression changes observed in patient-derived melanoma models and an immunotherapy-resistant syngeneic mouse model.

Results

Spatial multi-omic analysis of melanoma tissues from patients identified 12 meta-niches composed of distinct cell populations with unique molecular features. Although all tumors contained these meta-niches, those enriched in immunosuppressive cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and macrophages were significantly more common in tumors with NF1 loss. Conversely, niches enriched in cytotoxic CD8+ T cells were significantly reduced. In both human and mouse melanoma, NF1 loss was associated with impaired antigen-presentation programs and reduced CD8+ T cell infiltration. Mechanistically, EGFR signaling emerged as a prominent feature of NF1-deficient melanoma ecosystems and correlated with reduced expression of antigen-presentation genes and T cell exclusion. EGFR inhibition restored the expression of antigen-presentation programs and enhanced antitumor immune responses in a syngeneic Nf1 knockdown model resistant to ICIs.

Conclusions

These findings define spatially organized, functionally distinct meta-niches enriched in NF1-mutant melanoma that may contribute to their aggressive disease features and poor ICI response. Our study links an understudied melanoma driver to specific immune-evasion mechanisms and identifies EGFR inhibition as a candidate strategy to improve outcomes in patients with NF1-mutant melanoma resistant to immunotherapy.
