evidence_text:
DeSpaST: deconvoluting spatial transcriptomics signals to cell-level resolution using histology images. Advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies enable spatially resolved gene expression profiling, yet most platforms remain limited to spot-level resolution, where each measurement aggregates signals from multiple cells and obscures cell-specific programs and microenvironmental interactions. Existing computational approaches either provide limited sub-spot refinement or rely on matched single-cell RNA sequencing references that are costly and difficult to obtain. Here, we present DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network that deconvolves spot-level ST data into cell-level gene expression profiles using only paired histology images. DeSpaST extracts nucleus-level morphological features, constructs directed cellular interaction graphs, and integrates spatial and transcriptional information through message passing. Validated across four cancer datasets with orthogonal Xenium, immunofluorescence, ablation, and interslice evaluations, DeSpaST enhances spatial resolution, facilitates downstream cellular-level analyses, and provides deeper insights into tissue biology. Background  Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have made significant progress in transitioning transcriptomic research from the cell level to a 2D spatial cell system. This transition is crucial for investigating cell–cell communication, tissue heterogeneity, and the tumor microenvironment, offering new insights into intricate biological processes. In contrast to single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), which requires tissue dissociation, ST technologies profile gene expression and preserve the spatial composition of cells within the native tissue environment [ 1 ]. ST technologies (e.g. 10× Genomics Visium [ 2 ], Nanostring GeoMx DSP [ 3 ], HDST [ 4 ], and Slide-seq [ 5 ]) utilize unique spatial barcodes to label the spatial locations and capture the gene expression at thousands of barcoded spatial locations (referred to as spots) within one experiment [ 6 ]. While these methods achieve high detection efficiency, their spatial resolution is inherently limited. The barcoded spot area (Spot diameter: 10× Genomics Visium: 55 μm, Nanostring GeoMx DSP: 10 μm [ 7 ], and Slide-seq: 10 μm [ 8 ]) encompasses a diverse population of cells, ranging from a few cells up to 200 cells [ 9 ]. To accurately distinguish the mixed-cell populations and uncover biological inferences from the ST data, it is essential to develop computational models that can enhance the resolution of ST data.  Several computational methods have been developed to improve the spatial resolution of ST data. Bayesian-based methods such as BayesSpace [ 10 ] refine gene expression to sub-spot resolution, only yielding modest improvement. Deep-learning-based approaches such as SPOTlight [ 11 ], Tangram [ 12 ], cell2location [ 13 ], and CARD [ 14 ] integrate ST data with scRNA-seq data, mapping related gene expression cells to ST coordinates or reconstructing the ST landscape from various cell combinations. However, the reliance on scRNA-seq data significantly raises the experimental costs and introduces constraints, including limited cell types and potential biases in spatial reconstruction accuracy.  Instead of relying on the scRNA-seq data, integrating histology images with ST data presents a more feasible and promising way to enhance ST resolution. Most ST platforms, such as Visium and HDST, typically provide corresponding histology images, like hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining images, which offer high-resolution morphological and spatial information for individual cells across the tissue sections. Deep-learning-based methods such as TESLA [ 15 ], XFuse [ 16 ], and iStar [ 17 ] have been developed to integrate the histology image with ST data to enhance ST resolution. However, these methods primarily enhance resolution at the pixel level but fall short of achieving cell-level gene expression resolution. Furthermore, these methods focus on extracting pixel level histological features [e.g. pixel intensities in red, green, blue (RGB) channels], neglecting true cell features and cell–cell interactions, which compromises model accuracy. A specialized model that directly incorporates actual cell-level features is necessary to improve the biological application of ST data.  Many fundamental biological questions—including the delineation of cell-type boundaries, characterization of the tumor microenvironment, and inference of cell–cell communication—inherently require cell-level resolution. However, true single-cell spatial assays such as Xenium or MERFISH remain expensive, limited in gene panel size, and not universally available, making spot-level ST the dominant modality in practice. Moreover, matched scRNA-seq data from the same tissue, which several existing deconvolution methods depend on, is not always obtainable and may introduce additional biases when tissue dissociation alters cell-type composition. A computational approach that can reliably infer cell-level expression directly from spot-level ST data and routine histology images therefore addresses a practical and widely encountered gap in the field.  In this work, we developed an innovative model called DeSpaST (Deconvoluting Spatial Transcriptomics Signals to Cell-Level Resolution Using Histology Images), which incorporates the cell level features from histology image with ST data using dynamic edge–conditioned graph convolution neural network ( Fig. 1 , and  Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Starting with a histology image, we perform cell segmentation and explicitly extract cell morphological and spatial interaction features, followed by constructing the cellular graphic interaction structures of the tissue. We then build a graph deconvolution model that combines ST data with these morphological features and interaction structures to deconvolute spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression profiles. In contrast to the previous methods that primarily rely on pixel-level information and use convolutional neural network (CNN)-like structures to encode the features, which often failing to capture cell–cell interaction information. DeSpaST leverages the graph convolutional networks (GCNs) to fully capture the cellular interaction topologies by constructing cellular interaction graphic structures. Unlike conventional CNNs, GCNs operate on non-Euclidean data structures, enabling comprehensive modeling of diverse cellular interaction topologies.    Figure 1   Illustration of DeSpaST in uncovering cell-level gene expression. (a) Workflow of DeSpaST: The DeSpaST model integrates histology images with spatial transcriptomics (ST), encompassing cell segmentation, extraction of cell features, construction of cellular graphic structures, and the application of Graphic Convolution blocks for the precise deconvolution of cell-level gene expression. (b) Illustration of DeSpaST's application to human breast cancer tissue. Two genes  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  are shown as examples. From left to right includes H&E image, H&E image with pathologist annotations, DeSpaST  ERBB2  gene expression, Visium  ERBB2  gene expression, TESLA  ERBB2  gene expression, DeSpaST  MS4A1  gene expression, Visium  MS4A1  gene expression, and TESLA  MS4A1  gene expression. (c) Zoomed-in sub-region for detailed representation of orange box in panel b H&E image. (d) Zoomed-in sub-region for detailed representation of red box in panel (b) H&E image.            Multi-panel scientific figure showing the DeSpaST workflow and its application to breast cancer tissue. The workflow combines H&E histology, spatial transcriptomics, cell segmentation, cellular graph construction, and graph convolution to predict cell-level gene expression. Tissue maps compare H&E images, pathologist annotations, and ERBB2 and MS4A1 expression from DeSpaST, Visium, and TESLA, with zoomed regions highlighting tumor and immune-cell boundaries.         DeSpaST offers several practical advantages. First, it does not require scRNA-seq references, reducing experimental cost and avoiding dependence on matched dissociated-cell datasets. Second, it leverages morphology and local tissue architecture to improve spatial localization and denoising within spots, which is particularly valuable in heterogeneous tumors where boundaries and niches vary over short distances. Third, DeSpaST’s inferred cell-level expression supports downstream analyses that are difficult at spot resolution, such as cell-type mapping at cellular granularity, spatial domain characterization, and trajectory inference. In our experiments, these advantages manifest as improved agreement with orthogonal measurements (e.g. Xenium), clearer spatial patterns, and improved recovery of spatial domains, with robustness supported by ablations demonstrating that performance depends on both transcriptional input and morphology rather than visual cues alone. Together, these considerations motivate DeSpaST as a practical and interpretable approach for cell-level resolution inference from spot-based ST, while clarifying the conditions under which it is most reliable.    Result   Overview of the DeSpaST model  DeSpaST requires only two inputs: a histology image and ST data ( Fig. 1a ). Histology images offer the individual cell spatial organization and morphology characterization, while the ST data provide gene expression at the spot level. To explicitly extract the cell spatial and organization characterizations from the histology image, we first employed the HD-staining deep-learning algorithm [ 18 ,  19 ] to segment and classify the cell nucleus from the tissue image. Alternatively, other methods for cell or nuclei segmentation could also be applied at this step. We then extracted the morphology features for each cell to construct the cellular graphic structures (see  Fig. 1a  and  Method  section for details). DeSpaST builds the graphic convolution networks by performing the four following steps: (i) extract image patches based on the spot coordinates in the ST data; (ii) construct a directed cellular graphic structure for each patch using nearest neighbors based on the Euclidean distance from a cell to its neighbors; and (iii) derive features from the directed cellular graphic structures to incorporate the spatial and morphology information of the cells into the graph convolutional network. Each node in the graph represents a cell. Node features include cell size, shape, and other morphological features. Edges denote spatial and morphological relationships between cells. Edge features include cell spatial proximity, cell connectivity angle, and interaction edge categorization ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ) [ 4 ]. The model is then constructed using two convolutional layers and one fully connected layer ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). All cell nodes are updated through a message passing from all neighboring nodes in each convolutional layer, which incorporates both morphological and cell–cell spatial interaction features of neighboring cells. In this study, we demonstrate DeSpaST’s ability in accurately capturing cell-level gene expression to overcoming spatial resolution limitations in ST data, using breast, lung, and ovarian cancer datasets as examples. DeSpaST offers a new convenient tool for advancing biomedical research, with broad applicability to diverse spatial transcriptomics datasets.    DeSpaST effectively enhances gene expression resolution  To assess the efficacy of DeSpaST, we applied the model to a well-studied breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. We then conducted a comparative analysis of DeSpaST’s performance against the TESLA model [ 15 ], which is a machine-learning framework designed to enhance gene expression to pixel-level resolution [ 15 ]. DeSpaST demonstrated notable advancements in elucidating gene expression patterns. To illustrate, we present two marker genes,  MS4A1  and  ERBB2 , as representative examples ( Fig. 1b ). The  MS4A1  gene encodes the surface molecule CD20, which serves as a widely recognized marker indicative of B-cell lineage [ 21 ].  ERBB2  encodes the human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2) protein [ 22 ], which is used as a tumor marker in breast cancer diagnosis [ 23 ,  24 ]. For each gene, the cell-level gene expression profile from DeSpaST, spot-level gene expression pattern from Visium ST data, and the pixel-level gene expression patterns from TESLA ( Fig. 1b ), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ) were plotted separately. Compared to Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse, DeSpaST showed the gene expression profiles with highest clarity and precision for both genes, successfully enhancing the gene expression resolution. Notably, the gene expression patterns from DeSpaST correlated well with the pathologist-annotated regions. DeSpaST high  ERBB2  gene expression cells closely matched the pathologist-annotated tumor regions. Also, the DeSpaST high  MS4A1  expressed cells were well aligned with the annotated immune cell regions. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse did not achieve the same level of visual clarity as DeSpaST in these regions. The  MS4A1  gene expression profile is particularly noteworthy because it is nearly imperceptible in the Visium ST data and in the reconstructions produced by TESLA ( Fig. 1b , right), iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3b ), whereas DeSpaST accurately discerns the  MS4A1  gene expression pattern and immune cell regions.  Remarkably, DeSpaST’s cell-level gene expression predictions demonstrate its capability and reliability in distinguishing between different cell layers. In three specific areas ( Fig. 1c  and  d , and  Supplementary Fig. S4 ), pathologists meticulously annotated the invasive carcinoma and immune cell regions to delineate their boundaries in the H&E images. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST effectively differentiated between these immune cell and tumor cell regions. DeSpaST accurately captured the elevated expression of ERBB2 in tumor regions and the elevated expression of MS4A1 in immune cell regions. The distinct gene expression patterns of MS4A1 and ERBB2 predicted by DeSpaST ( Fig. 1c  and  d  ,  and  Supplementary Fig. S4b ) precisely delineated the tumor and immune boundaries. In contrast, Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse could not accurately delineate these cell layers and boundaries ( Supplementary Fig. S3a  and  b ); instead, they only provided ambiguous patterns, which indicates a lack of precision in defining the regions. Moreover, as shown in  Supplementary Fig. S4c , DeSpaST demonstrated exceptional potential in precise cell type annotation. Beyond the highly expressed ERBB2 tumor region, DeSpaST identified an additional layer outside the tumor region with abundant MS4A1 expression, which had not been previously annotated. Upon closer examination of the H&E image by the pathologist, the layer was found to be a lightly stained layer, containing fibrous connective tissues interspersed with inflammatory cells, crucial for restricting tumor expansion. This finding of interspersed immune cells is consistent with the MS4A1 gene expression pattern predicted by DeSpaST.    DeSpaST accurately predicts cellular-level gene expression  The above comparison between pathology annotation and DeSpaST highlights the resolution enhancement power of DeSpaST. To further evaluate the model’s performance, we conducted a direct and comprehensive comparison of cellular-level expression for individual genes. In addition to the Visium spot-level gene expression measurement, Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] also measured the cellular-level gene expression of hundreds of genes through the Xenium experiment. We applied DeSpaST to this breast cancer Visium dataset from Janesick  et al . [ 25 ], segmented and classified the cell nucleus from the H&E image ( Supplementary Fig. S5 ), and deconvolving spot-level ST signals into cell-level gene expression profiles. Despite the inherent limitations of adjacent-section comparisons (e.g. local distortion, cell displacement, and microenvironmental differences), DeSpaST showed strong concordance with Xenium in spatial distribution patterns. For example, for the breast cancer marker gene  CCND1  [ 26 ,  27 ] ( Fig. 2a ) and T-cell marker gene  CD69  [ 28 ,  29 ] ( Fig. 2b ), DeSpaST accurately predicted the gene expression patterns, in agreement with the observed patterns in the Xenium. Both Visium and TESLA failed to resolve these patterns adequately, especially in the complex tissue regions. Consider the top of the tissue section ( Fig. 2c  and  Supplementary Fig. S6a ) where intricate tumor and immune cell domains are present. Only DeSpaST successfully captured gene expression within intricate microenvironments ( Fig. 2d  and  e ), accurately reflecting the patterns observed in the Xenium experiment. Conversely, TESLA and Visium failed to capture these spatial variations in gene expression, resulting in unclear expression patterns. In the case of the  CD69  gene ( Fig. 2b ), the Visium ST data are noisy and lack a clear expression pattern. Although TESLA reduces some noise, it fails to capture the inherent gene expression patterns accurately. In contrast, DeSpaST effectively eliminates noise and accurately discerns the true gene expression pattern.    Figure 2   Evaluation of DeSpaST in cell-level gene expression prediction. (a) Comparison of CCND1 gene expression patterns across platforms: Visium (top left), DeSpaST (top right), Xenium (bottom left), and TESLA (bottom right). (b) Comparison of CD69 gene expression patterns across platforms: Visium (top left), DeSpaST (top right), Xenium (bottom left), and TESLA (bottom right). (c) A zoomed-in subregion of H&E image. (d) Zoomed-in subregion showcasing detailed CCND1 gene expression patterns. (e) Zoomed-in subregion showcasing detailed CD69 gene expression patterns. (f) Bar plots showing Pearson correlations with Xenium gene expression for DeSpaST, Visium, and TESLA (left, CCND1; right, CD69). (g) Pearson correlation analysis of all examined genes in Xenium: the left plot compares DeSpaST versus Visium performance ( x -axis: Visium correlation,  y -axis: DeSpaST correlation). The right plot compares TESLA versus Visium performance ( x -axis: Visium correlation,  y -axis: TESLA correlation).            Multi-panel comparison of cell-level gene expression prediction in breast cancer tissue. Spatial maps show CCND1 and CD69 expression from Visium, DeSpaST, Xenium, and TESLA. Zoomed H&E and expression panels highlight local tissue regions, and bar and scatter plots summarize Pearson correlations with Xenium for selected genes and all examined genes.         With the gene pattern identified by DeSpaST, our next step involves a quantitative assessment of the performance enhancement achieved by the DeSpaST model. To facilitate this assessment, spot-level gene expression was reconstructed by taking the average expression of cells inside each spot. For quantitative comparison across methods, we reconstructed spot-level expression by averaging the predicted cellular expressions within each Visium spot and then computed gene-wise Pearson correlations against Xenium for DeSpaST, raw Visium, TESLA, iStar, and XFuse ( Supplementary Fig. S3 ). DeSpaST exhibits a stronger correlation to Xenium ( r  = 0.754 for  CCND1  gene and  r  = 0.665 for  CD69  gene) than both Visium ( r  = 0.477 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.239 for  CD69  gene) and TESLA ( r  = 0.720 for  CCND1  gene, and  r  = 0.424 for  CD69  gene) ( Fig. 2f  and  Supplementary Fig. S3c ). Similar enhancements in clarity and noise reduction in gene expression patterns were observed in other genes as well, such as the  ERBB2  and  MS4A1  genes ( Supplementary Fig. S7 ). DeSpaST demonstrated strong consistency with Xenium experiments for both of these genes, achieving a correlation of  r  = 0.850 for the  ERBB2  gene and  r  = 0.610 for the  MS4A1  gene ( Supplementary Fig. S7c  and  d ). In addition to the above genes, to assess transcriptome-wide generalizability, we computed spot-level Pearson correlations for all examined Xenium genes and summarize the overall trend using correlation density plots ( Fig. 2g ;  Supplementary Fig. S3c ): DeSpaST achieves higher overall agreement with Xenium (median  r  = 0.518) than Visium (median  r  = 0.198) and TESLA (median  r  = 0.479), and the top 20% highest-density region summary consistently favors DeSpaST, indicating systematic improvement beyond a small set of marker genes.  To address the concern that histology-guided models might rely on visual cues and to validate key graph-construction hyperparameters, we performed a comprehensive set of ablation and sensitivity analyses ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). First, randomizing the input transcriptional counts (“Random count”) caused a substantial collapse in performance—gene-wise correlation with Xenium dropped (CD69:  r  = 0.188; CCND1:  r  = 0.379), the overall summary decreased (top 20% high-density mean correlation: 0.174), and downstream spatial domain agreement deteriorated (NMI: 0.033; ARI: 0.0196)—demonstrating that accurate transcriptional signals are essential and that morphology alone cannot recover meaningful spatial expression. Second, randomizing morphology features (“Random image info”) also reduced performance relative to the full model (e.g. CD69:  r  = 0.423 versus 0.665; top 20% high-density mean: 0.202 versus 0.582; NMI: 0.169 versus 0.194; ARI: 0.0910 versus 0.1167), indicating that morphology provides complementary information but is not solely responsible for DeSpaST’s gains. Finally, we evaluated the robustness of the k-nearest-neighbor (kNN) cell-graph parameter by varying        on the breast dataset: extreme values were suboptimal (e.g. top-20%-density mean correlation = 0.161 at        and 0.220 at       ), while intermediate values (      –12) consistently achieved higher performance (0.58–0.64) and stable domain-detection agreement, supporting our choice of        as a balance between locality and connectivity ( Supplementary Fig. S8 ). Together, these analyses show that DeSpaST integrates both transcriptional and morphological information and that its performance is stable across a biologically reasonable range of neighborhood sizes.  To further test whether the deconvoluted outputs preserve biologically meaningful spatial structure beyond individual marker genes, we evaluated each method using a downstream spatial domain detection task on the breast cancer 10× Visium dataset [ 20 ]. As shown in ( Supplementary Fig. S9 ), we used the manually annotated domains as ground-truth labels. For each tool, we took the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as input, constructed (i) an expression kNN graph in PCA space and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in 2D coordinate space, fused them into a hybrid connectivity matrix, and inferred domains using Leiden community detection (parameters reported in Supplementary Information). We then quantified concordance with manual annotations using NMI and ARI ( Supplementary Fig. S9b ; higher is better). DeSpaST achieved the best agreement with manual labels (NMI = 0.194; ARI = 0.117), outperforming iStar (NMI = 0.182; ARI = 0.056), XFuse (NMI = 0.033; ARI = 0.011), and TESLA (NMI = 0.143; ARI = 0.031), indicating that DeSpaST’s deconvolution better preserves domain-level organization for downstream spatial analyses.  Supplementary Fig. S9c  further visualizes the inferred domains from each method, where DeSpaST produces domain boundaries that are qualitatively more consistent with the expert annotations.  The remarkable cell-level resolution achieved by DeSpaST creates new possibilities for examining cell–cell communications within a spatial context. For instance, within the cellular milieu surrounding the breast ducts ( Supplementary Fig. S10 ), we detected elevated expressions of breast cancer marker genes  CCND1  and  ERBB2  ( Supplementary Fig. S10a  and  c ). In contrast, immune cell marker genes  CD69  and  MS4A1  ( Supplementary Fig. S10b  and  d ) exhibited high expression in the outside layer adjacent to the tumor cells. The gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST align with the Xenium gene panel, while TESLA failed to predict them accurately. DeSpaST’s findings suggest possible interactions between immune and tumor cells, highlighting its potential for further studies on the tissue microenvironment and cell–cell communication.    DeSpaST accurately captures the cell-level protein expression  As products of gene expression, protein expressions are generally correlated with differentially expressed mRNAs [ 30 ,  31 ]. Next, we evaluate whether the gene expression patterns obtained by DeSpaST could reflect protein expressions at the cell level [ 25 ]. We plotted and compared the  MS4A1  and  ERBB2  gene expression patterns with the corresponding HER2 and CD20 protein immunofluorescence (IF) signals ( Fig. 3a  and  b ). Interestingly, the gene expression patterns predicted by DeSpaST closely align with protein expression profiles, while Visium and TESLA are not able to capture them. We calculated the correlations between predicted  MS4A1  gene expression and Xenium IF CD20 protein signals. DeSpaST exhibits superior performance compared to TESLA and Visium with higher correlation ( r  = 0.622 for DeSpaST versus  r  = 0.420 for Visium and  r  = 0.401 for TESLA;  Fig. 3c ). DeSpaST also demonstrated a notably higher correlation of ERBB2 gene expression with HER2 protein expression ( r  = 0.839) when compared to Visium ( r  = 0.821) and TESLA ( r  = 0.660), as illustrated in  Fig. 3d . Although Visium and TESLA also showed good correlations with the HER2 IF signals, DeSpaST significantly outperformed them in predicting fine-grained details gene expression patterns ( Supplementary Fig. S11 ). Notably, only DeSpaST accurately captured the comprehensive pattern of ERBB2 gene expression, depicting the tumor’s shape around the breast duct in alignment with IF protein signals. In contrast, Visium and TESLA predicted a vague outline of ERBB2 expression, lacking finer details and failing to depict a clear pattern. Application of DeSpaST for cell type identification  Given the highly precise cell-level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST, we employed DeSpaST for downstream analysis. This involved leveraging the predicted cell-level gene expression to delineate the spatial distribution of various cell types. Unlike ST data, where one spot may contain multiple cells, DeSpaST’s cellular-level resolution offers a superior depiction of cell-type distribution. Utilizing DeSpaST’s gene expression predictions as input, we applied the cell-type identification algorithm ScType [ 32 ] to assign the cell type to each single cell. The resulting cell-type profiles were mapped back onto the spatial location and detected locations for tumor cells, lymphocytes, fibroblasts, and macrophages ( Supplementary Fig. S12a ). To validate the cell-type distribution by DeSpaST, we implemented the ScType algorithm with the Xenium data and plotted the cell-type distribution in  Supplementary Fig. S12b . The spatial distributions of annotated cell types from DeSpaST closely resemble the cell types obtained from Xenium, which further substantiate the accuracy of DeSpaST. To reveal the tumor’s immunological response, we specifically focus on tumor cells and immune cells ( Fig. 4a  and  b ). Both DeSpaST ( Fig. 4a ) and Xenium panel ( Fig. 4b ) delineated similar tumor and immune cell regions. Heterogeneous areas are found at the upper and middle portion of the tissue where tumor and immune cells closely interact, which indicates the recognition and attack of activated immune cells that impede tumor spread. In contrast, tumor regions at the lower portion of the slides appear less confined, forming dense and more aggressive tumor areas where there is a lack of immune cell control. Both Xenium and DeSpaST accurately classify these complex cell environments. While Xenium served as a valuable reference here, DeSpaST exhibits greater potential and offers the flexibility to include more marker genes for cell type classification analysis. Unlike Xenium's panel of 306 genes, DeSpaST can leverage the transcriptomic level gene expression data from ST data. This enables the inclusion of a wider range of cell-type markers, leading to more accurate classification.    Figure 4   Application of DeSpaST in spatial cell-level downstream analysis. The partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) method was used to construct the topological graph and a cluster with high expression of cancer stem cell marker  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ] was selected as the root node ( Supplementary Fig. S13 ). Discussion  In this paper, we presented DeSpaST, which is a graphic deconvolution model that integrates the cell morphology features from histology images with spatial transcriptomic data to predict the cellular resolution gene expression for cells across the tissue section. Unlike other methods that only enhance the ST resolution, DeSpaST stands out as the first model to directly infer cell-level gene expression from histology images and ST data. DeSpaST is innovative and beneficial in that it takes advantage of the histology images and explicitly models the spatial organization of cells. By constructing the cellular graphic structure, cell morphology and interaction information from histology images were successfully input to the GCN model as nodes and edges, respectively. GCN, with its capability to handle complex non-Euclidean structures, enables deconvolution at cell-level resolution by well aligning with the diverse and intricate cellular interaction topologies. We demonstrated the high accuracy, resolution, robustness, and efficacy of DeSpaST in this paper. This model can be easily applied to diverse types of tissues and ST data.  The cellular-level gene expression inferred from DeSpaST offers powerful support to many biomedical applications. In this study, we applied DeSpaST’s output to the spatial cell type annotation and inferred the pseudotime trajectories of tumor development. DeSpaST offers the cellular resolution for cell type identification compared to traditional spot-level cell type identification. DeSpaST clearly illustrates the cell types for individual cells, enabling the revelation of cell–cell interaction in the tumor microenvironment and providing valuable insights into tumor immunology studies. Pseudotime analysis further uncovers the pseudo-temporal trajectories of tumor progression, revealing distinct clusters of early- and late-stage cancer cells. The high precision of DeSpaST establishes a reliable foundation for subsequent spatial transcriptomics analyses, such as deriving differentially expressed genes and exploring cell–cell communication inference.  A key limitation of our evaluation is that the Xenium measurements used for validation are obtained from an adjacent FFPE section, rather than the exact same section profiled by Visium. Although adjacent-section validation is often necessary in practice because assays are destructive or mutually exclusive, it is inherently imperfect: consecutive sections can exhibit local tissue distortion during sectioning and mounting, cell displacement, partial-volume differences, and subtle microenvironmental heterogeneity (e.g. immune infiltration near boundaries). These factors can weaken strict quantitative comparability even when broad spatial trends remain visually similar. Therefore, the agreement we observe between DeSpaST predictions and Xenium should be interpreted primarily as qualitative and semi-quantitative evidence that DeSpaST recovers coherent spatial gene-expression patterns and microenvironmental structure, rather than as an absolute quantitative ground truth at single-cell resolution. To mitigate this limitation, we emphasize evaluations that do not require one-to-one cell correspondence across sections—such as region-level pattern concordance, marker-consistent localization, and spot-level correlations computed after aggregating predicted cells within each Visium spot—and we further assess whether predicted cell-level signals support consistent tissue organization using downstream spatial domain analyses.  Beyond the cross-section validation constraints discussed above, several additional limitations should be noted. First, DeSpaST’s accuracy depends on the upstream nucleus segmentation step; segmentation errors such as missed nuclei, over-segmentation, or misclassification propagate to the graph construction and deconvolution. Second, genes with very low or near-zero expression in the Visium data are inherently difficult to deconvolve, as there is minimal transcriptional signal to distribute among cells. Third, standardized simulation frameworks that jointly model realistic histology with spatially structured single-cell expression are not yet available, and matched single-cell spatial datasets with paired Visium and H&E inputs remain scarce, precluding direct ground-truth validation at single-cell resolution. Despite these limitations, DeSpaST demonstrates consistent improvements across multiple complementary evaluation criteria and tissue types.  In addition to uncovering cellular gene expression in ST data, DeSpaST holds the potential for deconvoluting cellular protein expression in spatial proteomics. Recently, numerous spatial proteomic methods have been developed to enable the direct detection of protein molecules with spatial variability. However, the resolution remains limited, typically operating at spot sizes around 20–100 μm [ 42–45 ]. The application of DeSpaST to improve the resolution of spatial proteomics encourages further exploration of spatially cellular protein expression.  DeSpaST is designed for broad applicability, leveraging histology images and ST data as input to uncover cellular-level expression. Its capabilities can be further extended by incorporating additional data sources. For example, if single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are available from the same tissue or a similar sample, DeSpaST can integrate it as a cell type constraint, potentially improving the deconvolution accuracy. This is particularly valuable when dealing with very weak sequencing signals in ST data, as scRNA-seq offers higher sequencing depth. An additional enhancement for DeSpaST could involve its extension to 3D spatial transcriptomes. Recently, spatially resolved transcriptomic atlases in high-dimensional data have emerged to revolutionize the understanding of cell interaction and gene regulation within the organ. Organ-level 3D spatial transcriptomics [ 46–48 ] or proteomics [ 49 ] were reconstructed from serial 2D tissue sections. DeSpaST, with a potential 3D GCN version, could leverage these data’s complexity to learn 3D spatial cell features and deconvolute gene expression. This is particularly relevant as current 3D spatial transcriptomes often miss data between sections. DeSpaST can potentially address this gap and provide a more complete picture of the 3D spatial transcriptomic landscape.    Method   Datasets   Human breast cancer datasets 1  Two human breast cancer datasets were employed for constructing and validating the DeSpaST model. The first human breast cancer dataset consists of Visium ST data for DCIS and Invasive Carcinoma FFPE human breast cancer tissue. This dataset contains 2518 spots, with 5244 median genes per spot and a sequencing depth of 32 524 reads per spot.    Human breast cancer datasets 2  The second human breast cancer dataset is associated with a recently released Xenium  in situ  platform [ 25 ]. This research conducted a comprehensive analysis with three complementary technologies (Chromium, Visium, Xenium) on a single breast-cancer FFPE tissue. The Visium output ST data were used to deconvolute the cell-level gene expression using DeSpaST, which contains 4992 spots, with 5712 median genes per spot and 40 003 mean reads per spot. The Xenium panels were used as a reference standard to evaluate DeSpaST’s cell-level resolution prediction. Additionally, IF staining was performed after Xenium to assess the expression profiles of HER2 and CD20 proteins. The results from both the Xenium panel and the subsequent IF staining were then used to verify the effectiveness of DeSpaST.    Human ovarian cancer dataset  The human ovarian cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 4674 spots, with 8792 median genes per spot.    Human lung cancer dataset  The human lung cancer dataset is obtained from 10× Genomics and contains 6195 spots, with 10 087 median genes per spot.     Spatial transcriptomics data preprocessing and image feature extraction  Spatial transcriptomics data were first preprocessed prior to analysis. Gene expression values in the spot barcode profile matrix were normalized to counts per million (CPM). To mitigate the impact of outliers, the normalized CPM values were scaled to the 95th percentile.  The cell morphology features were extracted from H&E images using HD-Staining (Histology-based Digital Staining of Pathology Images) [ 18 ], which is an automatic deep-learning model that simultaneously segments and classifies cell nuclei, as well as provides morphology information about each identified cell nucleus. The extracted morphological features encompassed the centroid position, cell area, convex area, eccentricity, extent, filled area, major axis length, minor axis length, orientation, perimeter, solidity, and probability. In addition, we further enriched DeSpaST by incorporating 1024-dimensional intermediate box features and 256-dimensional mask features derived from the HD-Staining model. These cell morphological features were incorporated into the construction of DeSpaST.    Cellular graphic structure construction  We initially divided whole-slide H&E images into 250 × 250-pixel patches centered on the Visium spots. In total, we generated 2518 patches for the 10× Visium human breast cancer dataset, 4992 patches for the Janesick  et al . [ 25 ] human breast cancer dataset, 4674 patches for the human ovarian cancer dataset, and 6195 patches for the human lung cancer dataset. For each patch, we first obtain each cell location by performing cell segmentation, then construct a directed graph structure by connecting the cells based on their spatial proximity. This graph structure was designed to incorporate at least eight nearest neighbors. Pairwise Euclidean distances between cell coordinates were computed to identify the nearest neighbors. For those patches with very low cell density (<8 cells), DeSpaST dynamically resized the patch to include at least eight neighboring cells. These directed graph structures captured the spatial relationship and connectivity among cells in the tissue.  Each graph structure consisted of two main components: nodes and edges. Nodes represent morphological features extracted through HD-Staining for individual cells. These node features have undergone global scaling as part of the preprocessing. Edges store information on edge categorization and edge spatial representation ( Supplementary Fig. S2 ). Edge categorization is determined based on the types of cells connected by each edge, which provides insight into the type of interactions between the connected cells. Here, we included a total of 49 combinations of edge categorizations across seven cell types ( Supplementary Fig. S2a ). Edge spatial representation refers to the spatial aspects of cell interactions, including the Cell Connectivity Angle and Spatial Proximity. Cell Connectivity Angle indicates the connectivity between neighboring cells and the directionality of these connections. Spatial Proximity reflects the physical distance between cells. Both nodes and edges collectively constitute the cellular graphic structure, which synergistically contributes to the definition of complex cellular relationships.    Auto graph convolutional network for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution  Following the construction of the cellular graphic structure and thoughtfully derived essential node and edge features, we employed dynamic edge-conditioned convolution to manage graphs of varying size and connectivity. This process is mathematically represented in Equation ( 1 ). The embedding vector of the convolution filter is then used to deconvolve the spot-level gene expression into cell-level gene expression. Our model-specific architecture comprises of three layers: two ECC (Edge-Conditioned Convolution) [ 50 ,  51 ] GCN layers [ 52 ,  53 ] followed by a ReLU activation function [ 54 ], and one linear transformation layer. Each ECC layer incorporates both node and edge feature embeddings for propagating information across the graph ( Supplementary Fig. S1 ). Image registration and result comparison   Immunofluorescence image and Xenium panel registration to hematoxylin and eosin images  In order to register the IF image and Xenium panel to the Visium corresponding H&E images and facilitate the comparison to the protein/RNA expression experiment, we employed skimage.transform package for image transformation. To achieve a precise and efficient registration, we systematically tested various combinations of angles and scales between the IF and H&E images. To optimize computing efficiency, we initially conducted tests with 10% scaled-down images to obtain approximate scale and angle adjustments. Subsequently, we fine-tuned the registration using the original scale.    DeSpaST model validation  We validate DeSpaST through the assessment of RNA expression and protein expression by utilizing data from the Xenium panel and IF images, respectively. Using the spatial information from Visium spot locations, we reconstructed the spot-level expression for DeSpaST, TESLA, Xenium panel, and IF protein expression. The accuracies of Visium ST data, TESLA, and the DeSpaST model were evaluated using the Pearson correlation coefficient with the Xenium panel and IF image.     Cell type analysis  To assign cell types to each predicted single cell, we adopted a fully automated cell-type identification algorithm, ScType [ 32 ], which utilizes the Xenium-tested marker gene as the selected cell markers. The cellular level gene expression predicted by DeSpaST was used as input. The Seurat package was used to normalize the data with the default LogNormalize method. We then use the Seurat FindNeighbors function with parameter dims = 1:50 and FindClusters function with resolution = 0.9, which results in 23 clusters. ScType was also applied with Xenium Breast Cancer Cell Marker panel. Each cluster was assigned to the cell type with the highest score, and clusters assigned the same cell type were merged into larger clusters.    Pseudotime analysis  The gene expression of tumor cells predicted by DeSpaST was extracted for pseudotime analysis. We first reduced the gene expression dimension using principal component analysis (PCA). Then, cell clustering was performed using the Leiden algorithm, which is a fast approach to ensure that all cells are well connected for downstream optimal trajectory inference [ 55 ]. Partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) [ 56 ] is used to construct a topological graph based on the cell partitions. The cluster with high expression of  ALDH1A 3 [ 33 ,  34 ], a gene marker of cancer stem cells, was selected as the trajectory root node. The Diffusion Pseudotime (DPT) method [ 57 ] was then applied to estimate pseudotime values, which represented the tumor cell dynamics. All analyses were performed using the SCANPY [ 58 ] Python packages.    Spatial domain detection  To assess whether each deconvolution method preserves biologically meaningful spatial structure at the domain level, we performed downstream spatial domain detection using the predicted cell-by-gene expression matrix together with per-cell spatial coordinates as inputs. For each method, we first constructed two neighborhood graphs: (i) an expression kNN graph in a low-dimensional transcriptomic space, obtained by PCA on the predicted expression matrix and kNN graph construction using Scanpy, yielding an expression connectivity matrix       ; and (ii) a spatial kNN graph in the 2D coordinate space using Euclidean neighbors, yielding a symmetric binary adjacency matrix       . We then fused these graphs into a hybrid connectivity matrix via a linear combination,        where       balances spatial proximity and transcriptional similarity. Finally, we applied Leiden community detection on       to infer spatial domains for each tissue section, using identical processing across methods; all parameters are reported in the Supplementary Information. Domain assignments were benchmarked against manual domain annotations (when available) using Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) and the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI).    Key Points    DeSpaST introduces a dynamic edge-conditioned graph convolutional network for deconvolving spot-level ST data into true cell-level-resolution gene profiles.    DeSpaST integrates spatial and morphological features from histology images to model cell–cell organization and improve accuracy.    Extensively benchmarked across multiple cancer datasets, outperforming existing methods in resolution and precision.    DeSpaST enables diverse applications, including cell-type annotation, tumor trajectory analysis, and cell–cell communication discovery, demonstrating its potential to provide new insights in various biological contexts. evidence_text:
Molecular characterization of large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung by multilayered omics analysis. Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is a rare type of lung cancer with a very poor prognosis, and its underlying molecular features remain elusive. Here, multi-omics analysis of 27 LCNEC cases along with seven small cell lung carcinomas is performed. The genomic and epigenomic alterations as well as the correlation of the genomic mutations with the pathological subtypes are characterized, which are not always consistent. Spatial omics analyses are also conducted, and most of the cases are successfully grouped into a high ASCL1 neuroendocrine (NE) subtype and high ASCL2 or YAP1 non-NE subtypes; however, an ambiguous state is observed for some specimens, which shows the simultaneous expression of NE and non-NE lineage markers. The findings of this study indicate that LCNEC may transit toward the NE or non-NE directions. By controlling the transcriptional regulatory networks of such elasticity, a new approach may be contemplated to overcome the pleiotropic therapeutic responses of LCNEC. Introduction  Lung cancer accounts for a large fraction of the high cancer mortality rate worldwide. To eradicate lung cancer, molecular characterization has rapidly progressed not only at the genome level, but also at the transcriptome, epigenome, and proteome levels. For the major subtypes, such as lung adenocarcinomas, mutations in driver genes have been identified, and molecular targeted drugs have been developed  1  . Immune cell-targeting approaches have also been established for the major cancer types  2  , including detailed clinical regimens for immune checkpoint blockage (ICB). Given the advances in treatment, the prognoses of lung cancer patients have markedly improved, particularly for those having drug-matched driver mutations or immune cell “hot” tumors, including tumors exhibiting a high tumor mutational burden (TMB) and tumors infiltrated with highly active immune cells  3  . Nonetheless, a large number of patients with lung cancer still lack rational therapies because the molecular pathology remains unclear.  Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) is a minor lung cancer type. It has a very poor prognosis with a 5-year survival rate of 17–57%  4 , 5  . Although it is relatively rare, it accounts for nearly 3% of total lung cancer cases; however, its molecular features are largely undefined. This lack of molecular data for each of the phenotypes hinders their precise diagnosis and optimal treatment, which render chemotherapy the standard treatment  6  , although the association between the genomic mutation patterns and the pathological phenotypes is unclear.  Some pioneering studies have been conducted for small cell lung carcinomas (SCLCs), which also belong to the same high-grade neuroendocrine carcinomas (HGNECs) along with LCNEC. SCLC also has a poor prognosis, with a 5-year survival rate of 5%  4  . Clinically, SCLCs are classified into neuroendocrine (NE) and non-neuroendocrine (non-NE) subtypes. Pathologically, the NE and non-NE subtypes may be further subdivided on the basis of the immunostaining patterns of lineage-associated transcription factors and activators, including the  ASCL1  and  NEUROD1  subtypes in NE and the  POU2F3  and  YAP1  subtypes in non-NE (designated as SCLC-A, SCLC-N, SCLC-P, and SCLC-Y subtypes)  7 , 8  . Some SCLC subtypes are also classified by inflammation patterns. SCLC-I may respond to ICB therapy because a large amount of immune cell infiltration is observed, which indicates that immunotherapy will show high efficacy  9 , 10  . The tumors of SCLC-I also exhibit high expression levels of epithelial–mesenchymal transition-related genes and various differentiation phenotypes. Recent studies have suggested that SCLC-I may overlap primarily with SCLC-Y  11 , 12  .  Based on the knowledge obtained from SCLC, several attempts have been made to characterize LCNEC at a molecular level, but only a limited number of studies have been published. This may be partly due to not only because LCNEC is a rare cancer subtype but also because the rate of cancer progression is so rapid that surgery is not an option for the majority of cases. Nevertheless, George et al.  13  , successfully generated the first dataset of LCNECs, in which the cases were classified in accordance with mutation patterns, with Type 1 having a  TP53  mutation only and Type 2 having  TP53  and  RB1  mutations. Another subtype, namely Type SCLC, is also defined by considering the expression patterns of a group of marker proteins. The first attempt was made to associate these types with the pathological (NE or non-NE; ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, or YAP1 types) subtypes, which were similarly defined as a case of SCLC; however, its correlation with clinical phenotypes remains unclear. In addition, the genomic mutational patterns may be even more complex, leaving a substantial number of relevant genomic features overlooked, such as large structural variants (SVs) and mutations occurring in repetitive regions  14 , 15  . Thus, extensive long-read whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analysis is necessary  16 – 18  , in which the DNA methylation status can be determined  19  .  The transcriptome knowledge of LCNEC remains even poorer, although transcriptome subtyping of LCNEC is expected to yield important information to reveal highly heterogeneous or versatile changes of their cancer cell phenotypes. Notably, LCNEC can display different expression profiles. The co-occurrence of lung adenocarcinoma or lung squamous cell carcinoma has been observed in approximately 12% of the cases  20  , indicating that parts of LCNEC may originate from a subgroup of these cancers, possibly through trans-differentiation. After emergence, the elastic nature of the transcriptome programs may be retained, thereby enabling a wide variety of phenotypes. To precisely understand the gene expression changes in LCNEC, further in-depth analysis of omics features is necessary, including those of the surrounding stromal and immune cells.  To elucidate the heterogeneous transcriptomic profiles of tumors in general, various spatial transcriptome technologies have been recently developed  21 – 23  . Using these spatial transcriptome techniques, various gene expression profiles are associated with tumor cell proliferation, and their changes into more malignant phenotypes in the complex tumor microenvironment (TME) have been established. Moreover, new insights into these phenotypes have been obtained, which cannot be clarified solely by analyzing their genomic mutations. The key factors influencing heterogeneous tumor phenotypes have been identified  24 , 25  . For LCNEC, such an approach will enable the precise molecular characterization of the genomic and multi-omics aberrations in LCNEC. Furthermore, this approach will provide insights into the biology of HGNEC.  Here, we show a series of systematic multi-omics studies of LCNEC, including WGS for 34 HGNEC specimens (27 and seven cases of LCNEC and SCLC, respectively). Moreover, 21 cases (LCNEC) were further subjected to long-read WGS analysis for SV and DNA methylation analyses. Spatial RNA profiling using Xenium in situ hybridization was conducted for all 34 HGNEC cases. Using the Xenium data, each cancer cell, even within a single case, was classified into one of the aforementioned subtypes. A similar characterization was also conducted for the surrounding stromal and immune cells. For network level analyses, sequence-based approaches were used, which included single-nucleus RNA-seq (snRNA-seq), Visium, and STOmics. The transcriptome profiles of tumor cells were also elucidated at the whole transcriptome level.    Results   Study design  Multi-omics analysis was conducted for 34 HGNEC cases (27 LCNEC and seven SCLC cases; Fig.  1a ). Based on pathological analysis using immunohistochemistry (IHC), these cancers were classified into four subtypes: 16, 3, 10, and 5 cases of ASCL1-positive (A-type), NEUROD1-positive (N-type), POU2F3-positive (P-type), and YAP1-positive (Y-type) subtypes, respectively (Supplementary Table  S1 ). Long-read WGS analysis (average sequencing depth of 58.5×; N50 read length of 14.5 kb in tumor genomes) was also conducted for 21 LCNECs (Supplementary Table  S2 ). The spatial gene expression data were collected for all 34 cases using Xenium (version 1 using the custom panel of 302 genes, Supplementary Table  S3 ). To validate the expressions of key genes, 13 cases were also analyzed by Xenium 5 k (Supplementary Table  S4 ). Visium analysis was conducted for 19 of the cases (Supplementary Tables  S5 ). The datasets of short-read WGS (average sequencing depth of 91.1× in the tumor genomes) and parts of the spatial omics analysis, which have been obtained for our previous study  26 , 27  , were also used. The statistics for the generated datasets are described in the supplementary information.    Fig. 1   Characterization of the LCNEC genomes.   a  Overview of the study.  b  OncoPrint of the point mutations and SVs for 21 cases. The samples in the plot are arranged by four subtypes (ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, and YAP1). TMB is shown above the plot. The percentages shown to the right of the plot indicate the mutation rate for the 21 samples. Genes were selected from highly mutated genes associated with cancer or reported in previous studies  13 , 91 , 92  . Gray squares indicate no mutation. Point mutations are all one colored square, but SV is displayed shorter than the point mutation.  c  Lollipop plots showing the locations of the mutations in the ADAMTS family. Blue, red, and green lollipops indicate a frameshift with deletion, nonsense mutations, and missense mutations, respectively. The vertical axis represents the number of mutations.  d  Mutations and IHC scores for cases classified by the George et al. subtype (G-subtype)  13  . The upper part shows the  TP53 ,  RB1 ,  STK11 , and  KEAP1  mutations, whereas the lower part shows the IHC score for ASCL1, NEUROD1, POU2F3, and YAP1. Gray squares indicate no mutation. The higher the IHC score, the darker the purple color. Type 1 was classified as a case with mutations in  TP53  and  STK11/KEAP1  and expressing NE markers. Type 2 was classified as a case with mutations in  TP53  and  RB1  but not expressing NE markers. Type SCLC was classified as a case with  TP53  and  RB1  mutations and expressing NE markers, and the others were classified as “Others”.  e  IHC scores of TTF-1 and ASCL1 by cases classified by the G-subtype. TTF-1 is shown in green, and ASCL1 is shown in red bar plots. Source data are provided as a Source Data file for ( e ).                     Genomic mutational features of LCNECs  Using the WGS data of the 21 LCNEC cases, their mutation patterns were characterized. Short and long-read datasets were used for detecting mainly point mutations and SVs, respectively. Overall, the average number of detected point mutations was 15.4 per Mb, which is far higher compared with other lung cancer subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S1a )  28  . This difference may be partly due to the fact that most patients with LCNEC (20 cases, 95%) have a smoking history, which is further supported by the observation that their mutational signatures showed a high proportion of tobacco-related signatures, including SBS4, ID3, and DBS2 (Supplementary Fig.  S1b ).   TP53  and  RB1  mutations are present in 90% (19 cases) and 57% (12 cases) of the cases, respectively (Fig.  1b , Supplementary Fig.  S1c ), which is consistent with a previous study  13  . The long-read data were also used to detect mutations that were not covered by short-read data. For example, a 46.5-kb duplication was detected in  RB1 , and a 37.7-kb deletion included the  STK11  region. In the present study,  RB1  mutations were detected in all P-type cases. Mutations in other tumor-suppressor genes, such as  STK11  (five cases), were spread across the subtypes. Interestingly, a series of mutations was detected in the ADAMTS family genes as frequently as those in the LCNEC signature genes (76%, Fig.  1c , Supplementary Fig.  S1d ).  ADAMTS12  was previously reported as a frequently mutated gene in LCNECs  13  . The  ADAMTS20  gene was also mutated in six cases, followed by three cases containing  ADAMTS9  and  ADAMTS12  mutations, thereby indicating their potential application as marker genes for this cancer subtype. Moreover, all three  ADAMTS12 -mutant cases were classified as A-type tumors. This gene family encodes a metalloprotease, and it is associated with anti-tumor immunity and inflammation  29  . Several studies have indicated that this gene family may have a functional role in lung cancers (also see below section of the in vitro assays)  30  .  Among all LCNEC cases, the overall mutation rate was highly variable. The total number of mutations in protein-coding genes showed no significant difference between the NE and non-NE subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S1e ). A case of the highest mutation rate (tkbhgnec6) involved a patient who received neo-adjuvant therapy, which could be explained by the effects of the anti-cancer drug. Two of the cases (tkbhgnec10 and tkbhgnec13), which showed low mutation rates, involved younger patients. Compared with other cases, no  TP53  mutation was detected in these two cases. One of the cases, tkbhgnec10, harbored a  KRAS  G12 mutation, which is a well-known driver mutation for lung cancers  31 , 32   but very rare in LCNEC.    Relationship of genomic mutations with clinical or pathological subtypes  In this study, the relationship between the clinical/pathological subtypes and the observed mutational patterns was precisely examined. Based on George et al. classification scheme  13   (referred to as the “G-subtype” in this study), the 21 LCNEC cases were classified into Type 1 (NE type:  TP53  [and  STK11/KEAP1 ] mutation-positive and  RB1  mutation-negative) and Type 2 (non-NE type:  TP53  mutation-positive and  RB1  mutation-positive). In this study, only two and five cases were categorized as Type 1 and 2, respectively (Fig.  1d ). Five cases were classified as Type SCLC with NE properties. The remaining nine (43%) cases were unclassified.  The relationship between the IHC profiles of the representative diagnostic markers and the subtypes was also examined. The results showed that Type 1 cases overlapped with the NE type and exhibited a high expression of ASCL1. The expression level of TTF-1/NKX2-1 was also high (Fig.  1e ), which is consistent with a previous report indicating that TTF-1 is involved in the maintenance of NE properties (Supplementary Fig.  S1f ,  g )  33  . However, no TTF-1/NKX2-1 expression was detected in Type 2 LCNEC cases, which belong to the non-NE type. Most of the P-type cases belonged to Type 2, whereas all of the Type SCLC tumors exhibited TTF-1/NKX2-1 expression along with ASCL1 expression. Overall, no significant correlation was observed between ASCL1 and TTF-1/NKX2-1 expression (Pearson’s correlation coefficient = 0.10, Fig.  1e ), indicating that these two networks may be under distinct regulatory programs. Interestingly, in several cases, IHC showed a double-positive (DP) pattern for ASCL1 and YAP1 (Fig.  1d ), although their expression was supposed to be mutually exclusive as subtype markers (see spatial transcriptome analysis below for further details on this issue). These patterns have also been reported in other studies  10 , 34  .    Long-read data detects complex genomic structures in the LCNEC genome  We hypothesized that the patterns of the SVs or aberrant DNA methylation as detected by the long reads may be useful for the classification of LCNECs. For SVs, LCNEC genomes harbored a large number of rearranged regions compared with other lung cancer types analyzed in previous studies  16 , 18  . In addition, the SV patterns were distinct from that of point mutations for each subtype (Fig.  2a ). The N-type tumors harbored significantly lower numbers of SVs ( P  < 0.05; Welch’s  t -test, Fig.  2b ), whereas the Y-type tumors contained a larger number of SVs compared with other subtypes ( P  = 0.11; not statistically significant, Fig.  2b ). Moreover, in many cases, the SVs were associated with repetitive regions, including long interspersed element 1 (L1, LINE-1), which is a mobile repeating element in the human genome. Abnormal L1 retrotranspositions have been identified in several tumors, and they may cause the deletion of tumor-suppressor genes, complex structural abnormalities, and oncogenes amplifications  35 , 36  . For example, a large number of L1 insertions were detected in tkbhgnec8 (a case categorized as “Others” in the above-mentioned G-subtype classification), indicating that L1 transposition became active at a certain phase of tumor progression (Fig.  2c ). Using the single breakend SV module of Nanomonsv  37  , which enables repeat-associated ambiguous alignments, candidate SVs were successfully detected in a comprehensive manner (Fig.  2d ). SVs frequently overlapped with known cancer-related genes. In tkbhgnec3 (another case of “Others”),  NF1  was disrupted by a rearrangement occurring at the repetitive region (Fig.  2e ). The disruptions in  PTEN  were detected in two cases, which were both non-NE tumors (Fig.  2e ). For tkbhgnec8, which contained the largest number of L1-associated SVs,  PTEN  translocations with chromosome 2 were detected. A partial human L1 sequence was inserted into the breakpoint, indicating that the L1 transposition event may have initiated cancer progression. Long-read analysis also detected the LCNEC genomes, which occasionally harbored a large number of high copy number regions, including extrachromosomal DNAs (ecDNAs). ecDNA is a recently characterized class of copy number aberrations, in which a particular genomic region is dissected from the chromosome and forms an independent replication unit  38 , 39  . Seven ecDNA candidates were detected in five cases that were assigned to only A- or P-types (Fig.  2f , Supplementary Fig.  S2a , Supplementary Table  S6 ). For example, in jichihgnec28, a 1.5-Mb region, including the  MYCN  gene, was detected as a candidate ecDNA (left, Fig.  2f ). In tkbhgnec2, a 476-kb region, including the  MYB  gene, was detected as a region of heavy amplification (CN = 12.07; right, Fig.  2f ). The transcription factor  MYB  and its amplification/overexpression promoted cell proliferation  40  . Several ecDNA candidates were also detected as homogenously staining regions (HSR) located within chromosomes (Supplementary Fig.  S2b ). To validate these ecDNA, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis was conducted. Furthermore, the  MYC  ecDNA candidate in jichihgnec25 was verified (Fig.  2g ). Compared with the control (jichihgnec23 without  MYC  aberrations), significant  MYC -amplified signals were detected in tumor cells of jichihgnec25 (Fig.  2h ).    DNA methylation patterns in the LCNEC genome  The DNA methylation features were also characterized (Fig.  3a , Supplementary Fig.  S3a ). We found that hypo-methylation occurred in most cases (Fig.  3b ). In particular, five cases exhibited lower methylation patterns. No significant difference was detected in the genome-wide methylation pattern among the four subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S3b ). No significant correlation was also observed between the degree of hypo-methylation and mutation frequency (Fig.  3c ), although genome-wide hypo-methylation has been frequently associated with genomic instability in other cancer subtypes  41 , 42  . The degree of DNA methylation was most diverse in the non-NE type, as the most relevant hypo-methylated and hyper-methylated cases were identified in the Y-type (tkbhgnec1, “Others”) and P-type (jichihgnec28, “Type 2”) groups, respectively (Fig.  3b ). The methylation rates in the CpG islands (CGIs) and promoter regions were low in the tumor and normal samples for all cases. On the contrary, the CGI shores, enhancers, and LINE-1 regions showed more diverse methylation patterns (Fig.  3d , Supplementary Fig.  S3c ), which similar to the trend observed in lung adenocarcuinoma  18  . For example, in the  APC  gene, one of the alternative promoters (promoter 1a) was differentially methylated in four cases (Supplementary Fig.  S3f ). The hyper-methylation of  APC  promoter 1a has been reported previously in various cancers  18 , 43 , 44  . We also reported that a pattern occurs in an allele-specific manner in lung adenocarcinomas  18  . The alternative promoter of the  ERBB2  gene was also methylated in NE cases (Supplementary Fig.  S3f ). Moreover, the methylation status of CGIs, particularly at the CGI shore, was distinct for the P-type (type 2) cases (Fig.  3 f, g). Although the functional relevance of these diverse patterns remains elusive, distinct DNA methylation patterns may represent the lineage background of tumor cells.    Association of genomic and epigenomic patterns with pathological subtypes  Despite intensive analysis of the obtained genomic DNA data, the association between the revealed genomic features of LCNECs and the pathological subtypes remained unclear. The point mutation patterns were not significantly different among subtypes, except for  RB1  mutations. Regarding SVs, a larger number, particularly those associated with repeat elements, were enriched in Y-type cases, whereas ecDNA candidates were detected in A-type or P-type cases; however, those features were not always decisive. Alternatively, most of the differences, which render this cancer type distinct from other lung cancer types, were not clearly evident from these analyses.    Diverse transcriptome features in LCNEC tissues  The transcriptome of the specimens was examined to determine whether they were associated with various pathological subtypes. Using Xenium equipped a full custom 302-gene panel  18  , data for 37 tissue sections representing 34 HGNECs (27 LCNEC and seven SCLC cases; Supplementary Table  S3 ) were successfully generated. A total of 14,110,579 cells were classified into 34 clusters and assigned to 14 cell types (Fig.  4a , Supplementary Fig.  S4a ). Immune and stromal cells were readily separated from tumor cell clusters. A total of 8,190,322 epithelial cells were extracted and assigned to NE and non-NE tumor cells along with normal epithelial cells. The tumor cells showed specific expression profiles among the patients, particularly those belonging to different subtypes (broken line, Fig.  4b ). On the contrary, the microenvironmental stromal and immune cells showed diverse expression patterns, but they were not separated by the patients (left side, Fig.  4b ). For a more precise classification, particularly for epithelial cells consisting of tumor cells, a second round of clustering was conducted, in which 26 sub-clusters were identified (Fig.  4c ). A clearer association was observed compared with genomic DNA analysis between the pathological and molecular subtypes (Supplementary Fig.  S4b ). Most of the A- and N-types were assigned to the NE type (highly  ASCL1 -expressing cells were defined as the NE type because  NEUROD1  probes were not included in the custom Xenium panel; see further discussion in Supplementary Fig.  S5 ), whereas the P-type cells were assigned to non-NE tumors. Y-type tumor cells exhibited diverse patterns depending on the case, with clusters located in the bridging area of other clusters. Notably, for some of the Y-type cases, although YAP1 is related to the non-NE epithelial lineage, tumor cells expressing NE markers, such as  CALCA , were also identified (Supplementary Fig.  S4c ). A series of validation analysis for the v1 panel was conducted using the 5 k panel from a viewpoint of the wider variety of genes (Supplementary Fig.  S6 ).  In general, non-NE tumors were divided into two subtypes based on the expression of  YAP1  and  ASCL2  (the  ASCL2  gene was utilized instead of  POU2F3  because the  POU2F3  gene was not included in the Xenium panel; however, the gene expression patterns mostly overlap with  ASCL2   45 , 46  . The overlapping expression pattern of  POU2F3  and  ASCL2  is shown in Supplementary Figs.  S5 ,  S6 ). When we examined the clustering pattern, some sub-clusters showed a neutral pattern between the NE and non-NE type tumor cells (in purple; Fig.  4c, d ). In addition, the cells expressed NE ( ASCL1 ) and non-NE ( YAP1  or  ASCL2 ) marker genes (designated “DP” type). Five cases contained these DP-type tumor cells as a large proportion of the total cells (Supplementary Fig.  S4d ). For example, for tkbhgnec6, which was classified into Y-type cases,  ASCL1  was also expressed in addition to  YAP1  (Fig.  4e ). A significant amount of  ASCL1/YAP1-  or  ASCL1/ASCL2 -DP cells were detected in the DP cases (Fig.  4f ). To validate the presence of DP cells, snRNA-seq was conducted using strictly dissociated cells for representative cases (Fig.  4g , Supplementary Table  S7 ). Again, the simultaneous expression of NE and non-NE marker genes within a single cell was observed in these cases. Even in some cases in which the tumor cells were categorized as NE, some cells contained these DP features but to a lesser extent.  To characterize DP cases, genes in which mutations were over- and under-represented in DP cases were detected (Supplementary Fig.  S4e ). First, DP cases did not harbor any  RB1  mutations (Fig.  4d ). On the contrary, six genes, including  STK11 , were highly mutated in DP types. In a previous study  13  , cases having  STK11  mutations were classified into Type 1 LCNECs. They reported that Type 1 LCNECs shared mutation profiles with lung adenocarcinomas and squamous cell carcinomas. The fact that DP types overlapped with Type 1 LCNECs and harbored evident non-NE profiles should be in line with the previous study. No obvious driver (gain-of-function) mutation was found in this subtype, which was attributed to the observed ambiguous phenotype of DP cases. The lack of evident drivers in the DP type, together with the  STK11  mutation, may allow the multi-faceted activation of the pathways, which are activated occasionally in adenocarcinomas or squamous cell carcinomas. The DNA methylation patterns of the DP cases were also re-examined, which exhibited low DNA methylation levels in the promoters and enhancers of the  ASCL1  and  YAP1  genes. This pattern may result in the transcriptional activation of both genes in these cells (Supplementary Fig.  S4f ).  In addition, other six sections (five cases) contained pure NE and non-NE tumor regions in the same tissue section (Fig.  4d , Supplementary Fig.  S4g ; designated as “Mixed” type). It is highly unlikely that these two regions originate from independent cancers based on the genomic mutation profiles (Supplementary Fig.  S4h ,  i ). We also validated that these tumors arouse from the single origin by conducting multiregion genome sequencing (Supplementary Fig.  S7 ; the detailed analysis of the data will be published elsewhere). It is rather more likely that these cases also represent the highly dynamic nature of the transcriptome in this cancer subtype. To further clarify this hypothesis, the expression profiles of the NE and non-NE regions of these mixed cases were examined. Based on the Xenium trajectory (Fig.  5a, b ), the NE and non-NE tumors were primarily included within the overall clusters of the respective groups, although they did not reside in the cluster core. These results indicated that the LCNEC cells could be differentiated into the NE and non-NE types through transcriptome changes.
