Drug-Target Mendelian Randomization Shows No Evidence of a Causal Effect of Genetically Predicted CD36 Expression on LUAD Risk  Drug-target MR using CD36 cis-eQTLs (65 instruments, 64 harmonized; F-statistic range, 30–2094;  Figure 7 ,  Supplementary Table S3 ) provided no evidence that genetically predicted CD36 expression affects LUAD risk: IVW odds ratio = 0.98 (95% confidence interval 0.95–1.01;  p  = 0.17), with concordant weighted-median (0.96; 0.92–1.01), MR–Egger (0.96; 0.91–1.00; intercept  p  = 0.22), independent cis-instrument (1.02; 0.94–1.11) and FinnGen (0.95; 0.86–1.05; 571 cases) estimates, no heterogeneity (Cochran’s Q  p  = 0.42), and robust leave-one-out and funnel-plot analyses ( Figure 7 A,D–F). Reverse-direction MR, with LUAD liability as exposure and CD36 expression as a continuous outcome, gave β = 0.009 (95% confidence interval −0.052 to 0.069;  p  = 0.78). Colocalization was analyzed separately: coloc.abf assigned posterior probabilities of 85.3% to an association with CD36 expression only (H1), 14.0% to associations with both traits through distinct variants (H3) and 0.7% to a shared causal variant (H4) ( Figure 7 B;  Supplementary Table S4 ). The dominance of H1 reflects the absence of any LUAD association in the region (minimum LUAD  p  = 0.002 across 3861 SNPs; 7 SNPs with  p  < 0.01 against 39 expected by chance) despite 889 SNPs reaching  p  < 5 × 10 −8  for CD36 expression ( Figure 7 C). Colocalization therefore does not support a shared variant, but it does not establish distinct variants either; H4 remained ≤6.7% for p12 between 1 × 10 −6  and 1 × 10 −4 , and because the CD36 locus contains several independent eQTL signals, the single-causal-variant assumption of coloc.abf is likely to be violated [ 44 ]. The conclusion that there is no evidence for an effect of genetically predicted CD36 expression on LUAD risk therefore rests on the MR estimates and their confidence intervals; colocalization is consistent with it but adds no independent evidence. This is an absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence: the 95% confidence interval (0.95–1.01) remains compatible with effect sizes ranging from a ~5% decrease to a ~1% increase in odds per unit increase in genetically predicted CD36 expression, and the analysis had 80% power (alpha = 0.05) to detect odds ratios of at least 1.043 or at most 0.959 but only 51% and 26% power for odds ratios of 1.03 and 1.02. Lung-specific instruments could not be used because, in GTEx, v8 CD36 had only nine significant lung cis-eQTL variant–gene pairs (versus 230 in whole blood), all rare (minor allele frequency 0.8–1.9%) and absent from the European LD reference panel and from the LUAD summary statistics ( Supplementary Table S10 ). The eQTLGen instruments therefore index genetically determined systemic expression rather than intratumoral regulation of CD36.     4. Discussion  This study identifies a macrophage state in primary LUAD—CD36-enriched LAM—that combines a lipid-handling and lysosomal program with resident-like features and was recovered in two independent single-cell cohorts and in every patient examined by criteria that do not depend on the genes used to select it. Relative CD36 enrichment, by contrast, was its least reproducible feature. In one Xenium section and, under a pre-specified plan, in an independent Visium HD specimen, exhausted CD8 +  T cells were modestly over-represented next to this population, although part of the association reflected transcript depth and regional co-occurrence. Expression-based inference nominated LXR (NR1H3) as a candidate regulator, and ligand–receptor inference nominated Galectin-9 and MIF as candidate but non-specific interactions. Drug-target MR provided no evidence for an effect of genetically predicted CD36 expression on LUAD risk. Its most strongly up-regulated genes in both cohorts were not canonical LAM genes but the resident-like markers SLC40A1, SELENOP and FOLR2, together with the C1Q genes, whereas SPP1 was enriched only in the replication cohort. Pan-cancer and cross-tissue single-cell atlases describe several conserved tumor-associated macrophage states, including lipid-associated (TREM2 + ), SPP1 + , complement-high and resident-like populations [ 47 , 48 ], and tumor-associated macrophages can arise from tissue-resident as well as monocyte-derived precursors [ 49 ]. CD36-enriched LAM thus combines a lipid-handling program with resident-like features rather than corresponding to a single previously described state, and its ontogeny cannot be resolved from transcriptomic data. Resident-like macrophages are not uniformly immunosuppressive: FOLR2 +  tissue-resident macrophages in breast cancer localize near CD8 +  T cells, prime effector CD8 +  T cells ex vivo and are associated with better survival [ 50 ], whereas tissue-resident macrophages in early non-small cell lung cancer provide a pro-tumorigenic niche [ 51 ]. The over-representation of exhausted CD8 +  T cells next to CD36-enriched LAM is therefore compatible with several explanations—macrophage-mediated suppression, co-residence of both cell types in T-cell-rich niches in which chronically stimulated T cells accumulate, or T-cell-derived signals that shape the macrophage state—which the present data cannot distinguish.  Several components of this hypothesis have experimental precedent but in other systems. CD36 can be inhibited pharmacologically by sulfo-N-succinimidyl oleate; in mouse models, CD36 blockade or ferroptosis inhibition restores CD8 +  T-cell effector function and synergizes with anti-PD-1 therapy [ 14 ], CD36 inhibition acts additively with anti-PD-1 through intratumoral regulatory T cells [ 12 ], and myeloid-specific CD36 deletion suppresses tumor growth [ 13 ]. Notably, the T-cell studies concern CD36 expressed by T cells rather than by macrophages. The present data do not address whether these mechanisms operate in human LUAD macrophages. Our results add a description of a reproducible human LUAD macrophage state with relative CD36 enrichment and of its spatial relationship to exhausted CD8 +  T cells; the sequence from CD36-mediated lipid uptake through LXR to Galectin-9- or MIF-mediated T-cell suppression is a hypothesis, each step and link of which remains to be tested ( Table 1 ). In particular, the Galectin-9 and MIF interactions were predicted from dissociated cells, were not specific to CD36-enriched LAM and lacked spatial support for the TIM-3 pair, so they are weaker candidates than CD36 itself. Galectin-9 is also not uniformly immunosuppressive: in triple-negative breast cancer, high Galectin-9 expression was associated with more stromal tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes and better overall survival [ 52 ].  LXR (NR1H3) emerged as a candidate regulator rather than a demonstrated driver. NR1H3 mRNA and an LXR-target program that excludes all population-defining genes were higher in every patient, and inferred NR1H3 activity remained higher after removal of the population-defining genes (11 of 11 and 8 of 9 patients), but its magnitude depended largely on APOE, a population-defining target, and on the regulon resource, and the difference was not consistent in the discovery cohort once the top 100 markers had also been removed. LXR activation downstream of efferocytosis has been described in human macrophages in vitro [ 45 ], and LXR modulators are being studied in atherosclerosis and metabolic disease; whether LXR regulates the CD36-enriched LAM program and whether its modulation alters this program or adjacent T cells require perturbation experiments.  The drug-target MR analysis addresses a different question from the tumor-microenvironment analyses: whether lifelong, genetically determined variation in systemic CD36 expression influences LUAD risk. Its contribution to target prioritization is therefore limited and negative. The null result, with a confidence interval that excludes moderate effects (80% power for odds ratios of at least 1.043 or at most 0.959; 90%, 51% and 26% power for odds ratios of 1.05, 1.03 and 1.02), does not support CD36 as a target for LUAD risk reduction, so any rationale for targeting CD36 must rest on its tumor-microenvironmental context rather than on germline genetic evidence. MR does not address whether CD36-enriched macrophages within established tumors affect immune evasion or treatment response, and it neither shows that systemic genetic variation is irrelevant to CD36 biology in LUAD nor establishes that locally targeted delivery would outperform systemic modulation. Lung-specific eQTL instruments were considered but could not be used: in GTEx v8, CD36 had only nine significant lung cis-eQTL variant–gene pairs (versus 230 in whole blood), all of them rare (minor allele frequency 0.8–1.9%) and absent from the European LD reference panel and from the LUAD summary statistics ( Supplementary Table S10 ). The whole-blood-derived eQTLGen instruments therefore index genetically determined systemic expression rather than intratumoral or macrophage-specific regulation of CD36.  This study has several limitations. First, all findings derive from transcriptomic and genetic data without protein-level or functional validation. The identity of CD36-enriched LAM, CD36 protein expression and lipid uptake, LXR activity and the Galectin-9/MIF interactions require confirmation by multiplex immunofluorescence or immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, lipid-uptake and co-culture assays, and perturbation in immunocompetent models (for example, myeloid-specific CD36 deletion or pharmacological CD36, LXR, Galectin-9 or MIF inhibition). Because CD36 is also expressed by monocytes (this study), regulatory T cells and CD8 +  T cells [ 3 , 12 , 41 ], protein-level validation should establish its cellular source and focus on the macrophage compartment. Second, different findings were examined in different datasets ( Supplementary Table S11 ): population identity and core transcriptional features in two single-cell cohorts; functional enrichment and CellChat inference in the discovery cohort only; and the spatial association in one Xenium section and one Visium HD specimen, each from a single patient. The Visium HD analysis used bins rather than segmented cells, and its secondary, distance-based endpoints were only partly consistent with the Xenium findings. Within-specimen resampling quantifies stability inside each section but cannot establish reproducibility across patients or capture inter-tumoral heterogeneity, and the exhaustion and LAM labels were based on transcript detection, which depends on sequencing depth. Multi-patient spatial cohorts with protein-level phenotyping are needed. Third, CD36 enrichment was weaker and inconsistent in the replication cohort, which spans pre-invasive and invasive lesions and combines two chemistries; the cause could not be determined with nine patients. Fourth, the replication criteria were defined post hoc, after the replication cohort had first been analyzed, rather than pre-specified. Fifth, the MR analysis provides no evidence for an effect of genetically predicted CD36 expression on LUAD risk; power was adequate only for moderate effects, and whole-blood cis-eQTL instruments reflect systemic rather than intratumoral regulation. Sixth, the exploratory association between the barrier signature and anti-PD-1 response was not consistent across two small cohorts ( n  = 27 and 16), the larger of which did not reach significance; it is reported only in the  Supplementary Materials  as hypothesis-generating and provides no evidence for patient selection or for guiding combination immunotherapy. Finally, cell-level comparisons use cells as the statistical unit, so very small  p  values partly reflect cell number; the major comparisons were therefore repeated at patient level ( Supplementary Tables S5–S8 ), but with 11 and 9 patients, these analyses have limited power, and the patient-level correlation between the CD36-enriched LAM fraction and CD8 +  T-cell exhaustion was not significant.    5. Conclusions  CD36-enriched LAM is a macrophage state in LUAD whose identity and core lipid-handling and lysosomal program were reproduced in two independent single-cell cohorts, whereas its CD36 enrichment was less consistent. In one Xenium section and an independent Visium HD specimen, it showed a modest spatial association with exhausted CD8 +  T cells, part of which reflected transcript depth and regional co-occurrence. CD36, LXR (NR1H3), Galectin-9 and MIF are candidate, experimentally testable components of a hypothesis linking lipid-handling macrophages to T-cell exhaustion; their functions in these cells and the connections between them were not tested here and require protein-level and functional studies. evidence_text:
Protocol for integrated multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium and MACSima. Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment. Graphical abstract                     Highlights    •  Multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on a single tissue section    •  Detailed Xenium and MACSima workflow protocol for single-section spatial multi-omics    •  Registration and integration of transcriptomic and proteomic data at single-cell level      Publisher’s note: Undertaking any experimental protocol requires adherence to local institutional guidelines for laboratory safety and ethics.    Combining same-section spatial transcriptomics with high-plex protein imaging enables comprehensive characterization of the tissue microenvironment while preserving spatial information. Here, we present a protocol for multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling using Xenium transcriptomics and MACSima cyclic protein imaging. We describe steps for tissue preparation, hybridization, and RNA imaging, followed by slide recovery, antigen retrieval, and MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS). We provide Python scripts for data registration and integration to generate a single-cell multimodal map of the tissue microenvironment.     status  released    display-pdf  yes    is-olf  no    is-manuscript  no    is-preprint  no    is-journal-matter  no    is-scanned  no    is-retracted  no       Collection date 2026 Dec 18.       Before you begin   Protocol overview  This protocol describes multimodal spatial RNA and protein profiling on the same tissue section using Xenium (10x Genomics) and MACSima Imaging Cyclic Staining (MICS, Miltenyi Biotec). The workflow was established using human tonsil and tumor tissue sections; however, it can be adapted to other tissue types with appropriate optimization of RNA probe panels, antibody panels, and tissue processing conditions.    Innovation  This protocol introduces a novel workflow for multimodal spatial profiling by integrating Xenium spatial transcriptomics with highly multiplexed protein imaging using MICS on the same formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue microarray (TMA) section. Alternative multimodal workflows have demonstrated the combination of Xenium with other hyperplex protein imaging platforms, including PhenoCycler and COMET.  1   ,   2   Building upon these advances, this protocol provides the first detailed experimental and computational workflow for integrating Xenium with the current-generation MACSima platform, which supports significantly higher antibody plexity than comparable technologies. This workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima analysis includes optimized requirements and procedures for sample processing, antigen retrieval, and iterative cyclic immunofluorescence that preserve tissue integrity and enable single-cell RNA and protein measurements on the same section. In addition to the experimental workflow, this protocol provides scripts for accurate registration of Xenium and MACSima imaging data, enabling direct correlation of transcriptomic and proteomic features within the same spatial framework. Importantly, both the laboratory workflow and computational approach can be adapted to other spatial multi-omics combinations, offering a flexible framework for integrating transcriptomic and proteomic data. Together, these advances address key technical challenges in spatial multi-omics and provide a reproducible and scalable approach for multimodal tissue analysis.    Institutional permissions  Experiments involving human-derived tissues require approval from the appropriate institutional ethics committee. Researchers must ensure that ethical approval is obtained and that informed consent is secured from all donors prior to sample collection. All specimens used in this study (see  key resources table ) were obtained with informed consent and handled in accordance with institutional regulations and approved protocols.    Tissue selection and preparation 
   1.  Obtain FFPE TMA samples with preserved morphology and RNA integrity.   
          CRITICAL:  Following proper handling, storage, preparation and sectioning of the FFPE tissues according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ) is critical to ensure preservation of morphology and RNA integrity.  
   2.  Optimize sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time for the block and floating time of the sections in the water bath of the Section Transfer System (STS) before mounting on slides to prevent cutting artefacts.    3.  Assess tissue quality, morphology and RNA integrity of the blocks prior to mounting on Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.    4.  Place sections on Xenium slides and store them according to standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).   a.  If the tissue blocks are of optimal quality, section them at 4–6 μm thickness using a microtome and mount the sections on Xenium slides.    b.  Dry the slides appropriately as per standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).      
          Pause point:  Slides can be stored at room temperature (RT, 20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in tubes with desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and Xenium workflow.  
   Xenium assay version compatibility 
    Note:   The workflow for sequential Xenium and MACSima is compatible with the v1 as well as the 5K Prime Xenium assay versions. It is also compatible with the Xenium In situ Multimodal Cell Segmentation which has now become standard in the Xenium workflows. Since the MACSima workflow uses directly conjugated antibodies, the antibodies in the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit do not pose a risk of cross-detection (10x Genomics,  CG000750 ).  
   Xenium probe panel design 
   5.  Select a pre-designed Xenium probe panel and/or design a custom Xenium probe panel (to be used as a standalone panel or as an add-on to the pre-designed panel) targeting genes of interest relevant to the biological question.    6.  Validate the custom probe panel performance in control samples, if available.   
    Note:   Perform add-on panel design in line with the guidelines provided in the  Technical Note: Xenium Add-on Panel Design  (10x Genomics,  CG000643 ). Transcript abundance and cell type specificity should be taken into consideration when designing a panel.  
    Note:   Reference to existing single-cell RNA-seq data, ideally from matched sample types, can guide panel design by enabling identification of cell type specific genes and transcript abundance.  
    Note:   The custom probe panel performance can be cross-validated post-Xenium run by comparing with existing single-cell RNA-seq and / or Xenium datasets for sensitivity in terms of number of transcripts detected and for specificity in terms of biologically relevant co-expression patterns of different genes.  3    
   Antibody panel design for MACSima 
   7.  Select antibodies targeting proteins of interest for multiplex imaging and check for compatibility of antibodies with the respective sample type (FFPE).    8.  Optimize antibody concentrations and staining conditions in a mock Xenium-MACSima experiment using control samples, if available, to test the compatibility of sequential Xenium and MACSima staining (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).   
          CRITICAL:  Antibodies must be tested for compatibility within the Xenium-MACSima workflow (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).  
          CRITICAL:  Ensure that tissue processing conditions, such as working in an RNase-free environment, sectioning thickness, and optimal slide recovery and antigen retrieval conditions post-Xenium are compatible with both Xenium RNA detection and downstream protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Check for tissue integrity after post-Xenium imaging slide recovery (steps 12 and 13 in the  step-by-step method details ) before continuing with the protein staining.  
          CRITICAL:  Optimize post-Xenium antigen retrieval conditions to achieve sufficient epitope accessibility for protein staining while preserving tissue integrity. Harsh antigen retrieval conditions can compromise tissue integrity and spatial registration between modalities.  
   Instrument and software preparation 
   9.  Prepare the Xenium Analyzer instrument and required reagents according to manufacturer guidelines (10x Genomics,  CG000584 ).    10.  Prepare the MACSima imaging system for cyclic staining and imaging. Install the MACS iQ View software on a data-analysis workstation.    11.  Install the scripts for the registration workflow, including required software dependencies ( Table 1 ).   a.  Clone the repository.  >git clone https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium.git    b.  Create the venv environment.  >python3 -m venv macsima_xenium    c.  Activate the venv environment.  >source macsima_xenium/bin/activate    d.  Install the Python package for the Xenium-MACSima analysis workflow from its repository in GitHub.  >pip install ./MACSimaXenium/    Note:   Ensure sufficient data storage and computational resources for handling large imaging datasets (see requirements listed in  materials and equipment ).        
   Table 1   Packages and resources required for data processing      Package or Resource  Version  IDENTIFIER  Reference      Python  ≥3.11   https://www.python.org/  RRID: SCR_008394  Programming language  Python Software Foundation    xenium_macsima_core_registration  1.0.0   https://github.com/scOpenLab/MACSimaXenium/   This protocol    harpy-analysis  ≥0.4.2   https://github.com/saeyslab/harpy   Rombaut et al.  4      Bioio  ≥3.3.0   https://github.com/bioio-devs/bioio   Brown et al.  5      bioio-ome-tiff  ≥1.4.0   https://github.com/bioio-devs/bioio-ome-tiff   Brown et al.  5      opencv-python-headless  ≥4.13.0.92   https://github.com/opencv/opencv-python   Alekhin et al.  6          Upstream data preparation (prerequisites)  The registration workflow in this protocol assumes that single-cell data and Xenium-MACSima region of interest (ROI) correspondences have been established beforehand. The following upstream processing steps are performed once per slide before the per-core registration loop and are summarized here for context. The code for these steps is experiment-specific and is not included in the shared repository; however, the analysis workflow follows standard practices using scanpy  7   and the Segment Anything Model (SAM).  8      12.  Build AnnData  9   feature matrix.   a.  Load each Xenium output folder by reading the transcript table (transcripts.parquet).    b.  Filter for quality value (QV) ≥ 20, remove control probes, and aggregate transcript counts per nucleus using nucleus boundary polygons (nucleus_boundaries.parquet).    c.  Store the resulting count matrix, centroid coordinates, and nucleus areas as an AnnData object.       13.  Segment TMA cores.   a.  Identify individual TMA cores using the Segment Anything Model (SAM1, ViT-H) applied to a 2D cell density histogram (binned centroids at approximately 50 μm per pixel). Each detected mask corresponds to one TMA core.    b.  Assign a position label to each cell according to which mask their centroid falls within and flag cells outside all masks with is_in_core = False.       14.  Perform quality filtering.   a.  Remove cells that are not assigned to a core and filter the remaining cells according to transcript counts and/or size.          Note:   A commonly used approach for cell-level quality filtering is to exclude cells with fewer than ten transcripts and genes expressed in less than five cells ( https://squidpy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/notebooks/tutorials/tutorial_xenium.html ).  10   However, transcript counts per cell are dependent both on the tissue and gene panel  11   and thus the use of more or less stringent thresholds taking into account also the area of the cell might be required.  12   Finally, a visual inspection of the spatial distribution of the excluded cells can help to identify biases in the filtering by highlighting the presence of spatially organized clusters of excluded cells.  11       15.  Match the TMA cores between Xenium and MACSima data.   a.  Match the Xenium TMA core positions and MACSima ROI numbers manually by comparing a spatial scatter plot of Xenium cell positions (colored by core position) with the MACSima ROI overview image.    b.  Write this mapping as a CSV file with one column named “xenium” and the other named “macsima”.         Planning of multimodal data integration  This protocol describes the cross-modal alignment of Xenium spatial transcriptomics data (10x Genomics) with MACSima multiplexed cyclic immunofluorescence imaging data (Miltenyi Biotec) for TMA samples. Integration is performed per TMA core and produces multi-modal SpatialData  13   objects saved as Zarr  14   archives.           CRITICAL:  Accurate image registration is essential for reliable analysis of RNA and protein data at single-cell resolution.     Data requirements 
   16.  Provide Xenium and MACSima data sets, along with mappings that link Xenium cells to TMA cores and Xenium TMA cores to MACSima ROIs ( Table 2 ).   
          CRITICAL:  Maintain consistent orientation and handling of tissue sections and ROIs throughout the workflow.  
   Table 2   Input files for the Xenium and MACSima registration workflow      Files  Explanation      Xenium folder  Xenium output folder produced by the Xenium Onboard Analysis pipeline.  15      Annotated H5AD  AnnData Object  9   containing Xenium TMA core membership (position column) and MACSima slide_name identifier (e.g., TMAN02-1-1) for each Xenium cell.    MACSima folder  Path to the preprocessed MACSima folder generated after stitching and background subtraction with the MACS iQ View software.  16      Xenium-MACSima ROI matching CSV file  The Xenium TMA core positions and MACSima ROI numbers are mapped in a CSV file with one column named “xenium” and the other named “macsima”.     Step-by-step method details 
    Note:   The protocol was optimized for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow with Cell Segmentation Staining, using a Prime 5K Human pan Tissue and Pathways panel (10x Genomics, PN-1000724) and a custom 100-gene add-on panel. For alternative Xenium workflow formats, workflow parameters may require adaptation. Xenium processing should always be performed according to the corresponding manufacturer-recommended protocols. In addition, performance of downstream antibody staining following Xenium processing may vary depending on the selected Xenium assay configuration.  
  Preparation of FFPE TMA sections 
          Timing: 3 days when performing steps consecutively. Approximately 1.5 days are required for sectioning optimization, slide mounting, drying, and quality assessment. Another day is required for sectioning, mounting to Xenium slides, and drying. Half a day is required for deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of sections.   
 This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA samples for the Xenium Prime 5K workflow, including sectioning of the FFPE blocks, tissue mounting, deparaffinization, and decrosslinking of sections. Sample preparation is performed according to the demonstrated protocol  Xenium In Situ for FFPE – Tissue Preparation Handbook  (10× Genomics,  CG000578 ).           CRITICAL:  Sectioning conditions, such as rehydration time of the FFPE TMA block in ice-cold water, should be optimized depending on tissue type, degree of dehydration, and the age of the paraffin block. Similarly, the floating time of sections in the water bath prior to mounting on Xenium slides needs to be adjusted to prevent wrinkling, folding, or tearing of the sections.     1.  Assess tissue quality and RNA integrity.    Note:   Evaluate tissue quality and RNA integrity of the FFPE TMA samples prior to placement of sections onto Xenium slides by performing DAPI staining, H&E staining, and/or DV200 analysis.     a.  Mount serial sections on SuperFrost Plus slides and deparaffinize according to the standard protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 ).    b.  Perform DAPI and H&E staining as outlined in the demonstrated protocol (10x Genomics,  CG000578 , Appendix).    c.  Image the slide to assess nuclear integrity, tissue morphology, sectioning artefacts, and the presence of necrotic or degraded regions.    d.  For RNA quality assessment, collect approximately four 10 μm sections (for samples ≤ 6.5 × 6.5 mm) for RNA extraction and DV200 analysis.          CRITICAL:  Samples with DV200 values below 30 % are considered suboptimal and may result in reduced median transcript counts per cell in downstream Xenium analysis.         2.  Section the FFPE TMA block and dry the sections.          CRITICAL:  During sectioning, maintain RNase-free conditions by wiping the microtome with RNase Zap ™ solution and filling the water bath of the STS with nuclease-free water.     a.  Prepare the FFPE TMA block for sectioning by rehydrating it in ice-cold Milli-Q water for a previously optimized duration (typically 10–30 min, depending on tissue type and degree of dehydration).    b.  Trim the block until the area of interest is fully exposed. For previously sectioned TMA blocks, discard the first 5–10 sections to obtain uniformly hydrated and intact tissue sections prior to collection.    c.  Section FFPE TMA block at a thickness of 5 μm using a microtome. Let the sections slide via the STS into its water bath filled with nuclease-free water and maintained at 42°C–45°C.    d.  Incubate the sections in the water bath for a previously optimized duration (typically 10 s to 3 min for most FFPE tissues) to allow the section to fully flatten and to minimize wrinkles, folds, or tearing prior to mounting.          CRITICAL:  Excessive incubation times in the water bath may lead to tissue distortion or reduced adherence during downstream processing.      e.  From the water bath, mount the sections carefully onto the Xenium slides (10× Genomics, PN-1000465), within the designated sample area.          CRITICAL:  Avoid placing the sections covering the fiducials, specifically the top and bottom fiducials.            CRITICAL:  Monitor the section adhesion on Xenium slides throughout the workflow to ensure that sections remain intact and properly attached during all processing steps.      f.  Following section placement, incubate the slides at 42°C for 3 h to promote adhesion of the sections to the Xenium slide surface.    g.  After incubation, place the slides in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing desiccant and store them overnight (16–24 h) at RT (20°C–25°C) to allow complete drying of the tissue sections.          Pause point:  Following section mounting, Xenium slides can be stored at RT (20°C–25°C) or at 4°C in the presence of desiccant sachets for up to 4 weeks prior to deparaffinization and further processing with the Xenium workflow.         3.  Perform deparaffinization, rehydration, and decrosslinking of the sections.   a.  Incubate the slides at 60°C for 2 h, followed by cooling at RT (20°C–25°C) for 7 min prior to further processing.    b.  Sequentially incubate the slides in two Coplin jars containing xylene for 10 min each.    c.  Perform two washes in 100 % ethanol for 3 min each.    d.  Perform two washes in 96 % ethanol for 3 min each.    e.  Perform one wash in 70 % ethanol for 3 min.    f.  Perform a final rinse in nuclease-free water for 20 s.    Note:   Xylene and ethanol incubation steps should be performed in a fume hood.      g.  Assemble the slides into Xenium cassettes.    h.  Perform decrosslinking using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation Reagents  (10x Genomics, PN-1000720) (included in the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  kit, 10x Genomics, PN-1000742).    i.  Immediately proceed with the Xenium in situ gene expression workflow.         Probe hybridization for Xenium Prime  in situ  gene expression 
          Timing: 2–3 days; with the Xenium  in situ  multimodal cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 3 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, and cell segmentation staining. Day 3 includes post-staining washes, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining. Without cell segmentation staining, the workflow spans 2 days: day 1 includes priming and probe hybridization. Day 2 comprises post-hybridization washes, ligation, amplification, autofluorescence quenching, and nuclear staining.   
 This section describes the preparation of deparaffinized and decrosslinked FFPE TMA sections for the Xenium workflow, enabling subsequent imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer. The entire workflow is performed according to the  Xenium Prime In Situ Gene Expression with optional Cell Segmentation  user guide (10x Genomics,  CG000760 ) using the  Xenium Prime Sample Preparation with Cell Segmentation with Slides  reagents (10× Genomics, PN-1000742).    4.  Perform priming and probe hybridization.   a.  Hybridize priming oligos to decrosslinked RNA.    b.  Perform RNase treatment and a polishing reaction to release the RNA strand from the hybridized oligos, thereby enabling subsequent hybridization of Xenium probes to the target RNA (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).    c.  Perform hybridization overnight (16–24 h) at 50°C in a thermocycler (Bio-Rad, C1000) using the Xenium Prime 5K probes ( Xenium Prime 5K Human Pan Tissue and Pathways Assay  kit, 10× Genomics, PN-1000671) together with an optional custom human add-on panel comprising up to 100 additional genes.       5.  Perform post-hybridization washes, ligation, and amplification.   a.  Perform post-hybridization washes to remove unbound probes, followed by ligation of hybridized probes, and enzymatic rolling circle amplification to generate amplified signal products for downstream imaging.       6.  Perform optional multimodal cell segmentation staining.   a.  To facilitate morphology-based cell segmentation, perform overnight (16–24 h) staining using the Xenium cell segmentation staining reagents, which label nuclei, cell boundaries, and intracellular RNA-rich regions according to the manufacturer’s instructions (10× Genomics,  CG000760 ).       7.  Perform autofluorescence quenching and nuclear staining.   a.  After amplification (and optional cell segmentation staining), perform autofluorescence quenching, brief drying at 37°C for 5 min and subsequent nuclear staining according to the manufacturer’s instructions.    b.  Upon completion of the workflow, store the slides in 0.05 % PBST until imaging and analysis using the Xenium Analyzer.                Pause point:  After completion of the Xenium sample preparation workflow and prior to loading onto the Xenium Analyzer, slides can be stored in 0.05 % PBST at 4°C in the dark for up to 1 week using a new Xenium cassette lid.      Note:   During the drying step following autofluorescence quenching, inspect the slides to ensure that the Xenium slide fiducials, particularly the top and bottom fiducials, remain free of tissue coverage. If fiducials are obstructed, carefully remove the tissue from these regions at the end of sample preparation, as covered fiducials may interfere with subsequent imaging and alignment on the Xenium Analyzer.      Note:   At the end of sample preparation, clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 70 % ethanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.     Xenium  in situ  gene expression imaging 
          Timing: 2.5–5 days; half a day is needed for hands-on preparation, including buffer preparation and setup of the Xenium Analyzer. An additional 2–5 days are required for instrument run time, depending on the Xenium assay version (e.g., Xenium v.1, Xenium Prime 5K), whether cell segmentation staining is performed, and the size and number of ROIs.   
 This section describes the setup and operation of the Xenium Analyzer for imaging and preliminary analysis of FFPE TMA sections prepared using the Xenium workflow.           CRITICAL:  In cases where a custom panel (add-on or standalone) is used, obtain the corresponding JSON file for the panel and upload it to the Xenium Analyzer prior to initiating the run.            CRITICAL:  Slides processed using different Xenium workflows cannot be run simultaneously in the same instrument run. However, slides processed with different probe panels within the same workflow can be run together during a single instrument run.      Note:   For the Xenium Prime workflow, ensure that the Xenium Analyzer software version is XA v3.0 or higher.     8.  Prepare buffers and set up the Xenium Analyzer.   a.  Prepare all required buffers and decoding reagents and set up the Xenium Analyzer for processing of slides generated using the Xenium workflow according to the  Xenium Analyzer User Guide  (10× Genomics,  CG000584 ). Use the  Xenium Prime 5K Decoding Reagents  (10× Genomics, PN-1000740),  Xenium Decoding Consumables v2  (10× Genomics, PN-1000726), and  Xenium Reagent Bottles  (10× Genomics, PN-1000730).          Note:   Transfer the  Xenium Prime Decoding Reagent Module B  (sealed in the mylar bag) from −20°C to 4°C at least one day before the run and allow it to thaw at 4°C for 16–72 h.      Note:   Prepare the Xenium Probe Removal buffer in a fume hood due to the hazardous nature of DMSO.     9.  Define ROIs.   a.  Following the overview scan, define one or more ROIs consisting of fields of view (FOVs) that encompass the tissue of interest while excluding blank areas, and initiate the run.          Note:   Up to eight ROIs can be defined per slide.      Note:   For TMAs, define a single ROI encompassing all FOVs containing TMA cores and excluding blank FOVs.     10.  Clean the instrument and store slides.   a.  After completion of the run, clean the instrument according to the standard protocol (10× Genomics,  CG000584 ).    b.  Replace the buffer on the slides with 1 mL 0.05 % PBST and store the slides at 4°C until further processing.       11.  Store and prepare post-Xenium slides for transport.   a.  Fill two 50 mL Falcon tubes with 0.05 % PBST up to the brim.    b.  Remove the Xenium slides from the Xenium cassettes and place each of them in a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with 0.05 % PBST. Ensure that the slides are completely submerged.    c.  Seal the lid of the Falcon tube with parafilm.    d.  Transport them at 4°C on cool packs.          Note:   For long term storage, transfer the slides into a 50 mL Falcon tube and replace the 0.05 % PBST weekly to prevent contamination or sample drying.      Note:   Alternatively, slides may be stored or transported in 50 mL Falcon tubes containing MACSima Running Buffer. In this case, exchange the buffer every four weeks.            Pause point:  Slides can be stored in MACSima Running Buffer at 4°C. In our experience, slides stored for up to nine months still yielded MACSima data meeting established QC criteria; longer storage periods have not been systematically evaluated.      Note:   Slides can be stored long term at this stage while awaiting Xenium analysis results and potential adjustment or optimization of the downstream antibody panel.     Post-Xenium sample preparation for MACSima imaging cyclic staining 
          Timing: 4–5 h; quencher removal requires approximately 30 min. Preparation of the TEC buffer and antigen retrieval require approximately 2–3 h, while DAPI pre-staining and removal of dust particles prior to imaging require an additional 30 min.   
 This step describes the preparation of FFPE TMA sections for MICS after the Xenium run and includes quencher removal, antigen retrieval, DAPI pre-staining, and dust particle removal. Following Xenium imaging, perform quencher removal as recommended in  Xenium In Situ Gene Expression – Post-Xenium Analyzer H&E Staining  (10x Genomics,  CG000613 ) to reduce residual Xenium-associated background signals and improve compatibility with downstream cyclic immunofluorescence imaging using MACSima.    12.  Remove the quencher (see  problem 1  in  troubleshooting ).   a.  In a fume hood, prepare quencher removal solution by weighing 17.4 mg sodium hydrosulfite and transfer it to a conical tube containing 10 mL Milli-Q water.    b.  Cap the tube tightly and vortex for 10 s until the reagent is fully dissolved.    c.  Keep the solution at RT (20°C–25°C) until use.          CRITICAL:  Prepare quencher removal solution immediately before each use to ensure optimal performance, as its effectiveness decreases after 10 min.      Note:   Because sodium hydrosulfite is hazardous, prepare the solution in a fume hood.      Note:   Vortexing may be performed outside the fume hood if the tube is tightly capped.      Note:   Do not use alternative chemicals for quencher removal.      d.  Add 10 mL quencher removal solution into the slide mailer.    e.  Prepare three slide mailers with 10 mL Milli-Q water each.    f.  Gently immerse Xenium slide into the slide mailer with quencher removal solution and incubate for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).    g.  Immerse slide in each Milli-Q water containing slide mailer for 1 min, then move to the next one.    h.  Transfer the Xenium slide into a 50 mL Falcon tube filled with MACSima Running buffer until further use.    Note:   Alternatively, transfer Xenium slide into a MACSwell One Small imaging frame ( Figure 1 A, right) and add 1.5 mL quencher removal solution. After 10 min incubation at RT (20°C–25°C), wash slide with 1.5 mL Milli-Q water three times, waiting for 1 min each time.      Note:   Residual purple staining after Xenium processing indicates the presence of autofluorescence quencher and should disappear following successful quencher removal ( Figure 1 B).         13.  Perform heat-induced epitope retrieval (HIER).   a.  Prepare the 10× stock solution of TEC antigen retrieval buffer at pH 9.0.    Note:   The 10x stock solution can be stored at 4°C for up to 3 months.      b.  Immediately before use, dilute the 10x stock to 1x working solution.    c.  Adjust the pH to 9.0.    d.  Preheat the 1× working solution to 95°C in a pressure cooker.    e.  Place the Xenium slide in a slide mailer and immerse it in the preheated TEC buffer. Incubate for 20 min at 95°C.          CRITICAL:  Ensure the slide is fully submerged and does not touch the pressure cooker container.            CRITICAL:  Avoid using open-bottom slide mailers, as air bubbles could directly contact the tissue section and cause partial lifting or detachment from the slide surface.      Note:   Depending on the antibody panel, alternative antigen retrieval buffers may be required (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ).      f.  After incubation, remove the pressure cooker container and transfer it to a pre-cooled water bath (ice-cold) for cooling.    g.  When the buffer has reached RT (20°C–25°C), carefully remove the slide from the buffer.    h.  Dry the edges with a lint-free wipe to remove excess liquid.    i.  Mount the slide onto a MACSwell One Small imaging frame.    Note:   The MACSwell One Small imaging frame accommodates the Xenium imaging area optimally and enables complete coverage of the imaged region ( Figure 1 A).      j.  Add 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer.       14.  Pre-stain the sample with DAPI and remove dust particles.   a.  Incubate the Xenium slide with DAPI staining solution at a 1:5 dilution using MACSima Running Buffer (final concentration 1 μg/mL) in the dark for 10 min at RT (20°C–25°C).          CRITICAL:  Protect the slide from light during DAPI incubation to prevent photobleaching.      Note:   Ensure the staining solution fully covers the section.      b.  Wash the slides three times with 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer to remove excess dye.    c.  Check the TMA section under bright transmitted light to ensure there are no dust particles or debris in the experimental area.    d.  Remove any visible dust or debris, as these can interfere with imaging quality.    e.  Cover the slide with a final experimental volume of 550 μL MACSima Running Buffer and seal with pierceable aluminum foil.    Note:   Clean the underside of the Xenium slides using 2-propanol and lint-free wipes to remove residues and prevent fibers or debris from interfering with subsequent imaging.            Pause point:  Store slides in running buffer at 4°C for ≤1 week.           Figure 1   Preparation of Xenium slides for subsequent MACSima imaging  (A) Xenium slide assembled in a Xenium cassette during Xenium sample preparation and imaging (left) and mounted in a MACSwell One imaging frame for subsequent MACSima imaging cyclic staining (MICS) (right).  (B) Representative tissue microarray (TMA) sections following Xenium processing, displaying a slight purple discoloration caused by the Xenium autofluorescence quencher before quencher removal (left), and the same sections after successful quencher removal, appearing colorless (right).                     MICS 
          Timing: 20–240 h; imaging duration depends on the size of the antibody panel and the number and size of selected ROIs.   
 This section describes staining of FFPE TMA sections using fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies and automated cyclic imaging using the MACSima platform.  2   ,   12   The workflow enables high-dimensional spatial characterization of protein expression following Xenium imaging and includes experimental setup, reagent and procedure configuration, reagent preparation, ROI selection, autofocus definition on each ROI and automated cyclic image acquisition. Basic information of the control software is based on the  MACS® iQ View Software Control Module 1.0 User manual  (Miltenyi Biotec).    15.  Register the sample and configure the sample setup.   a.  Open the Sample Setup tab and create a new sample entry.    b.  Enter all required metadata for each sample, including sample type, species, and fixation method. Additional experimental information is recommended where available.    c.  Assign samples to the appropriate imaging wells according to the selected MACSwell imaging frame configuration.          Optional:   Create duplicate sample entries or sample groups for organizational purposes.      Note:   Sample groups are intended for organization only and do not affect imaging or analysis settings.      Optional:   For multiple tissue sections located within the same well (e.g., TMAs), samples can be defined as a complex sample.     16.  Configure the sample and reagent rack.   a.  Generate a new rack configuration within the Sample Setup tab.    b.  Select the appropriate rack type corresponding to the MACSwell imaging frame and reagent plate format used in the experiment.    c.  Assign the sample to the correct well position within the rack layout by dragging it to the correct well.          Note:   Not every well requires a sample assignment.     17.  Register antibodies and define the reagent panel.   a.  Under the Reagent Definition tab, register pre-validated Miltenyi Biotec antibodies using the integrated reagent registration system or manually enter reagent information.    Note:   Pre-validation data for the antibodies is provided to confirm compatibility with acetone-, PFA-fixed, or FFPE tissues; however, they have not been tested for compatibility after Xenium.      b.  Add non-Miltenyi antibodies by specifying antibody type, species reactivity, antigen target, fixation compatibility, and fluorochrome assignment.    c.  Create reagent panels by combining antibodies from the reagent inventory into predefined staining panels.    d.  Review fluorochrome assignments and reagent compatibility prior to experiment setup.          CRITICAL:  Use fluorochromes compatible with cyclic imaging workflows (e.g., FITC, PE, APC) and directly conjugated primary antibodies to avoid issues when using the Xenium multimodal cell segmentation kit.            CRITICAL:  Include DAPI staining in regular intervals (e.g., every 3–4 imaging cycles) to facilitate reliable image registration and alignment across staining cycles for the MACSima images.      Note:   Evaluate antibody compatibility, for example by performing a mock Xenium experiment followed by a MACSima run (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ). A representative example of antibody panel validation and resulting multiplex protein staining on human tonsil tissue is shown in  Figure 2 , illustrating the expected staining quality and marker performance achievable with this workflow.      Note:   Antibody compatibility should be assessed based on specificity, signal-to-background ratio, reproducibility, and preservation of the expected staining pattern after Xenium processing. Compatible antibodies show the expected cellular and subcellular localization, clear separation of positive signals from background, and staining consistent with previous MACSima or immunohistochemistry validation and reference databases (see  problem 2  in  troubleshooting ). Representative examples of antibodies that fulfilled ( Figures 3 C–3E, 3G, and 3H) or failed to meet ( Figures 3 B and 3F) these criteria are shown in  Figure 3 .      Note:   Selected examples of antibody performance for the panel used in this study, following the Xenium Prime 5K workflow with an additional custom panel of 100 transcripts, are shown in  Figure 4 . Antibody compatibility and staining quality may vary depending on tissue type, Xenium assay design, and experimental conditions and should therefore be validated for each application.      Alternatives:   While pre-validated multiplex panels help streamline optimization, their compatibility with the Xenium-MACSima workflow must be confirmed experimentally.         18.  Set up the cyclic imaging procedure.   a.  Open the Procedure Creation tab and create a new procedure from an existing template or generate a new procedure.    b.  Add reagent panels and/or individual antibodies to the procedure.    c.  Adjust staining and imaging parameters as needed, including dilution factor, incubation time, exposure settings, bleaching conditions, and wash parameters.    d.  Recalculate imaging cycles after all reagents and parameters have been defined or assign the antibodies to the individual cycles manually.    Note:   When manually assigning antibodies to imaging cycles, consider the following guidelines:     i.  Avoid placing multiple markers targeting the same cell type in the same cycle.    ii.  Preferably place low-abundance, transiently expressed, activation-dependent markers, cytokines, and chemokines in earlier cycles, as their detection can be more challenging.    iii.  Place abundant, constitutively expressed, or structural proteins in later cycles, as they provide more robust signals.    iv.  Evaluate receptors and ligands individually based on antigen abundance, subcellular localization, and expected staining performance.    v.  Avoid FITC for broadly expressed or critical phenotyping markers because of its relatively low photostability and potential signal loss during image acquisition.    vi.  For alternative fluorochromes (e.g., Alexa Fluor dyes), empirically determine the bleaching intensity required for efficient signal removal or perform at least two bleaching cycles before staining with the subsequent conjugated antibody in that channel.    vii.  Avoid combining strongly expressed FITC signals with weak PE signals in the same cycle to minimize spectral overlap and signal interference.          CRITICAL:  Validate any modifications to exposure times, bleaching settings, or wash parameters empirically prior to large-scale experiments.            19.  Create and configure the experiment.   a.  In the Experiment Planning tab, create a new experiment.    Note:   When duplicating an experiment, ROIs from earlier runs can be reloaded and reused.      b.  Enter experiment metadata and assign the corresponding sample racks.    c.  Assign cyclic staining procedures to all occupied wells containing sections.    Optional:   Define the expected number and size of ROIs to obtain runtime and dataset size estimates.      d.  Export the pipetting scheme for antibody preparation and documentation purposes from the Reagent rack Info tab.       20.  Prepare the antibody plate.   a.  Dispense antibodies into a compatible deepwell reagent plate, distributing them into the designated wells according to the generated pipetting scheme.    Note:   Briefly centrifuge antibody tubes prior to pipetting and aspirate antibodies carefully from the top of the solution to avoid transferring antibody aggregates or clumps.      b.  Cover the prepared reagent plate with adhesive, pierceable aluminum foil to protect fluorochrome-conjugated antibodies from light exposure.       21.  Load the instrument and initiate the experiment.   a.  In the Experiment Planning tab, initiate the experiment by clicking the Run button or by right-clicking the experiment and selecting Run Experiment.    b.  Scan or manually register the reagent racks.    c.  Load sample racks onto the imaging stage according to the software instructions. Insert the MACSwell with the frosted labeling area of the slide facing the front of the device.    d.  Load the reagent rack into the instrument.    Optional:   During reagent loading, include the MACSima Stain Support Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-127-574) when using REAlease® antibodies or predefined commercial antibody panels according to the manufacturer’s recommendations.      e.  Verify waste bottle status and ensure sufficient storage solution, running buffer, and system buffer volumes prior to starting the experiment.    f.  Start the experiment and allow the system to perform the preview scan.          CRITICAL:  Monitor buffer levels and waste bottle capacity daily during long imaging runs to avoid interruptions.         22.  Define ROIs and autofocus settings (see  problem 3  in  troubleshooting ).   a.  Define ROIs and autofocus settings following completion of the preview scan.    b.  Inspect the preview image and adjust brightness, contrast, and gamma settings as needed.    c.  Define ROIs using polygon, rectangle, or circular selection tools.    d.  Ensure ROIs encompass all regions to be analyzed while excluding empty imaging areas.          CRITICAL:  Avoid selecting large empty imaging areas within the ROIs, as image stitching and alignment rely on sufficient DAPI signal across the imaged region.      Note:   Large ROIs may be more prone to autofocus instability. Inspection of autofocus profiles and acquired images is recommended before proceeding with downstream analysis ( Figure 5 ).      e.  Configure autofocus settings for each ROI and refine parameters where necessary.   i.  Set the autofocus parameters, including Method, Exposure Time, Offset Range, and Z-Offset, to ensure optimal focus adjustment for each ROI.       f.  Accept autofocus settings and continue the experiment.    Note:   For TMAs, define a single ROI for each core and exclude blank regions.      Note:   Imaging duration depends on the antibody panel size and the number and size of selected ROIs. Long imaging experiments may require several days to complete.            CRITICAL:  Accurate ROI definition and autofocus settings are essential for optimal image quality across all imaging cycles.         23.  Complete the experiment and retrieve data.   a.  After completion of the imaging run, unload the instrument and retrieve the imaging data.    b.  Remove sample and reagent racks according to the software-guided unloading procedure.          CRITICAL:  Create a backup of raw and processed imaging data prior to deleting experiments from the instrument workstation.      c.  Continue downstream image analysis using MACS iQ View on external computational systems.       24.  Preprocess the data.   a.  Perform data preprocessing using the MACS iQ View’s Preprocessing Pipeline, selecting the appropriate processing settings.  16   ,   18     i.  Load the “RawData” folder into the “Preprocessing” tool in MACS iQ View by selecting “Open Raw Directory”.  This section describes the computational workflow for registering MICS multiplexed protein imaging data onto the Xenium spatial transcriptomics images, assembling the aligned data into a multi-modal SpatialData  13   object and quantifying per-cell protein signal. The workflow is implemented in the XeniumMacsimaRegistration class (MACSimaXenium/src/xenium_macsima_core_registration/xenium_macsima_core_registration.py) and demonstrated in the example notebook (example/align_one_core.ipynb). A batch processing script for full TMA slides is provided (MACSimaXenium/src/xenium_macsima_core_registration/match_rois_cores_fullslide.py) with the full workflow depicted in  Figure 6  and described below.    25. Define the mapping between Xenium TMA positions and MACSima ROI indices according to the mappings in the input CSV file ( Table 2 ).    d.  Visualize the mapping and save diagnostic plots.      Note:   The cell-type annotations and obs_name_orig identifiers are generated during upstream processing (see  before you begin ). The obs_name_orig field links each cell to its original Xenium cell boundary polygon.     26.  Load Xenium core mappings.   a.  Load the H5AD file, filter to the target slide and position, and retain only cells flagged as is_in_core.       27.  Load Xenium Spatial Data.   a.  Load cell/nucleus boundaries, cell labels, transcripts, expression matrix, and the morphology focus images from the Xenium output folder.       28.  Perform the per-core Registration Loop ( Figures 6 C and 6D).   a.  For each position-ROI pair, execute Steps 29–37 below. Pairs where the output Zarr folder already exists are automatically skipped.       29.  Align Observation Tables.   a.  Join annotated metadata with the Xenium cell table by cell_id/obs_name_orig. Filter to the highlighted position and set obsm['spatial'] from centroid coordinates (cell_centroid_x, cell_centroid_y).       30.  Load the MACSima images.   a.  Load the DAPI channel for the first cycle as well as all other non-DAPI and non-background channels.       31.  Compute Core Bounding Box.   a.  Derive the ROI bounding box in pixel coordinates from the spatial extent of the aligned cell table.       32.  Transform Cell/Nucleus Boundary Polygons and crop the Xenium dataset.   a.  Scale each polygon by the transform_factor (micrometers to pixels).    b.  Translate it by subtracting the bounding box origin multiplied by scale_factor, placing the boundaries in the same coordinate space as the full-resolution images.       33.  Perform a Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT)-Based Image Registration.  19     a.  Perform downscaling by scale_factor, using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform().  20      b.  Apply Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization (CLAHE)  21   with skimage.exposure.equalize_adapthist()  22   with default parameters: clip_limit = 0.01, kernel_size = 1/8 of image dimensions.    c.  Convert pixel values to uint8.    Note:   The downscaling by scale_factor = 3 reduces runtime and suppresses high-frequency photon noise during feature detection. If registration fails or produces poor results, try scale_factor = 2 for higher-resolution feature detection or adjust CLAHE parameters.  21        d.  Detect SIFT key points and match descriptors with Fast Library for Approximate Nearest Neighbors (FLANN)  23   (Parameters: KD-tree, 5 trees, 50 checks).    e.  Apply Lowe’s ratio test  19   with threshold 0.5 to retain high-confidence matches.    f.  Compute a 2D affine transformation from the surviving inlier matches using spatialdata.transformations.get_transformation_between_landmarks().    g.  Scale the translation components by scale_factor to obtain the full-resolution affine transformation matrix.    h.  Apply the full-resolution affine transformation to the entire MACSima image using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform().       34.  Assemble a multi-modal SpatialData Object containing the following data:   a.  macsima: aligned MACSima images.    b.  morphology_focus: Xenium morphology focus images (all channels).    c.  cell_boundaries: Xenium cell segmentation polygons.    d.  nucleus_boundaries: Xenium nucleus segmentation polygons.    e.  transcripts: cell expression table and spatially filtered transcripts.    f.  cell_labels: Xenium cell segmentation labels.       35.  Write the assembled object to: <output_folder>/Pos_<position>_ROI_<roi>.zarr.       Note:   All loaded MACSima channels are read and transformed using dask_image.ndinterp.affine_transform() and stored as an Image2DModel layer in the SpatialData object. Aggregate protein signal per cell. For each MACSima image layer, call harpy.tb.allocate_intensity() using the cell labels image as the spatial mask.          Note:   The mean pixel intensities within each cell mask are appended to the gene expression table and saved as rna_protein_table.     37.  Visualize the registration quality.   a.  Generate a 2×2 summary figure and save it as POS_<position>_registration_summary.png. CRITICAL:  Visually inspect the overlay to check the registration quality. Cell boundaries should fall on top of nuclear structures and the red and green channels of the RGB overlay should be highly overlapping for good quality registration. A poorly registered core will show systematic lateral or rotational offsets between the channels. In addition to visual inspection,  26   registration quality could also be evaluated quantitatively with several image-based metrics. For instance, the normalized mutual information  27   between the Xenium DAPI channel and the registered and the unregistered MACSima DAPI channel images can be calculated and compared. When processing a large number of slides, these metrics could facilitate the identification of potentially misaligned cores for further evaluation by virtual inspection or manual adjustment.
